glossary.definition: The negatively charged particle found in every atom, carrying −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. In copper about one electron per atom is free to move through the whole lattice, and these free electrons carry the current.

drills.prompt: What is the charge of one electron?

choices.feedback: That is the proton's charge. The electron's is the same size but negative.
A coulomb is the charge of about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons; one electron carries only −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
9.109 × 10⁻³¹ is the electron's mass in kilograms, not its charge.

drills.prompt: A copper wire carries 1 A. What moves along the wire to carry the current?

choices.text: Free electrons drifting through the lattice

choices.feedback: The copper ions are fixed in the lattice; they vibrate in place but don't travel. Moving ions carry current in an electrolyte, not in a metal.

choices.text: Protons, in the direction of conventional current
choices.feedback: Protons stay in the nuclei and never move along a wire. Conventional current is a sign convention, not a description of what moves.

drills.prompt: Which statement about the free electrons in a wire is true?

choices.text: They drift opposite to the conventional current arrow.
They drift in the direction of the conventional current arrow.
choices.feedback: Conventional current is the direction positive charge would move. Electrons are negative, so they drift the other way.

choices.text: The battery supplies them, and the load uses them up.
choices.feedback: The electrons were already in the wire, about one per atom in copper. The battery pushes them around the loop and gets back as many as it sends out; the load converts their energy, not the electrons.

drills.prompt: About how many electrons pass a point each second in a current of 1 A?

choices.feedback: That is the charge of one electron, in coulombs. The count is 1 C/s divided by it: 1 / (1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 6.24 × 10¹⁸ per second.
That is Avogadro's number, the atoms in a mole. A coulomb is about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons.
An ampere is one coulomb per second, and a coulomb is the charge of about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons.

glossary.unit: charge −e = −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; mass 9.109 × 10⁻³¹ kg
physics: Every atom is a small positive nucleus surrounded by electrons, and every electron carries the same charge, −e = −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. A neutral atom has as many electrons as its nucleus has protons, so its charges cancel. Charge in a circuit is always a whole number of electrons moved, but the numbers are so large that it behaves as a smooth quantity: 1 C is 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons, and a current of 1 mA carries 6.24 × 10¹⁵ electrons past a point every second.

In a metal, the outermost electron of each atom is not bound to any one atom. Copper has 29 electrons per atom, but only about one of them is free, which still gives about 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons in every cubic meter. They move in random directions at around 10⁶ m/s, scattering off the vibrating atoms about every 2 × 10⁻¹⁴ s, so with no field their average velocity is zero. A voltage across the metal sets up a field that adds a slow net drift, a fraction of a millimeter per second, and that drift is the current.

Electrons are negative, so in a wire they drift the opposite way to conventional current: out of the − terminal, around the circuit, and into the + terminal. Schematics, formulas, and simulators use conventional current, the direction positive charge would move, and give the same results. Electrons are not the only carriers: ions carry the current in an electrolyte, and in p-type silicon the current is described as holes, gaps in the bonds that move like positive charges.

One electron crossing 1 V gains or loses 1 electron-volt, 1 eV = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. That is the natural unit for the energy of a single carrier, such as the band gap of a semiconductor or the energy of a photon from an LED.

typical.what: drift speed, 1 A in 1 mm² copper

confusions.title: Electrons do not race from the battery to the lamp.
confusions.text: The wire is already full of free electrons, and the field that sets them all drifting spreads along it at a large fraction of the speed of light. Each electron drifts slowly: at 1 A in 1 mm² copper, about 0.073 mm/s, so crossing 1 m of wire takes about 13 600 s, nearly four hours.

confusions.title: Electron flow and conventional current give the same answers.
confusions.text: A current of 2 mA flowing clockwise in conventional terms is electrons drifting counterclockwise at the same rate, 1.25 × 10¹⁶ electrons per second. Only the sign convention differs; every voltage, current, and power comes out the same.

confusions.title: A battery does not supply the electrons.
confusions.text: The electrons are already in the wires and parts. A 2000 mAh cell moves 7200 C, about 4.5 × 10²² electrons, around the loop over its life, and the circuit holds as many electrons at the end as at the start. The cell supplies energy, not electrons.

confusions.title: Not every current is a flow of electrons.
confusions.text: In the electrolyte inside a cell, ions carry the current; in p-type silicon, holes do. Inside a lithium-ion cell, each ampere is about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ lithium ions per second crossing the electrolyte, while electrons carry the same current through the wires outside.

glossary.uses: Converting charge to particle counts (1 C = 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons), drift-speed estimates, photodiode and shot-noise calculations that count carriers, and the electron-volt for band gaps and photon energies.

glossary.definition: An atom or molecule with more or fewer electrons than protons, so it carries a net charge. In an electrolyte, including the one inside a cell, ions rather than free electrons carry the current.

drills.prompt: Inside a cell, what carries the current through the electrolyte between the two electrodes?

choices.feedback: An electrolyte has almost no free electrons; the current crosses it as moving ions. Electrons carry it only in the electrodes and the outside wires.
Holes are a semiconductor's carriers. In an electrolyte the carriers are ions.

drills.prompt: What makes an atom an ion?

choices.text: It has gained or lost electrons, so its charges no longer balance.
It has gained or lost protons.
choices.feedback: Changing the number of protons changes the element itself, a nuclear process. Chemistry moves electrons.

choices.text: It is moving through a liquid.
choices.feedback: Motion doesn't change charge: a neutral molecule moving through water is not an ion.

choices.text: It has more neutrons than protons.
choices.feedback: Neutrons carry no charge, so they make a different isotope, not an ion.

drills.prompt: A neutral sodium atom loses one electron. What is the charge of the ion?

choices.feedback: Losing a negative electron leaves one more proton than electrons, so the ion is positive.
The atom was neutral; taking away −1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C leaves +1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.
One elementary charge is 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C; a coulomb is about 6.24 × 10¹⁸ of them.

drills.prompt: Salt water conducts well and distilled water barely does. Why?

choices.text: The dissolved salt splits into ions that are free to move.
The salt adds free electrons to the water.
choices.feedback: Dissolved salt adds Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, not free electrons; the ions carry the current.

choices.text: The salt lowers the water's breakdown voltage.
choices.feedback: Conducting at a few volts needs mobile charge carriers, not breakdown. The salt supplies them as ions.

glossary.unit: charge: a whole number of elementary charges, ±z·e, with e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C
physics: An atom with an electron missing carries a net charge of +e: H⁺, Li⁺, and Na⁺ are examples. One with an extra electron, such as Cl⁻, carries −e. Groups of atoms can be ions too: OH⁻ carries −e and SO₄²⁻ carries −2e. An ion is thousands of times heavier than an electron, because it is a whole atom or molecule.

In a liquid, paste, or gel electrolyte, ions are free to move. A field drives positive ions one way and negative ions the other, and both make conventional current in the same direction: a positive charge moving right and a negative charge moving left both carry charge to the right. Because ions are heavy and collide with the solvent molecules around them, an electrolyte conducts far worse than a metal: seawater has a resistivity of about 0.2 Ω·m, more than ten million times copper's 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m.

Inside a cell, ions carry the current through the electrolyte and electrons carry it through the external circuit. At each electrode a chemical reaction hands the charge from one kind of carrier to the other. While a lithium-ion cell discharges, lithium ions cross the electrolyte toward the positive electrode while the same charge, as electrons, flows through the load outside; the charge per second is the same in both paths, as Kirchhoff's current law requires. Each ampere-hour moves 3600 C, about 2.2 × 10²² ions, which is about 0.26 g of lithium.

An ion locked in a solid carries no current. Dry table salt is made of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions, yet it insulates until it is melted or dissolved. In a PN junction, the depletion region is made of fixed dopant ions, positive on the n side and negative on the p side: they cannot move, so they carry no current, but their charge sets up the junction's built-in field.

confusions.title: Ions are atoms, not loose charges.
confusions.text: A current of ions moves matter. Each ampere-hour through a lithium-ion cell carries about 0.26 g of lithium from one electrode to the other, which is why a cell's chemistry changes as it discharges and why its capacity is limited.

confusions.title: Ions moving in opposite directions do not cancel.
confusions.text: If positive ions carry 0.6 A to the right and negative ions carry 0.4 A of conventional current to the right by moving left, the total is 1.0 A to the right. Opposite charges moving opposite ways add.

confusions.title: Fixed ions carry no current.
confusions.text: The ions in dry salt and the dopant ions in a depletion region are held in a crystal. Their charge makes fields, but with nothing free to move, the current through them is zero.

glossary.uses: Batteries and their internal resistance, electrolytic capacitors, electroplating and corrosion, the fixed dopant ions that set a PN junction's barrier, and conductivity sensors that measure the ions dissolved in water.

glossary.definition: A liquid, paste, gel, or solid that conducts by the movement of ions, not free electrons. It carries the current between the electrodes inside a cell, and in an aluminum electrolytic capacitor it makes contact with the oxide dielectric.

drills.prompt: Which of these conducts by moving ions rather than free electrons?

choices.text: The paste inside an alkaline cell

choices.feedback: Copper conducts by free electrons, about one per atom.
Silicon conducts by electrons and holes; its atoms stay fixed in the crystal.
Graphite conducts by electrons moving within its carbon layers.

drills.prompt: Which is true of an aluminum electrolytic capacitor?

choices.text: It is polarized: reversed voltage damages its oxide layer.

choices.feedback: The electrolyte conducts; it serves as the negative plate, in contact with the oxide. The dielectric is the thin aluminum oxide on the positive foil.

choices.text: It can be connected either way around.
choices.feedback: Its oxide dielectric is formed for one polarity. Reversed, the oxide breaks down, leakage current rises, and the capacitor can overheat or vent.

drills.prompt: Why does a cell's internal resistance rise when it gets cold?

choices.text: Ions move more slowly through the colder electrolyte.
The free electrons in its leads slow down.
choices.feedback: Metal leads conduct slightly better when cold. The rise comes from the electrolyte, where the ions move more slowly.
The EMF is set by the chemistry and changes little with temperature. The internal resistance is a separate thing, set largely by the electrolyte.

glossary.unit: none of its own; its resistivity, in Ω·m, sets much of a cell's internal resistance
physics: An electrolyte is a salt, acid, or base dissolved in water or another solvent (or held in a paste, gel, or polymer), with its ions free to move. It conducts ions but not electrons. That is what makes a cell work: the only path for electrons from one electrode to the other is the external circuit, so the chemistry can deliver its energy only by driving current through the load. If electrons could cross the electrolyte, the cell would discharge inside itself.

Ions are heavy and collide constantly with the solvent around them, so an electrolyte conducts far worse than a metal. Seawater has a resistivity of about 0.2 Ω·m, more than ten million times copper's. The current through a cell has to cross its electrolyte, and the electrolyte's resistance, with the electrodes and contacts, is the cell's internal resistance. A cold electrolyte is more viscous and its ions move more slowly, so a cell's internal resistance rises in the cold and its terminal voltage sags further under the same load.

In an aluminum electrolytic capacitor, the dielectric is a thin film of aluminum oxide grown on the etched anode foil. The electrolyte soaks the paper between the foils and reaches into every pore of the roughened oxide surface, so it acts as the second plate; a second foil only makes contact with it. Its resistance is a large part of the capacitor's equivalent series resistance, and it slowly dries out with heat and age, so that resistance rises over the capacitor's life.

confusions.title: Pure water is not what conducts.
confusions.text: Deionized water has a resistivity up to 1.8 × 10⁵ Ω·m; seawater, about 0.2 Ω·m, nearly a million times lower. The dissolved ions carry the current, not the water.

confusions.title: Electrons do not cross the electrolyte.
confusions.text: Inside the cell, ions carry the current; outside, electrons do. At each electrode a reaction converts one to the other, so 1 A through the load means 1 A of ion current through the electrolyte.

confusions.title: In an electrolytic capacitor, the electrolyte is not the dielectric.
confusions.text: The dielectric is the oxide film on the anode foil, nanometers thick; the electrolyte is a conductor that serves as the other plate. Reversing the voltage attacks the oxide, which is why polarity matters.

confusions.title: A cell's internal resistance is not fixed.
confusions.text: If the cold raises a cell's r from 0.15 Ω to 0.5 Ω, a 1.6 V cell delivering 1 A drops from 1.45 V at its terminals to 1.1 V, which may be below what the device needs.

glossary.uses: Batteries of every chemistry, aluminum electrolytic and supercapacitors, why batteries and electrolytic capacitors lose performance when cold or old, electroplating, and corrosion wherever wet ions meet two metals.

glossary.definition: The property of particles that makes them exert electric forces on each other, measured in coulombs (C). It is conserved: a circuit moves charge around a loop and never uses it up, and charging a capacitor moves charge from one plate to the other through the circuit, leaving the capacitor's total charge zero.

drills.prompt: Which unit measures electric charge?

choices.feedback: The ampere measures current, the rate of flow of charge: 1 A = 1 C/s.
The volt measures energy per unit charge: 1 V = 1 J/C.
The farad measures capacitance, charge per volt: 1 F = 1 C/V.

drills.prompt: A current of 2 A flows for 3 s. How much charge passes a point?

choices.feedback: Charge is current times time, Q = I·t = 2 A × 3 s = 6 C, not t/I.
That is I/t. Charge is current times time: Q = I·t = 6 C.
Joules measure energy. Charge is in coulombs: Q = I·t = 6 C.

drills.prompt: A cell is "dead." What has it run out of?

choices.text: The chemical energy that does work on the charge

choices.feedback: Charge is conserved: a cell moves charge around the loop and gets it all back. A dead cell has used up its reactants, the stored chemical energy.
Current is a rate of flow, not something stored. What a cell stores is chemical energy.

drills.prompt: A capacitor is charged to 5 V. What is the total charge on it, both plates together?

choices.text: Zero: +Q on one plate and −Q on the other
Q = CV, all on the positive plate
choices.feedback: Charging moves Q from one plate to the other through the circuit, so one plate holds +Q and the other −Q. "The charge on a capacitor" means Q on each plate, not a net charge.
The source pumps no net charge into the capacitor; it moves charge from one plate to the other, leaving +Q and −Q, a total of zero.

glossary.unit: coulomb (C) = A·s; 1 mAh = 3.6 C
physics: Charge comes in two signs. Like charges repel and opposite charges attract, with a force that falls as the square of the distance: two charges of 1 C held 1 m apart would exert a force of 9 × 10⁹ N on each other. Ordinary matter is neutral because its protons and electrons balance exactly, and charge comes in whole multiples of e = 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

Charge is conserved: it is never created or destroyed, only moved. A circuit moves charge around a loop, so the charge entering any part each second equals the charge leaving it. With a steady current, the charge moved is Q = I·t: 1 mA for 1 s is 1 mC, and 1 A for an hour is 3600 C.

The forces between charges are so strong that a circuit never separates much charge. Charging a 10 µF capacitor to 5 V moves 50 µC from one plate to the other: one plate holds +50 µC, the other −50 µC, and the capacitor as a whole stays neutral. What it stores is energy, ½CV² = 125 µJ, in the field between the plates.

A small object has a capacitance of only picofarads, so a little charge makes a large voltage, V = Q/C. A person is about 100 pF to the surroundings (the human-body model used in static-discharge testing), so 0.5 µC on the body is 5 kV, enough to damage a MOSFET's gate.

typical.what: 10 µF at 5 V, on each plate
a person charged to 5 kV (100 pF)

confusions.title: A charged capacitor holds no net charge.
confusions.text: A 10 µF capacitor at 5 V has +50 µC on one plate and −50 µC on the other: zero in total. "Charging" it means separating charge and storing energy, 125 µJ here.

confusions.title: A battery's mAh is charge it moves, not charge it holds.
confusions.text: A 2000 mAh cell can drive 7200 C around a circuit before it is flat, for example 200 mA for 10 h. That charge comes from the wires and parts and returns to them; the cell's chemistry supplies the energy, 3.7 V × 7200 C ≈ 27 kJ for a lithium-ion cell.

confusions.title: Charge is not used up in a load.
confusions.text: A lamp drawing 0.5 A for an hour takes in 1800 C at one terminal and gives out 1800 C at the other. It converts the energy the charge carries, V joules per coulomb, into heat and light.

confusions.title: A coulomb is a lot of separated charge.
confusions.text: Circuits move many coulombs per second, but almost none is ever left separated. Two isolated charges of 1 C at 1 m would push apart with 9 × 10⁹ N; static charges are measured in nanocoulombs and microcoulombs.

glossary.uses: Battery capacity in mAh (1 mAh = 3.6 C), the charge on a capacitor, Q = CV, the charge a gate driver must deliver to switch a MOSFET, and static-discharge protection.

glossary.definition: The rate at which charge passes a point, I = Q/t, in amperes (1 A = 1 C/s). Schematics draw conventional current, the direction positive charge would move, opposite to the electrons' drift in a metal.

drills.prompt: 1 A is the same as:

choices.feedback: A joule per second is a watt, a rate of energy. Current is a rate of charge: 1 A = 1 C/s.
A joule per coulomb is a volt. 1 A = 1 C/s.
Volts per second measures how fast a voltage changes, as in a slew rate. 1 A = 1 C/s.

drills.prompt: A lamp is in series with a battery. Compare the current into the lamp with the current out of it.

choices.text: Less comes out, because the lamp uses some of it.
choices.feedback: Charge doesn't pile up in the lamp, so as much current leaves as enters. What the lamp uses is energy: the charge leaves it at a lower potential.

choices.text: It depends on which way the electrons drift.
choices.feedback: Whichever way the carriers move, the current is the same at both terminals of a two-terminal part; only the sign convention depends on direction.

drills.prompt: Which measurement needs the meter in series, breaking the circuit to insert it?

choices.feedback: A voltmeter goes across two points, in parallel; a voltage belongs to two points.
An ohmmeter goes across a part with the circuit unpowered; it doesn't go in series with a live loop.

drills.prompt: Which relation defines current?

choices.feedback: Q·t grows with time; current is charge per unit time, I = Q/t.
That is Ohm's law, a property of a resistance. Current itself is the rate of charge flow, I = Q/t, in any part.
From P = V·I, I = P/V, not P·V; and the definition is I = Q/t.

glossary.unit: ampere (A) = C/s
physics: Current is the rate at which charge passes a point: I = Q/t, or I = dQ/dt when it changes. One ampere is one coulomb per second, 6.24 × 10¹⁸ electrons per second. In a wire it is the slow drift of a vast number of free electrons, I = nAe·v_d.

Charge cannot pile up anywhere in a steady circuit: a growing excess at any point would raise that point's voltage and push the charge on. So whatever charge enters a part each second leaves it, and in a single loop the current is the same at every point, before and after every part. A lamp or resistor converts the energy the charge carries; it does not use up the charge.

The circuit, not the source alone, sets the current. A 9 V battery drives 9 mA through 1 kΩ and 90 mA through 100 Ω (a little less, for its internal resistance). To measure a current, the circuit is broken and an ammeter is put in series, so the current passes through it; an ammeter has a very low resistance so that it barely changes what it measures.

Schematics draw conventional current, from the + terminal through the circuit to the − terminal, the way positive charge would move. In a metal the electrons drift the other way; the current, and every formula, is the same.

glossary.definition: The energy each coulomb gains or gives up between two points, V = W/Q, in volts (1 V = 1 J/C). A voltage always belongs to two points; a node voltage is measured from ground.

drills.prompt: 1 V is the same as:

choices.feedback: A coulomb per second is an ampere. A volt is energy per charge: 1 V = 1 J/C.
A joule per second is a watt. 1 V = 1 J/C.

drills.prompt: A meter shows "the voltage at node B" as 3.3 V. What does that mean?

choices.text: Node B is 3.3 V above ground.

choices.feedback: Voltage doesn't flow; current does. A voltage is between two points, here node B and ground.

choices.text: Node B holds 3.3 V of charge.
choices.feedback: Charge is measured in coulombs. A node voltage is the potential difference from ground to node B.

drills.prompt: 2 C of charge gains 18 J passing through a source. What is the voltage across the source?

choices.feedback: V = W/Q = 18 J / 2 C = 9 V, not W·Q.
That is Q/W. Voltage is energy per charge: V = W/Q = 9 V.
18 J is the energy for all 2 C; each coulomb gains 9 J, so V = 9 V.

drills.prompt: Two points are joined by a wire of negligible resistance carrying 2 A. What is the voltage between them?

choices.feedback: V = I·R with R ≈ 0 gives about 0 V, whatever the current.

choices.text: It can't be known without the source voltage
choices.feedback: The source voltage drops across the other parts; across a near-zero resistance V = I·R ≈ 0.

glossary.unit: volt (V) = J/C = W/A
physics: Moving a charge against an electric field takes work, which is stored as electric potential energy; moving with the field releases it. The voltage between two points is that energy per unit charge, V = W/Q. One volt is one joule per coulomb, so a coulomb crossing a 12 V lamp delivers 12 J, and 0.5 A through it delivers 12 V × 0.5 A = 6 W.

A voltage always belongs to two points. A voltmeter has two leads, one on each side of what it measures. When a schematic says a node is at 5 V, it means 5 V above ground, the node chosen as 0 V. Only differences matter: shifting every potential by the same amount changes no force and no energy, so moving ground changes every node voltage but no voltage across a part.

A source raises the energy of each coulomb by its EMF; the parts around the loop take it back. The voltage across each part is its share, and the shares around any closed loop add up to the source's voltage: Kirchhoff's voltage law.
Current flows through a part; voltage is across it. A 9 V battery on a shelf has 9 V across it and no current. A closed switch carrying 2 A has almost no voltage across it.

confusions.title: There is no voltage at one point.
confusions.text: "The output is at 4 V" means 4 V between the output and ground. Move ground to a node at 1 V, and the output reads 3 V; the voltage across every part stays the same.

confusions.title: Voltage does not flow.
confusions.text: Current flows through a part; voltage is across it. A 9 V battery with nothing connected has 9 V across it and 0 A through it.

confusions.title: Zero volts across does not mean zero current.
confusions.text: A closed switch carrying 2 A has only a few millivolts across it. An open switch in a 12 V loop is the opposite: 12 V across it and no current.

confusions.title: A higher voltage does not always mean more power.
confusions.text: Power is V·I. A 5 V USB port delivering 2 A supplies 10 W; a 12 V adapter delivering 0.5 A supplies only 6 W.

glossary.uses: Reading node voltages on a schematic, probing with a voltmeter or scope, supply rails, logic levels, and every energy calculation: the energy delivered is W = Q·V.

glossary.definition: Electromotive force: the work a source does on each coulomb passing through it, from its chemistry or from a changing magnetic field, in volts. A source's terminal voltage equals its EMF only when no current flows.

drills.prompt: In what unit is EMF measured?

choices.feedback: Despite its name, EMF is not a force: it is work per unit charge, joules per coulomb, which is volts.
EMF is energy per charge, in volts; the current it drives depends on the rest of the circuit.
EMF is energy per coulomb (volts), not energy per second (watts).

drills.prompt: A cell has an EMF of 1.5 V and an internal resistance of 0.5 Ω, and delivers 0.4 A. What is its terminal voltage?

choices.feedback: That is the EMF, what it reads with no current. With 0.4 A flowing, 0.4 A × 0.5 Ω = 0.2 V drops inside, leaving 1.3 V.
While the cell delivers current, the internal drop subtracts: V = ℰ − I·r = 1.3 V. It adds only while the cell is being charged.
0.2 V is the drop inside the cell; the terminals show what's left: 1.5 − 0.2 = 1.3 V.

drills.prompt: When does a voltmeter across a cell read its EMF?

choices.text: When no current flows from the cell

choices.feedback: Shorted, the terminal voltage is near zero: the whole EMF drops across the internal resistance.

choices.text: When it delivers its rated current
choices.feedback: Delivering current, it loses I·r inside, so the terminals read less than the EMF.

drills.prompt: Which of these produces an EMF?

choices.text: A coil whose magnetic flux is changing

choices.feedback: A resistor has a voltage across it, but it takes energy from the charge (V = I·R); it doesn't do work on it. An EMF does work on the charge.

choices.text: A wire at rest in a steady magnetic field
choices.feedback: A steady field through a stationary loop induces nothing; an EMF needs the flux through the loop to change.

glossary.unit: volt (V) = J/C: the work the source does on each coulomb passing through it
physics: Outside a source, the electric field drives charge from + to −. Inside, something else must drive it the other way, from − to +, against that field. In a cell it is the chemical reactions at the two electrodes; in a generator, the magnetic force on the charges in a moving conductor; in a solar cell, light freeing carriers that the junction's field separates. The work this does on each coulomb is the electromotive force, ℰ, in volts.

A real source is an ideal EMF in series with an internal resistance r. With a current I, the drop I·r inside it is lost as heat, so the terminal voltage is V = ℰ − I·r. Only with no current does a voltmeter on the terminals read the EMF itself, which is why an unloaded reading says nothing about r.

The chemistry sets a cell's EMF, not its size. An AA and a D alkaline cell both start near 1.5–1.6 V; the D cell holds more reactants, so it lasts longer, and its larger electrodes give it a lower internal resistance. A cell's EMF falls slowly as it discharges: a lithium-ion cell goes from 4.2 V full to about 3.0 V empty.

A generator's EMF follows Faraday's law: a coil of N turns whose flux changes at dΦ/dt has ℰ = N·dΦ/dt across it, so it grows with speed. The same EMF in a running motor is its back-EMF, which opposes the supply.

typical.value: about 0.6–0.7 V open circuit; about 0.5 V at full power

confusions.title: The terminal voltage is not the EMF under load.
confusions.text: A cell with ℰ = 1.6 V and r = 0.15 Ω reads 1.6 V with nothing connected and 1.6 − 0.5 × 0.15 = 1.525 V while it delivers 0.5 A.

confusions.title: EMF is not a force.
confusions.text: Despite the name, it is work per charge, in J/C = V. A 9 V battery does 9 J of work on every coulomb it moves through itself.

confusions.title: A bigger cell does not have a bigger EMF.
confusions.text: AA and D alkaline cells have the same 1.5 V chemistry. Four AA cells in series give 6 V; four in parallel still give 1.5 V, for longer and with a quarter of the internal resistance.

confusions.title: A source does not set the current.
confusions.text: A 9 V EMF drives 9 mA through 1 kΩ and about 90 mA through 100 Ω (less the internal drop). The EMF fixes the work per coulomb; the circuit decides how many coulombs per second.

glossary.definition: The resistance inside a source, from its electrolyte, electrodes, and contacts (or a generator's or transformer's windings). A current I drops I·r inside the source, so the terminal voltage is ℰ − I·r.

drills.prompt: A battery reads 9.0 V with no load and 8.0 V while delivering 0.5 A. What is its internal resistance?

choices.feedback: 9 V / 0.5 A is the resistance of the whole loop. Only the 1 V drop happens inside: r = 1 V / 0.5 A = 2 Ω.
8 V / 0.5 A = 16 Ω is the load. The internal drop is 9.0 − 8.0 = 1 V, so r = 1 V / 0.5 A = 2 Ω.
r = ΔV/I = 1 V / 0.5 A = 2 Ω, not I/ΔV.

drills.prompt: A shorted car battery can deliver hundreds of amperes; a shorted AA cell only a few. What is the main reason?

choices.text: The car battery's internal resistance is far lower.
The car battery's EMF is higher.
choices.feedback: 12 V against 1.5 V is a factor of 8, but the short-circuit currents differ by far more. I = ℰ/r is set mostly by r: milliohms for a car battery, a fraction of an ohm for an AA cell.

choices.text: The car battery stores more energy.
choices.feedback: Capacity sets how long it lasts, not how much current it can push at once; the short-circuit current is ℰ/r.

drills.prompt: A cell's voltage sags when a load is connected and recovers when it's removed. What explains this?

choices.text: The load current drops I·r across the internal resistance.
The EMF falls while current flows.
choices.feedback: The EMF is set by the chemistry and stays nearly the same; the drop is I·r inside the cell, and it goes away when the current stops.

choices.text: The wires to the load lose charge.
choices.feedback: Wires don't lose charge. The terminal voltage falls by I·r, the drop across the internal resistance.

glossary.unit: ohm (Ω): the fall in terminal voltage per ampere drawn
physics: The current through a cell has to cross its electrolyte, where ions drift and collide, and its electrodes and contacts. Those have resistance, so a real cell behaves as an ideal EMF ℰ in series with a resistance r. A generator's or transformer's windings give it an internal resistance in the same way.

With a current I, the drop I·r inside the source is lost as heat, and the terminals show V = ℰ − I·r: a straight line falling with current, of slope −r. With nothing connected, I = 0 and a meter reads ℰ, whatever r is. To find r, read the open-circuit voltage, then the voltage with a known load, and divide the difference by the load current: 1.600 V open and 1.524 V across 3 Ω give I = 1.524/3 = 0.508 A and r = 0.076/0.508 = 0.15 Ω.

A short across the terminals leaves r as the only resistance in the loop: I = ℰ/r, with all the power, ℰ²/r, heating the source. For a lithium-ion cell with 3.7 V and 30 mΩ, that is about 120 A and 460 W. The load gets the most power when R_L = r, but then the source dissipates as much as the load, an efficiency of 50%; batteries are used with R_L many times r.

r is not fixed. As a cell discharges, and when it is cold, its reactions slow and its electrolyte conducts less well, so r rises and the terminal voltage sags further under the same load. Cells in series add their internal resistances; identical cells in parallel divide it.

glossary.definition: The voltage across a part divided by the current through it, R = V/I, in ohms. For a wire or a film it is set by the material's resistivity, the length, and the cross-section: R = ρL/A.

drills.prompt: Which is the same as 1 Ω?

choices.feedback: A/V is the siemens, the unit of conductance, the reciprocal of resistance.
V·A is the unit of power (a watt for DC). Resistance is volts per ampere.
Ω·m is resistivity, a property of the material. A part's resistance is in ohms, V/A.

drills.prompt: A wire is replaced by one of the same metal, twice as long and with twice the cross-sectional area. Its resistance:

choices.feedback: Twice the length doubles R, but twice the area halves it: R = ρL/A is unchanged.
Length and area act in opposite directions in R = ρL/A: 2/2 = 1, so R is unchanged.
Twice the area halves R, but twice the length doubles it: R = ρL/A is unchanged.

drills.prompt: You double the voltage across a 1 kΩ resistor. What happens?

choices.text: The current doubles; the resistance stays 1 kΩ.
The resistance doubles and the current stays the same.
choices.feedback: Resistance is a property of the part (its material and shape), not of the voltage applied. For a resistor, I = V/R doubles.
Current is proportional to voltage, I = V/R. It's the power that quadruples, P = V²/R.

drills.prompt: Which has the higher resistance when lit: a 60 W, 120 V lamp or a 100 W, 120 V lamp?

choices.feedback: At a fixed voltage P = V²/R, so more power means less resistance: 240 Ω for 60 W against 144 Ω for 100 W.
Same voltage, different power: R = V²/P gives 240 Ω and 144 Ω.

glossary.unit: ohm (Ω) = V/A; its inverse, conductance G = 1/R, is in siemens (S)
physics: A voltage across a conductor sets up a field along it. The field speeds up the free electrons, but each one scatters off the vibrating atoms and impurities every 2 × 10⁻¹⁴ s or so and loses what it gained. The net result is a steady drift in proportion to the field, so in a metal at a fixed temperature the current is proportional to the voltage. That is Ohm's law, and the ratio R = V/I is the resistance.

The energy the field gives the electrons between collisions passes to the atoms as heat, which is why a resistor warms at the rate P = I²R. The charge leaves with the same current it entered with; it has given up energy, V joules per coulomb.

Resistance depends on the material and the shape: R = ρL/A. Twice the length needs twice the voltage for the same field; twice the area holds twice the free electrons in each slice. In a metal, R rises with temperature, about 0.39% per °C for copper.

Not every part is ohmic. A lamp filament's resistance rises steeply as it heats, and a diode's current grows exponentially with voltage. For them V/I is a different number at every point on the curve, and no single resistance describes the part.

glossary.definition: A property of a material, ρ in Ω·m: the resistance of a piece 1 m long with a cross-section of 1 m². Copper's is about 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m at 20 °C, and in a metal it rises with temperature.

drills.prompt: Resistivity is measured in:

choices.feedback: Ohms measure a piece's resistance, which depends on its shape. Resistivity belongs to the material: Ω·m.
Ω/m is the resistance per length of one particular wire, which depends on its cross-section. From R = ρL/A, ρ = R·A/L, in Ω·m.
S/m is conductivity, the reciprocal of resistivity.

drills.prompt: You cut a copper wire in half. What changes for each half?

choices.text: Its resistance halves; its resistivity is unchanged.

choices.feedback: Resistivity belongs to the material, copper, not to the piece. Only the resistance, R = ρL/A, halves with the length.

choices.text: Nothing: resistance is a property of copper.
choices.feedback: That describes resistivity. Resistance depends on the length too: R = ρL/A halves.

drills.prompt: As a copper wire warms up, its resistivity:

choices.feedback: In a metal the lattice vibrates harder when hot and scatters the free electrons more, so resistivity rises, about 0.4% per °C for copper. Falling with temperature is typical of semiconductors.

choices.text: stays the same: resistivity is a constant
choices.feedback: It is a property of the material at a given temperature; copper's rises about 0.4% per °C.

drills.prompt: A piece of material has resistance R, length L, and cross-sectional area A. Its resistivity is:

choices.feedback: From R = ρL/A, solve for ρ: multiply by A and divide by L, ρ = R·A/L.
V/I is the resistance of this one piece. Resistivity takes the shape out: ρ = R·A/L.

glossary.unit: ohm meter (Ω·m); tables also give µΩ·cm (1 µΩ·cm = 10⁻⁸ Ω·m) and Ω·mm²/m (1 Ω·mm²/m = 10⁻⁶ Ω·m)
physics: Resistance mixes the material with the shape. Resistivity separates them: R = ρL/A. A conductor twice as long needs twice the voltage for the same field along it, so R doubles; one with twice the cross-sectional area has twice as many free carriers in each slice to carry the current, so R halves. What is left, ρ, belongs to the material alone.

ρ depends on how many free carriers a material has per cubic meter and how freely they move between collisions. Metals have about one free electron per atom, so their resistivities are tiny: 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m for the annealed copper used in wire. Alloys such as nichrome scatter electrons on their mixed atoms and are about 60 times higher, which suits heating elements. Insulators have almost no free carriers and are higher by 18 to 30 orders of magnitude.

Temperature changes ρ. In a metal, a hotter lattice vibrates harder and scatters the electrons more often, so ρ rises: copper's rises about 0.39% per °C, giving R = R_20·(1 + 0.00393·(T − 20 °C)). Copper wire at 100 °C has 31% more resistance than at 20 °C. In carbon and in semiconductors, heat frees more carriers, so ρ falls as they warm.

confusions.title: Resistivity is not resistance.
confusions.text: Copper's ρ is 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m whatever the wire. One meter of 0.5 mm² wire is 1.72 × 10⁻⁸ × 1 / (0.5 × 10⁻⁶) = 34 mΩ; ten meters of it is 344 mΩ.

confusions.title: Units: area in square meters.
confusions.text: 0.5 mm² is 0.5 × 10⁻⁶ m², because 1 mm² = (10⁻³ m)² = 10⁻⁶ m². Converting it like a length, to 0.5 × 10⁻³ m², gives a resistance 1000 times too small; entering 0.5 as if it were already in m² gives one a million times too small.

confusions.title: A metal's resistance is not constant.
confusions.text: A copper winding with 2.00 Ω at 20 °C has 2 × (1 + 0.00393 × 80) = 2.63 Ω at 100 °C. A tungsten lamp filament goes much further: its resistance rises roughly tenfold from cold to working temperature.

confusions.title: Gold is not the best conductor.
confusions.text: Silver (1.59 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m) and copper (1.72 × 10⁻⁸) beat gold (about 2.2 × 10⁻⁸). Gold plates connectors because it does not corrode, not because it conducts better.

glossary.definition: A material with many free charge carriers, so a small voltage drives a large current; in copper, about one free electron per atom. A wire on a schematic stands for a conductor whose resistance is negligible.

drills.prompt: Which conducts best at room temperature?

choices.feedback: Pure silicon is a semiconductor, far more resistive than copper; doping helps but comes nowhere near a metal.
Pure water has very few ions, so it conducts poorly; tap water and salt water conduct because of their dissolved ions.
Glass is an insulator: its electrons are held in their atoms and bonds.

drills.prompt: What does a wire drawn on a schematic mean?

choices.text: A connection whose resistance is small enough to ignore: both ends are one node.
A connection with exactly zero resistance in the real circuit.
choices.feedback: Real wires and traces have some resistance; the schematic assumes it is negligible. Where it matters (long runs, large currents), it is drawn as a resistor.

choices.text: A path along which the voltage drops gradually.
choices.feedback: A schematic wire is ideal: both ends are at one voltage. Any drop that matters is drawn as a part.

drills.prompt: Why does a metal conduct so well?

choices.text: About one electron per atom is free to move through the lattice.
Its positive ions move toward the negative terminal.
choices.feedback: A metal's ions are fixed in the lattice; only the free electrons move through it.

choices.text: Its electrons are bound tightly to their atoms.
choices.feedback: That describes an insulator. In a metal, about one electron per atom is free.

glossary.unit: none; a metal's resistivity is about 10⁻⁸–10⁻⁶ Ω·m
physics: A conductor has many charge carriers free to move. In a metal the atoms share their outermost electrons, which belong to the whole piece rather than to any one atom: copper has 29 electrons per atom, and only about one of them is free, but that still makes about 8.5 × 10²⁸ free electrons per cubic meter. A small field sets them all drifting, so a small voltage drives a large current.

A wire on a schematic is an ideal conductor with zero resistance, so every point on it is at one voltage. A real wire comes close because its resistance is tiny next to the parts it joins: 1 m of 0.5 mm² copper is 34 mΩ, against a 1 kΩ resistor. The idealization fails at high current or with long runs: 3 A through 2 m of that wire (out and back) drops 0.21 V.

Conductors are not only metals. Electrolytes conduct by moving ions, doped semiconductors by electrons or holes, and carbon by its loosely bound electrons. What they share is free charge carriers; how many there are, and how freely they move, sets the resistivity.

typical.what: 10 cm of 0.25 mm PCB trace, 35 µm thick

confusions.title: A good conductor does not have more electrons; it has free ones.
confusions.text: Copper has 29 electrons per atom and glass has many too. In copper about one per atom is free to move; in glass essentially none are, so its resistivity is at least 10¹⁷ times higher.

confusions.title: A real wire is not a schematic wire.
confusions.text: Two meters of 0.5 mm² copper is 69 mΩ. At 3 A it drops 0.21 V and dissipates 0.62 W, enough to matter for a 3.3 V load at the far end.

confusions.title: Current in a conductor does not mean charge piles up in it.
confusions.text: A wire carrying 1 A takes in 1 C each second at one end and gives out 1 C at the other. It stays neutral; its free electrons drift, at about 0.07 mm/s in 1 mm² of copper.

glossary.definition: A material with almost no free charge carriers, such as glass, PVC, or air, because its electrons are held in their atoms and bonds. Its current is negligible until the field is strong enough to break it down.

drills.prompt: Which of these is an insulator?

choices.feedback: Aluminum is a metal, a good conductor.
Salt water conducts through its dissolved ions.
Graphite conducts by electrons moving within its carbon layers.

drills.prompt: Which is true of an insulator?

choices.text: A strong enough field breaks it down and makes it conduct.
It conducts no current at any voltage.
choices.feedback: Every insulator breaks down above its dielectric strength (dry air at roughly 3 kV/mm), and a tiny leakage current flows even below it.
Its atoms have as many electrons as any other material's; they are bound to their atoms and bonds, not free to move.

drills.prompt: Why does glass insulate?

choices.text: Almost none of its electrons are free to move.

choices.feedback: Glass is full of charge, electrons and nuclei; it is neutral overall, and the charges are not free to move.

choices.text: Its electrons drift too fast to be steered.
choices.feedback: Drift is the slow net motion of free carriers; glass has almost no free carriers to drift at all.

glossary.unit: none; its resistivity is above about 10¹⁰ Ω·m, and its breakdown field is given in kV/mm
physics: In an insulator every electron is held in its atom or in a chemical bond. Freeing one takes several electron-volts, while the thermal energy available at room temperature is only about 0.026 eV, so almost no carriers are free and the resistivity is enormous: around 10¹³ Ω·m for PVC, compared with 1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω·m for copper.

The current through an insulator is tiny but not zero. A 1 cm cube of PVC (ρ ≈ 10¹³ Ω·m) between two 1 cm² plates is 10¹⁵ Ω, so 100 V drives 0.1 pA through it. In practice, current along a dirty or damp surface is usually far larger than current through the bulk, which is why high-impedance circuits are kept clean and dry.

A field strong enough pulls bound electrons free; they accelerate, knock more loose, and the insulator breaks down into conduction. Air at sea level breaks down at about 3 kV per millimeter between smooth electrodes; sharp points and edges concentrate the field and arc over at much lower average fields, below 1 kV/mm. Solid insulators hold much more. Every insulation therefore has a voltage rating, and a capacitor's dielectric sets its voltage rating the same way.

A field also shifts the bound charges slightly, stretching each atom or molecule into a small dipole. This polarization carries no steady current, but it is what lets a dielectric raise a capacitor's capacitance.

typical.what: leakage through a 1 cm cube of PVC at 100 V
breakdown of air at sea level
typical.value: about 3 kV/mm, uniform field; less at sharp edges

confusions.title: An insulator does pass some current.
confusions.text: It is very small: 0.1 pA through a 1 cm cube of PVC at 100 V. That matters for picoamp measurements and for sample-and-hold capacitors, not for a 10 kΩ divider.

confusions.title: Every insulator has a voltage limit.
confusions.text: Above its breakdown field it conducts, often destructively. A 1 mm air gap between smooth electrodes arcs over at about 3 kV, and at less from a sharp edge, which is why high-voltage boards keep their traces far apart.

confusions.title: An insulator is not empty of electrons.
confusions.text: Glass and PVC hold as many electrons as metals; they are bound rather than free. In a field they shift slightly (polarize) instead of drifting away, so no current flows but the field inside is changed.

glossary.definition: A material such as silicon whose conductivity lies between a conductor's and an insulator's and is set mainly by doping: a trace of another element supplies free electrons (n-type) or holes (p-type). Diodes and transistors are made from it.

drills.prompt: What makes n-type silicon different from pure silicon?

choices.text: A trace of a donor element such as phosphorus supplies free electrons.
It carries a net negative charge.
choices.feedback: Doped silicon is neutral: each free electron is balanced by a fixed positive donor ion. The "n" names the majority carrier, not a net charge.

choices.text: Its atoms are packed more densely.
choices.feedback: Doping replaces only a tiny fraction of the atoms; the crystal is the same, but the number of free carriers rises enormously.

drills.prompt: As pure silicon warms up, its resistance:

choices.feedback: In a metal the number of carriers is fixed and they scatter more when hot. In a semiconductor heat frees many more carriers, so resistance falls.
Heat frees more carriers in a semiconductor, so its resistance falls steeply.

drills.prompt: In p-type silicon, the majority carriers are:

choices.text: positive ions moving through the crystal
choices.feedback: The acceptor ions are fixed in the crystal. What moves are holes: missing electrons in the bonds, which act as positive carriers.
Those are the minority carriers in p-type silicon; acceptors create holes.
Protons never leave the nuclei. A hole is a missing electron in the bonds that behaves like a positive carrier.

drills.prompt: Which part is made from doped semiconductor?

choices.feedback: Carbon film is a resistive film with no junction; it is not a doped semiconductor device.
Aluminum foil, oxide, and electrolyte: no semiconductor.

glossary.unit: none; silicon's resistivity runs from about 2 × 10³ Ω·m (pure) to about 10⁻⁵ Ω·m (heavily doped)
physics: In pure silicon, each atom shares its four outer electrons in bonds with four neighbors, so at absolute zero there are no free carriers at all. Freeing an electron from a bond takes the band gap, 1.12 eV, against about 0.026 eV of thermal energy at room temperature, so only a few bonds break: about 10¹⁶ free electrons per cubic meter, against 8.5 × 10²⁸ in copper. Each freed electron leaves a hole, a missing bond electron that neighboring electrons can hop into, so the hole moves through the crystal as a positive carrier.

Doping sets the conductivity. A phosphorus atom has five outer electrons; four go into bonds and the fifth is free, giving n-type silicon. A boron atom has three, leaving a hole: p-type silicon. One phosphorus atom per 5 million silicon atoms (10²² per m³) gives about a million times as many carriers as pure silicon has, and lowers the resistivity from about 2 × 10³ Ω·m to about 5 × 10⁻³ Ω·m.

Heat breaks more bonds, so a pure semiconductor conducts better as it warms: silicon's free carriers roughly double for every 10 °C near room temperature. That is the opposite of a metal, and it is how a thermistor with a negative temperature coefficient works. In doped silicon the dopants fix the majority-carrier count over the working range, but the minority carriers, which grow as n_i², still change fast with temperature: that is why a diode's leakage roughly doubles every 10 °C and its forward voltage falls about 2 mV/°C.

Where p-type meets n-type, the carriers near the boundary recombine and leave a depletion region of fixed ions with a built-in field. That junction, not the bulk material, is what makes diodes, transistors, LEDs, and solar cells work.

typical.what: free electrons in pure silicon at 300 K
silicon doped with 10²² phosphorus atoms per m³

confusions.title: A semiconductor is more than a poor conductor.
confusions.text: Its use is that its carriers can be controlled: doping changes silicon's resistivity by a factor of about 10⁸ across the usual range, from 2 × 10³ Ω·m pure to 10⁻⁵ Ω·m heavily doped, and a junction lets a voltage switch its current on and off.

confusions.title: Doped silicon is not charged.
confusions.text: Each free electron in n-type silicon leaves behind a phosphorus ion with one positive charge, so the crystal stays neutral overall: 10²² free electrons per m³ balanced by 10²² fixed positive ions.

confusions.title: Holes are not particles of their own.
confusions.text: A hole is a bond missing an electron. When a neighboring bound electron hops into it, the hole moves the other way, so it carries current as a positive charge would.

confusions.title: Heat lowers a pure semiconductor's resistance.
confusions.text: Pure silicon's free carriers roughly double for every 10 °C near room temperature, so its resistance roughly halves; copper's rises only 3.9% over the same 10 °C. Doped silicon is different: the dopants fix the carrier count, the mobility falls as it warms, and its resistance rises, which is why a MOSFET's on-resistance grows by about 1.5–2 times from 25 °C to 125 °C.

glossary.uses: Diodes, LEDs, transistors, and integrated circuits; solar cells and photodiodes; NTC thermistors; and Hall-effect sensors.

glossary.definition: The slow average velocity of the charge carriers along a conductor, v_d = I/(nAe), typically well under a millimeter per second in a copper wire. It is a small net motion on top of a fast random one that averages to zero.

drills.prompt: You flip a switch and a lamp 3 m away lights at once. Why, if the electrons drift so slowly?

choices.text: The field travels along the wire close to light speed and sets the electrons everywhere moving at once.
Electrons from the switch race to the lamp close to light speed.
choices.feedback: Each electron drifts well under 1 mm/s. The wire is already full of free electrons, and the field reaches all of them almost at once.

choices.text: The lamp lights only once electrons from the switch reach it.
choices.feedback: At under 1 mm/s that would take close to an hour or longer. The lamp lights because the electrons already in its filament start moving when the field arrives. On AC they never arrive at all; they only oscillate in place.

drills.prompt: The same current flows in a wire with twice the cross-sectional area. The drift velocity:

choices.feedback: v_d = I/(nAe): the same current spread over twice the area needs each carrier to move only half as fast.
v_d = I/(nAe) depends on A: twice the area, half the drift velocity.

drills.prompt: Roughly how fast do electrons drift in a 1 mm² copper wire carrying 3 A?

choices.feedback: That is how fast the field, the signal, travels along the wire, not the electrons. v_d = I/(nAe) ≈ 0.2 mm/s here.
That is the electrons' random speed in copper, which averages to zero. The net drift for 3 A in 1 mm² is about 0.2 mm/s.

glossary.unit: meter per second (m/s): v_d = I/(nAe)
physics: Picture a wire of cross-section A with n free carriers per cubic meter, each of charge e, all drifting at v_d. In a time t they advance v_d·t, so every carrier in a length v_d·t of the wire passes a given cross-section: n·A·v_d·t carriers, carrying n·A·v_d·t·e of charge. Dividing by t gives the current, I = nAe·v_d, so v_d = I/(nAe).

For copper, n ≈ 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³, so 1 A through 1 mm² needs only v_d = 1/(8.5 × 10²⁸ × 10⁻⁶ × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹) ≈ 7.3 × 10⁻⁵ m/s, about 0.07 mm/s. The current is large because there are so many carriers, not because they move fast.

The drift rides on fast random motion. The free electrons in copper move at around 10⁶ m/s in random directions, scattering off the lattice about every 2 × 10⁻¹⁴ s. Between collisions the field speeds each one up a little in one direction, and each collision scrambles that gain; the average result is a steady drift in proportion to the field, which is Ohm's law.

In a series loop the current is the same everywhere, but the drift speed is not: it depends on the area and on n. Halve the cross-section and the drift doubles. In moderately doped silicon (10²² carriers per m³), n is millions of times smaller than in copper, so the same current density needs a far faster drift: with 10²² carriers per m³, 1 A/mm² needs about 620 m/s.

typical.what: random speed of electrons in copper

confusions.title: The drift speed is not how fast a signal travels.
confusions.text: At 0.073 mm/s an electron takes nearly four hours to cross 1 m of wire, yet a lamp 1 m away lights within nanoseconds: the change in the field travels along the wire at about 2 × 10⁸ m/s and starts every carrier drifting at once.

confusions.title: It is not the electrons' actual speed.
confusions.text: Each free electron in copper moves at about 10⁶ m/s, ten billion times its drift speed of about 10⁻⁴ m/s, but in random directions that average to zero. The drift is the small average that a field adds.

confusions.title: The same current does not mean the same drift speed.
confusions.text: In a series loop, 1 A flows through 1 mm² of copper at about 0.073 mm/s and through a 0.5 mm² section at about 0.15 mm/s. The current is equal; the drift speed is inversely proportional to the area.

confusions.title: A slow drift is not a small current.
confusions.text: Multiply back: 8.5 × 10²⁸ m⁻³ × 10⁻⁶ m² × 7.3 × 10⁻⁵ m/s × 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C ≈ 1 A. The enormous number of carriers makes up for their slowness.

glossary.uses: Explaining why a circuit responds at once though its carriers creep, comparing metals with semiconductors through n, and the Hall effect, where the drift of the carriers in a magnetic field gives a measurable voltage.

glossary.unit: watt (W) = J/s = V·A
physics: Power is the rate at which energy is transferred: P = W/t, in watts (1 W = 1 J/s). In a circuit it follows from two definitions: a voltage is joules per coulomb and a current is coulombs per second, so their product is joules per second. For any two-terminal part, P = V·I, with V the voltage across that part and I the current through it.

For a resistance, Ohm's law gives two more forms: P = I²R and P = V²/R. Neither says a bigger resistance always gets hotter. At a fixed voltage a bigger R draws less current and dissipates less (V²/R); at a fixed current it dissipates more (I²R).

Because P = V²/R, power grows with the square of the voltage: twice the voltage on the same resistor gives twice the current and four times the power. A source delivers power (current leaves its + terminal); a load absorbs it (current enters its + terminal). Around a circuit, the power delivered equals the power absorbed.
Energy is power times time. A 10 W load running for 3 h uses 30 Wh, which is 108 kJ. Efficiency is output power over input power; the rest becomes heat.

glossary.unit: watt (W): the rate at which a part turns electrical energy into heat
physics: Inside a resistor, the field keeps speeding up the free electrons and they keep losing that energy in collisions with the lattice, which vibrates harder: the part warms. The rate is the power it takes in, P = V·I = I²R. A transistor or regulator dissipates in the same way, at the voltage across it times the current through it.

The hot part loses heat to its surroundings, through its leads into the board, into the air, and by radiation, faster the hotter it is. Its temperature climbs until the heat lost each second equals the power going in. That happens at about P·θ above the air around it, where θ is the thermal resistance from the part to the air in °C/W.

A power rating is the dissipation that brings the hottest spot to the highest temperature the materials tolerate, at a stated ambient temperature. In hotter surroundings there is less room to rise, so the allowed power falls: the part is derated. A resistor rated 0.25 W up to 70 °C that may reach 155 °C is allowed (155 − 85)/(155 − 70) × 0.25 W ≈ 0.21 W at 85 °C.

glossary.definition: The charge a capacitor holds per volt across it, C = Q/V, in farads. For parallel plates C = ε·A/d: larger plates, a thinner gap, and a dielectric of higher permittivity all raise it.

glossary.unit: farad (F) = C/V; real parts run from picofarads to millifarads (and farads for supercapacitors)
physics: A capacitor is two conductors separated by an insulator. Connect a voltage and the circuit moves charge off one plate and onto the other until the field between them matches the voltage. The charge moved is proportional to the voltage, Q = C·V, and the constant C is the capacitance: the charge moved per volt.

C depends only on the construction: C = ε_r·ε₀·A/d for parallel plates. A larger area holds more charge at the same field; a thinner gap gives a stronger field for each volt, which needs more charge on the plates; and a dielectric that polarizes partly cancels the field, so more charge is needed for the same voltage. One farad is enormous: plates 1 mm apart in air would need about 113 km² of area.

Because Q = C·V, the voltage can change only as fast as a current moves charge: i = C·dv/dt. A steady voltage means no current, so a capacitor blocks DC; a changing voltage means current in both leads, though no charge crosses the dielectric. Moving charge onto the plates against the growing field takes work, stored in the field: W = ½CV².
Parallel capacitors add, because their plate areas add. In series their spacings effectively add, so the total is less than either: two 10 µF in series give 5 µF.

drills.prompt: What sets a capacitor's voltage rating?

glossary.unit: none: its relative permittivity εr is a ratio, ε = εr·ε0, with ε0 = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² F/m
physics: A dielectric is the insulator between a capacitor's plates. In the field between the plates its atoms and molecules polarize: their bound charges shift slightly, leaving a thin layer of bound charge on each face, opposite in sign to the nearby plate. That bound charge partly cancels the plates' field, so for the same voltage the plates can hold more charge. The factor is the relative permittivity ε_r, and C = ε_r·ε₀·A/d.

The voltage across the gap is the field times the thickness, V = E·d, and every dielectric breaks down above some field. So a thinner dielectric gives more capacitance and a lower voltage rating, and for a given material and size the two trade against each other. Aluminum electrolytics reach large values by using an oxide film only nanometers thick on a deeply etched foil.

Real dielectrics are not ideal. They leak a little current, absorb some energy each cycle of an AC voltage, and their ε_r can depend on temperature and voltage. Class 1 ceramics (C0G) and polypropylene film are stable and low-loss, with a far lower ε_r; class 2 ceramics (X7R, X5R) reach ε_r in the thousands, but lose a large part of their capacitance as the DC voltage across them rises.

confusions.text: It is a ratio. Plates of 1 cm² 0.1 mm apart make 8.85 pF in air and about 40 pF with FR-4 (ε_r ≈ 4.5) between them: the same geometry, 4.5 times the capacitance.

confusions.title: A thinner dielectric is not free capacitance.
confusions.text: The breakdown field is a property of the material, so halving the thickness doubles C and halves the voltage the capacitor can hold.

confusions.title: In an electrolytic capacitor, the dielectric is not the electrolyte.
confusions.text: The dielectric is the aluminum oxide film; the electrolyte is a conductor that serves as the second plate.

glossary.definition: The magnetic flux linkage per ampere of a coil, L, in henries; it sets the voltage a changing current induces, v = L·di/dt. It grows with the square of the number of turns and with the core's permeability.

choices.feedback: A coulomb per volt is a farad.
From v = L·di/dt, L = v/(di/dt), in V·s/A, which is Ω·s, not Ω/s.
Inductance is flux linkage per ampere: 1 H = 1 Wb/A, not Wb·A.

drills.prompt: A coil's turns are doubled on the same core. Its inductance:

choices.feedback: Inductance goes with the square of the turns: twice the turns makes twice the flux, linked by twice the turns.
More turns give more inductance, in proportion to the square of the turns.

drills.prompt: An ideal 10 mH inductor carries a steady 2 A. The voltage across it is:

choices.feedback: v = L·di/dt, and a steady current has di/dt = 0, so v = 0. L·I is the flux linkage (20 mWb), not a voltage.

drills.prompt: The current in a 1 mH inductor rises at 1000 A/s. The voltage across it is:

choices.feedback: v = L·di/dt = 0.001 H × 1000 A/s = 1 V; the millihenry matters.

glossary.unit: henry (H) = V·s/A = Wb/A
physics: Every current is surrounded by a magnetic field. Wind the wire into a coil and the turns' fields add inside it; a core of iron or ferrite multiplies the flux many times for the same current. The inductance L is the flux linkage per ampere, the flux through each turn times the number of turns, divided by the current.

When the current changes, the flux changes, and by Faraday's law a voltage appears across the coil: v = L·di/dt, with a polarity that opposes the change (Lenz's law). One henry gives 1 V when the current changes by 1 A each second. Read it both ways: a steady current needs no voltage across an ideal inductor, and a fixed voltage V ramps the current in a straight line at V/L amperes per second.

L grows as the square of the number of turns: twice the turns make twice the flux for each ampere, and that flux passes through twice as many turns. It also grows with the core's permeability and cross-section and falls with the coil's length, roughly L = N²·µ·A/l. A ferromagnetic core can only be magnetized so far: above its saturation current, its permeability, and with it L, falls steeply.
The energy is stored in the magnetic field, W = ½LI²: 5 mJ for 10 mH at 1 A. Because the current cannot change instantly, interrupting it makes the voltage rise until something conducts.

glossary.definition: A voltage induced in a coil by changing magnetic flux, in the direction that opposes the change producing it. In an inductor it is L·di/dt and opposes any change of current (Lenz's law); in a turning motor it is generated by the rotation, grows with speed and opposes the supply, so a stalled motor has none and draws its largest current.

drills.prompt: When does a DC motor draw the most current?

choices.text: At standstill: stalled or just starting
At full speed with no load
choices.feedback: At speed the back-EMF nearly cancels the supply, so little current flows. At standstill there is no back-EMF, and only the winding resistance limits the current.
The back-EMF grows with speed and opposes the supply, so the current falls as the motor speeds up.

drills.prompt: A motor with 2 Ω windings runs from 12 V and generates 10 V of back-EMF. What current does it draw?

choices.feedback: 12 V / 2 Ω is the stalled current. Running, only the difference drives current: (12 − 10) / 2 = 1 A.
The back-EMF opposes the supply: (12 − 10) / 2 = 1 A, not (12 + 10) / 2.
10 V / 2 Ω uses the back-EMF alone; the current is set by the difference, (12 − 10) / 2 = 1 A.

drills.prompt: Why is a diode placed across a relay coil driven by a transistor?

choices.text: To clamp the voltage spike when the coil is switched off
To stop the coil's back-EMF from reversing the supply while the relay is on
choices.feedback: While the current is steady, di/dt = 0 and nothing is induced. Even at turn-on, the back-EMF only opposes the rising current, and the diode is reverse biased and does nothing. The spike comes at turn-off, when the current is forced to change fast.

choices.text: To make the relay switch faster
choices.feedback: The diode actually slows the release a little, since the coil current decays through it. It is there to clamp the turn-off spike.

drills.prompt: In a turning DC motor, the back-EMF is proportional to:

choices.feedback: The resistance only drops I·R; the generated back-EMF is proportional to the speed.
The current sets the torque. The back-EMF is generated by the rotation, in proportion to the speed.

glossary.unit: volt (V): L·di/dt in an inductor; proportional to speed in a motor
physics: When the magnetic flux through a coil changes, a voltage is induced across it: ℰ = N·dΦ/dt for N turns (Faraday's law). Its polarity opposes the change that caused it (Lenz's law). In an inductor the flux comes from the coil's own current, so the induced voltage is v = L·di/dt and opposes any change of that current. While the current rises, this voltage opposes the supply; that is why it is called back-EMF.

It opposes changes, not the current itself. With a steady current an ideal inductor has no voltage across it. When the current falls, the back-EMF reverses and acts to keep the current flowing. If a switch breaks a coil's current, di/dt becomes enormous: a 100 mH coil carrying 100 mA, cut off in 1 µs, would need L·di/dt = 10 kV, so the voltage rises until something conducts, often an arc across the switch or the breakdown of the transistor driving it. A flyback diode across the coil gives the current a path and holds the voltage to about 0.7 V beyond the supply.

A DC motor's turning armature is a coil moving in a magnetic field, so it generates an EMF in proportion to its speed, opposing the supply. The current is set by what is left over: I = (V − E_b)/R, where R is the winding resistance. A 12 V motor with R = 2 Ω draws 6 A when stalled (E_b = 0), but only 0.6 A when it turns fast enough to generate E_b = 10.8 V.

The back-EMF is where a motor converts electrical power to mechanical: E_b·I becomes mechanical power, 10.8 V × 0.6 A = 6.48 W in the example (some of it lost to friction), while I²R = 0.72 W heats the winding. A stalled motor converts nothing and turns all 72 W into heat.

typical.what: same motor at speed, E_b = 10.8 V
100 mH, 100 mA cut off in 1 µs
coil switched off with a flyback diode
typical.value: clamped about 0.7 V beyond the supply

confusions.title: Back-EMF opposes changes in current, not the current.
confusions.text: An ideal 10 mH inductor carrying a steady 1 A has 0 V across it. Ramp the current up at 1 A/ms and 10 V appears opposing the rise; ramp it down at the same rate and 10 V appears in the other direction, aiding the current.

confusions.title: A stalled motor draws more current, not less.
confusions.text: With the shaft held still there is no back-EMF to oppose the supply: the 12 V motor above draws 6 A and heats its winding at 72 W, against 0.6 A and 0.72 W when running.

confusions.title: The winding resistance does not set a running motor's current.
confusions.text: An ohmmeter reads the 2 Ω winding, and 12 V / 2 Ω suggests 6 A. Running, the motor draws 0.6 A, because the back-EMF of 10.8 V leaves only 1.2 V across the winding.

confusions.title: It is not a separate part.
confusions.text: Motor models draw the back-EMF as a voltage source in series with the winding resistance, but nothing in the motor is that source: the voltage comes from the coil itself, from its changing current or its motion. Stop the change or the motion and it is gone.

glossary.definition: How far a part's actual value may lie from its marked value as made (at 25 °C), such as ±5% for a resistor. Changes with temperature and age are specified separately and are not included in it.

drills.prompt: A new 1 kΩ ±5% resistor at 25 °C may measure anywhere from:

choices.feedback: 5% of 1000 Ω is 50 Ω, not 5 Ω.
± means either side of the marked value: 950 Ω to 1050 Ω.
That would be ±50%. 5% of 1000 Ω is 50 Ω.

drills.prompt: Which does a resistor's tolerance cover?

choices.text: Spread from the marked value as made

choices.feedback: Change with temperature is specified separately, as a temperature coefficient in ppm/°C.
Aging is a separate stability specification, such as the change after 1000 h at rated power.

drills.prompt: Two "10 kΩ ±5%" resistors from one bag measure 9.8 kΩ and 10.3 kΩ. That is:

choices.text: normal: both lie within 9.5 kΩ to 10.5 kΩ
a defect: parts from one bag should match
choices.feedback: The tolerance allows any value within ±5%, here 9.5 kΩ to 10.5 kΩ; both are inside it.

choices.text: a sign the meter is wrong
choices.feedback: Nothing here points to the meter: both readings are inside the ±5% band.

glossary.unit: percent of the marked value (±%), or an absolute value for small capacitors (such as ±0.25 pF)
physics: No two parts come out of production identical. A film resistor is trimmed to value, often by cutting a groove into its film, and the film, the cut, and the end contacts all vary slightly. The maker measures and guarantees a band: a 10 kΩ ±5% resistor lies between 9.5 kΩ and 10.5 kΩ as delivered, at the stated temperature.

Tolerance covers only how the part is made. In use its value moves for other reasons, each specified separately: temperature (a temperature coefficient in ppm/°C) and aging. A 100 ppm/°C resistor that warms by 50 °C moves another 0.5%.

A careful design works out the worst case, with each part at whichever end of its band makes the result worst. A divider of two 10 kΩ ±5% resistors from 12 V is 6 V nominally; with R1 high and R2 low it gives 12 × 9.5/(10.5 + 9.5) = 5.70 V, and the other way 6.30 V. The output moves ±5%, not ±10%: each resistor also sits in the sum R1 + R2, so in a 1:1 divider an error in either one moves the output by only half as much.

confusions.title: Tolerance is not drift.
confusions.text: A ±1% resistor with a 100 ppm/°C temperature coefficient can move another 0.5% over a 50 °C rise. That change is specified separately and comes on top of the tolerance.

confusions.title: A ±5% part is not 5% off.
confusions.text: It can be anywhere in the band: a 1 kΩ ±5% resistor may measure 1003 Ω or 951 Ω. The tolerance is a limit, not a prediction.

confusions.title: Worst-case errors do not always add.
confusions.text: In a divider of two equal ±5% resistors, the output can be off by ±5% (5.70–6.30 V from 12 V). If both resistors were 5% high, the ratio, and the output, would not change at all.

glossary.uses: Worst-case analysis of dividers, gain-setting resistors and RC timing, choosing between ±5% and ±1% parts, trimming where no tolerance is good enough, and the spacing of the E-series.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Ohm's and Joule's Laws, Resistor Ratings, and Electrical Safety" (last update 26 August 2024), sections 4.3 "Resistors" (p. 38), 6.2 "Resistor labeling" (p. 72) and 6.3 "Resistor parameters and types" (p. 75)

sources.note: Checked the color-code table (digits black 0 to white 9, multipliers 10⁰ to 10⁹ with gold ×0.1 and silver ×0.01, tolerances brown ±1%, red ±2%, gold ±5%, silver ±10%, none ±20%) and the band order: digit, digit, multiplier, tolerance for four bands; three digits, multiplier, tolerance for five.

glossary.definition: The standard component values of IEC 60063 (E6, E12, E24, E96, and others). Each divides a decade into n steps of nearly equal ratio, about 10^(1/n), so a calculated value is never far from a standard one; each series goes with a tolerance (E12 with ±10%, E24 with ±5%) roughly wide enough that neighboring values' ranges meet.

drills.prompt: Which value is in the E12 series?

choices.feedback: Not in E12 or E24; the nearest E12 values are 3.9 kΩ and 4.7 kΩ.
Not in E12: it has 5.6 and 6.8 (E24 adds 6.2).

drills.prompt: Roughly what ratio separates neighboring E12 values?

choices.feedback: That is E24's step, 10^(1/24): twice as many values per decade. E12's step is 10^(1/12) ≈ 1.21: twelve equal ratio steps make a factor of 10.
That is E6's step, 10^(1/6). E12's step is 10^(1/12) ≈ 1.21: twelve equal ratio steps make a factor of 10.

drills.prompt: Why are E-series values spaced by nearly equal ratios rather than equal differences?

choices.text: So any calculated value is within a similar percentage of a standard one, at every scale.
Because only those values can be manufactured
choices.feedback: Any value can be made; the series is a choice, so a short list per decade covers every scale evenly in percentage.

choices.text: So that values in series add up to other standard values
choices.feedback: They generally don't: 4.7 kΩ + 4.7 kΩ = 9.4 kΩ is not an E12 value. The point is even coverage in percentage.

drills.prompt: You calculate 5.3 kΩ and stock E24 parts. Which is the nearest standard value?

choices.feedback: 5.6 kΩ is about 5.7% away; 5.1 kΩ is about 3.8% away.
5.0 is not an E24 value; E24 has 4.7, 5.1, and 5.6 here.

glossary.unit: none: a list of values per decade, scaled by powers of ten (4.7 Ω, 47 Ω … 4.7 MΩ)
physics: A tolerance is a percentage, so a ±10% band around 1 kΩ is 200 Ω wide and one around 8.2 kΩ is 1.64 kΩ wide. To cover every value with bands that meet, the standard values must be spaced by a constant ratio, not a constant difference. The E-series of IEC 60063 divide each decade into n steps of ratio 10^(1/n): about 1.47 for E6, 1.21 for E12, 1.10 for E24, and 1.024 for E96.

Each series goes with a tolerance that makes neighboring bands meet. In E12 with ±10%, 1.0 reaches up to 1.10 and 1.2 reaches down to 1.08; in E24 with ±5%, 1.0 reaches 1.05 and 1.1 reaches down to 1.045. So any calculated value is within about one tolerance of a standard part.

The values are rounded: to two figures in E6, E12, and E24, three in E48 and finer. Some are also shifted from the formula for historical reasons: 10^(5/12) is 2.61, but the E12 value is 2.7; 10^(6/12) is 3.16, but the value is 3.3. Each coarser series is every second value of the next: E6 ⊂ E12 ⊂ E24.

typical.what: step ratio: E6, E12, E24, E96

figures.title: E12: equal ratios, not equal steps
figures.caption: the formula 10^(n/12) on a log scale; each dot is labeled with the E12 value it is rounded to

confusions.title: There is no 5 kΩ in E12.
confusions.text: The neighbors are 4.7 kΩ and 5.6 kΩ. E24 has 5.1 kΩ, and E96 has 4.99 kΩ and 5.11 kΩ. Pick the nearest value and check the circuit with it, or combine two parts.

confusions.title: The values are not evenly spaced.
confusions.text: From 1.0 to 1.2 is a step of 0.2; from 8.2 to 10 is a step of 1.8. Both are a ratio of about 1.2.

confusions.title: The values are rounded, not exact powers.
confusions.text: The formula gives 2.61, 3.16, and 4.64 where E12 has 2.7, 3.3, and 4.7. Use the listed values, never the formula, when choosing a part.

confusions.title: A finer series does not mean a tighter part.
confusions.text: The series and the tolerance are separate choices. A 4.7 kΩ ±1% resistor is common; the series only says which values are made.
