glossary.definition: The node chosen as the 0 V reference for node voltages, marked with a ground symbol. Every copy of the same ground symbol on a schematic is one node, whether or not that node is connected to earth.

drills.prompt: Two identical ground symbols sit at opposite corners of a schematic with no wire drawn between them. They are:

choices.text: separate nodes unless a wire joins them
choices.feedback: Every copy of the same ground symbol is one node; the symbols stand in for the wire.

choices.text: joined only if the circuit is connected to earth
choices.feedback: Earth doesn't matter here: the symbols are one node in the circuit either way.

drills.prompt: In a battery-powered circuit, "ground" is:

choices.text: the node chosen as 0 V, usually the battery's negative terminal

choices.feedback: A battery circuit usually has no earth connection at all; ground is only the reference node.
Current goes around a loop and back to the source; ground is just the reference for measuring voltages.

drills.prompt: Node A is at 5 V and node B at 2 V, both measured from ground. What is the voltage of A relative to B?

choices.feedback: V_AB = V_A − V_B = 5 − 2 = 3 V; node voltages subtract.
5 V is A's voltage from ground. Relative to B, which sits at 2 V, A is 5 − 2 = 3 V higher.

drills.prompt: You move the ground symbol to a different node. What changes?

choices.text: Every node voltage, but no voltage between two nodes and no current

choices.feedback: Ground is only the reference point; the circuit and its currents are the same.

choices.text: Nothing: ground is always the supply's negative terminal
choices.feedback: Ground is a choice. Node voltages are measured from it, so they all shift by the same amount.

glossary.unit: volt (V): 0 V by definition, the reference for every node voltage
physics: A voltage belongs to two points, so a schematic picks one node as the reference for all the others and marks it with the ground symbol. "The output is at 4 V" then means 4 V above ground. The choice is free: moving ground to another node shifts every node voltage by the same amount but changes no voltage across any part, because only differences of potential do anything.

Every ground symbol on a schematic is the same node, as if one wire joined them all. Ground is drawn as many small symbols only to keep the drawing clear. It is also an ordinary conductor: the current that leaves a source's + terminal comes back to its − terminal through ground. Real ground wires and traces have resistance, so a large return current shifts the local ground: 2 A through 10 mΩ of ground trace moves it by 20 mV, enough to upset a sensor read to millivolts.

Ground does not have to be the most negative point. Two 9 V batteries in series with ground at the junction give rails of +9 V and −9 V. A battery-powered circuit's ground is only its reference and needs no connection to the earth. In line-powered equipment, the metal case is tied to the earth through the outlet's round pin, so that a fault to the case trips the breaker instead of making the case live. That protective earth wire is not a current return: in normal use it carries no current, and it carries current only during a fault.

2 A of return current through 10 mΩ of ground trace
a voltmeter between two ground symbols

confusions.text: In the figure, 0.6 mA leaves the source's + terminal, passes R1 and R2, and returns through ground to the − terminal. Every ampere into ground comes back out of it.

glossary.definition: A set of points joined by wire, all at one voltage. Each terminal of a part connects to exactly one node, and the currents into a node sum to zero (Kirchhoff's current law).

drills.prompt: Wires join one end of a resistor, one end of a capacitor, and a transistor's emitter, with no part between them. These points form:

choices.feedback: Points joined only by wire are at one voltage, so they are one node.
No part separates any of them; points joined only by wire are one node.

drills.prompt: Three wires meet at a node. 2 A flows in on one and 3 A flows in on another. The third carries:

choices.feedback: The currents in must equal the currents out (KCL): 2 + 3 = 5 A out.
If all three carried current in, charge would pile up at the node. The third must carry 5 A out.

drills.prompt: Both terminals of a resistor end up on the same node. What follows?

choices.text: It is shorted: 0 V across it and no current through it
That can't happen in a real circuit
choices.feedback: It is easy: a wire across the resistor puts both terminals on one node.

choices.text: It carries the full loop current
choices.feedback: With both ends at one voltage, V = 0, so I = V/R = 0; the wire carries the current instead.

glossary.unit: a node has one voltage, in volts, measured from ground
physics: A node is every point joined together by wire. A schematic's wires stand for conductors with negligible resistance, so even the full current through them makes next to no voltage, V = I·R ≈ 0, and the whole node sits at one voltage, however long or winding the wire is drawn. Each terminal of a part connects to exactly one node, and a two-terminal part only "sees" the voltages of its two nodes.

All ground symbols are one node, and so are points with the same net label, wire or no wire. Wires that cross without a dot are not joined. Good drawings join wires in T-junctions, never four at a point, so a dot lost in printing cannot be mistaken for a crossing.

A node is a small piece of metal with almost no capacitance, so it cannot store charge: the currents into it add up to the currents out of it. That is Kirchhoff's current law, and it is why circuit analysis works node by node. Pick one node as ground; the voltages of the others are the unknowns, and nodal analysis writes one current-law equation for each. A simulator such as SPICE solves for exactly these node voltages.

typical.what: voltage between two points on one node

typical.value: N − 1 node voltages, less one for each voltage source that fixes a node

typical.what: stray capacitance of a node on a board

confusions.title: A node is not a dot.
confusions.text: It is the whole set of joined wire. In the figure, node a runs from R1 to R3; a meter between any two points on it reads 0 V.

confusions.text: R2 and R3 in the figure are drawn eight grid steps apart, but both connect a to ground: they share 4.5 V and are in parallel.

confusions.text: Two parts are in series only if the node between them touches nothing else. In the figure, R1 leads straight into node a and on to R2, but node a also feeds R3, so R1 carries 4.5 mA and R2 only 2.25 mA.

confusions.title: A real node is not perfectly one voltage.
confusions.text: The ideal wire is a model. At 1 A, 1 m of 0.5 mm² copper drops 34 mV from end to end, which matters for high currents and precise measurements.

glossary.definition: A path of near-zero resistance between two nodes, which holds the voltage between them near zero while the rest of the loop sets the current. Across a source, only the internal resistance is left to limit that current.

drills.prompt: A 1.5 V cell with 0.25 Ω internal resistance is short-circuited. What current flows?

choices.feedback: The internal resistance still limits it: I = ℰ/r = 1.5 V / 0.25 Ω = 6 A.

choices.text: 0 A, since a short has no voltage across it
choices.feedback: Zero volts across zero ohms allows any current; here it's set by the internal resistance: ℰ/r = 6 A.
That is ℰ·r. The current is I = ℰ/r = 1.5 / 0.25 = 6 A.

drills.prompt: Across a short circuit, which is near zero?

choices.feedback: The current can be very large; it's the voltage across the short that is held near zero.

choices.text: Both the voltage and the current
choices.feedback: A short carries current, often a lot; only the voltage across it is near zero.

drills.prompt: A solder bridge shorts one resistor in a series string. The current in the string:

choices.text: rises, because the total resistance falls

choices.feedback: That is what an open does. A short removes resistance, so the current rises.
The total resistance fell by that resistor's value, so the current rises.

glossary.unit: ohm (Ω): ideally 0 Ω; a real short is milliohms
physics: A short circuit is a path of near-zero resistance between two nodes. With R ≈ 0, V = I·R ≈ 0 whatever the current, so the short holds the two nodes at almost the same voltage, and the rest of the circuit decides how much current flows through it. Any part connected across a short has no voltage across it and carries no current: it has been bypassed.

Across a source, only the source's internal resistance is left in the loop. The current is ℰ/r, and all the power, ℰ²/r, heats the source: about 11 A and 17 W for a fresh AA cell (1.6 V, 0.15 Ω), and over 100 A for a lithium-ion cell. A bench supply instead holds the current at its set limit, and fuses and current limits are there to stop exactly this.

Inside a circuit, a short changes what the rest of it does. Shorting R2 of a 1 kΩ / 1 kΩ divider on 12 V takes the output to 0 V and doubles the current, from 6 mA to 12 mA, because R1 now has the whole 12 V across it.
Shorting a network's output is also a measurement. The short-circuit current of a linear network, with its open-circuit voltage, gives its Thevenin resistance: R_th = V_oc / I_sc.

typical.what: 10 cm of 0.2 mm² copper jumper wire

confusions.title: A short is not a high voltage.
confusions.text: It is the opposite: almost no voltage across it, and as much current as the rest of the loop allows. The danger is the current and the heat.

confusions.title: Shorting one part does not stop the current.
confusions.text: With 1 kΩ and 1 kΩ in series on 12 V, the current is 6 mA. Short one resistor and it rises to 12 mA through the other.

confusions.title: Current does not take "only the easiest path."
confusions.text: It divides between parallel paths in proportion to their conductance. A 10 mΩ short across 1 kΩ takes all but about one hundred-thousandth of the current; the resistor still gets that tiny share.

confusions.title: The short-circuit current is set by the source.
confusions.text: It is ℰ/r, so it depends on the source: about 11 A from a fresh AA cell and over 100 A from a lithium-ion cell, or the current limit of a bench supply.

glossary.definition: A break in a path, so no current flows through it whatever voltage is across it. With no current there is no internal drop, so an unloaded source reads its EMF.

drills.prompt: A lamp, a switch, and a battery form a loop, and the switch is open. Which is true?

choices.text: No current flows, and the full battery voltage appears across the switch.
No current flows, and there is no voltage across the switch.
choices.feedback: With no current the lamp drops nothing (V = I·R = 0), so the whole battery voltage appears across the gap.

choices.text: A smaller current still flows through the switch.
choices.feedback: An open passes no current at all.

drills.prompt: One resistor in a powered series string of three has failed open. A meter across each resistor reads:

choices.text: the full supply across the open one and 0 V across the others
a third of the supply across each
choices.feedback: That would need current through all three. With no current the good ones drop nothing, so the whole supply appears across the gap.
The good ones read 0 V, but the open one has the full supply across it.

drills.prompt: A 9 V battery with nothing connected reads 9.4 V on a voltmeter. That reading is:

choices.text: its EMF: with no current there is no internal drop

choices.feedback: With no current (a voltmeter draws almost none), I·r ≈ 0, so the reading is the EMF itself.

choices.text: the voltage it will hold under any load
choices.feedback: Under load, I·r drops inside the battery, so the terminals read less.

glossary.unit: ohm (Ω): ideally infinite; a real open is gigaohms or more
physics: An open circuit is a break: no conducting path, so no current, whatever the voltage across it. An open switch, a blown fuse, a cracked solder joint, and a reverse-biased ideal diode are all opens.

In a series loop, one open stops the current everywhere, because charge has no path around the loop. With no current, every resistor in the loop drops I·R = 0, so by Kirchhoff's voltage law the whole source voltage appears across the open: a blown fuse in a 12 V circuit has 12 V across it.

A source with nothing connected is open-circuited. No current means no drop across its internal resistance, so its terminals show its EMF. For any linear network, the open-circuit voltage at a pair of terminals is its Thevenin voltage.

A node connected only through an open is floating: the circuit no longer sets its voltage. A 10 MΩ voltmeter then pulls it toward its other lead and reads about 0 V, and a logic input left floating can drift and pick up noise.

typical.what: voltage across an open in a 12 V series loop

confusions.title: An open can have the full voltage across it.
confusions.text: No current flows, so nothing else in the loop drops any voltage. A meter across a blown fuse in a 12 V circuit reads 12 V; across a good fuse, nearly 0 V.

confusions.title: An open in one branch does not stop the others.
confusions.text: Two 12 V lamps in parallel draw 1 A each. If one filament breaks, the other still draws 1 A; only the supply current falls, from 2 A to 1 A.

confusions.title: A floating node is not at 0 V.
confusions.text: Its voltage is undefined. A multimeter reads about 0 V only because its 10 MΩ input pulls the node toward the meter's other lead.

confusions.title: An open-circuit reading does not show a source's health.
confusions.text: With no current, the internal drop is zero, so a worn cell with 0.6 Ω inside still reads near its EMF; under 0.5 A it would lose another 0.3 V.

glossary.uses: Fault finding (broken wires, blown fuses, cracked joints), measuring a source's EMF and a network's Thevenin voltage, switches, and pull-up resistors that give a floating input a defined level.

glossary.definition: A circuit that turns an input (line AC or a battery) into the DC voltage a circuit needs, usually regulated so it holds steady as the load current changes.

drills.prompt: A 5 V supply's output falls from 5.00 V with no load to 4.95 V at 1 A. Its output resistance is:

choices.feedback: 5 V / 1 A is the load. The supply's own resistance is ΔV/ΔI = 0.05 V / 1 A = 0.05 Ω.
4.95 V / 1 A is the load resistance. The supply's is ΔV/ΔI = 0.05 V / 1 A = 0.05 Ω.

drills.prompt: A "12 V, 1 A" adapter powers a load that needs 100 mA. The adapter:

choices.text: supplies 100 mA: the load sets the current, and 1 A is the most it can give

choices.feedback: A voltage supply sets the voltage; the load draws what it draws, I = V/R. 1 A is its maximum.

choices.text: is the wrong choice, since it would overload the circuit
choices.feedback: A higher current rating is only headroom; at 12 V the load still draws its own 100 mA.

drills.prompt: What does "regulated" mean for a power supply?

choices.text: Its output voltage holds steady as the load current and the input change.
Its output current is fixed, whatever the load.
choices.feedback: That describes a current source. A regulated voltage supply holds the voltage and lets the load set the current.

choices.text: It has a fuse against overcurrent.
choices.feedback: Protection is separate; regulation is about holding the output voltage steady.

glossary.unit: rated by its output voltage (V) and the most current (A) or power (W) it can deliver
physics: A linear supply works down a chain. A transformer steps 120 V RMS line voltage down to a safer secondary voltage; a bridge rectifier lets current flow only one way; a reservoir capacitor charges near each peak and feeds the load between peaks, sagging by the ripple ΔV ≈ I/(2fC); and a regulator turns that rippling voltage into a steady one. A 12 V RMS secondary peaks at 12 × √2 = 17.0 V; less two diode drops the capacitor charges to about 15.6 V, and with 1 A and 2200 µF it sags by 1/(120 × 0.0022) ≈ 3.8 V, to about 11.8 V, between peaks.

A linear regulator is a transistor in series with the load, adjusted by feedback until the output matches a reference. It passes the whole load current and drops all the excess voltage, so it dissipates (V_in − V_out)·I. In the example, a 5 V regulator fed an average of about 13.7 V at 1 A turns about 8.7 W into heat and delivers 5 W: the regulator's efficiency is about 37%. It also needs its input to stay above its output plus its dropout at the lowest point of the ripple.

A switching supply chops its input at tens of kilohertz to megahertz and filters the result with an inductor and capacitor. Because its transistor is either fully on or fully off, it wastes little power and typically reaches 85–95% efficiency, which is why phone chargers and laptop adapters are small and cool. Its price is switching noise on its output and around it.

A bench supply holds its set voltage until the load tries to draw more than its current limit; then it holds the current at the limit and lets the voltage fall. That makes it hard to damage a circuit, or the supply, with a short.

typical.what: linear regulator, 12 V in, 5 V out, 0.5 A

confusions.title: A supply does not force its rated current.
confusions.text: A 12 V, 2 A adapter driving 100 Ω delivers 12 V / 100 Ω = 0.12 A. The 2 A is the most it can deliver; the load decides how much it draws.

confusions.title: More input voltage is not a safety margin for a linear regulator.
confusions.text: Every volt above the output becomes heat: 5 V at 0.5 A from 12 V wastes 3.5 W; from 7 V, only 1 W.

confusions.title: A regulator cannot fix dips below its minimum input.
confusions.text: If the ripple valley falls below the output plus the dropout, about 7 V for a regulator with 2 V of dropout at 5 V out, the ripple passes straight through to the output.

confusions.title: 120 V RMS is not 120 V peak.
confusions.text: A 120 V RMS sine peaks at 120 × √2 ≈ 170 V. Components on the line side must be rated for the peak, and the line voltage is dangerous to touch.

glossary.definition: Two parts are in series when they share a node that nothing else connects to, so the same current must pass through both. Series resistances add, and the voltages across the parts add up to the voltage across the whole string.

drills.prompt: R1 and R2 are joined end to end, and a wire from their shared node also goes to R3. Are R1 and R2 in series?

choices.text: No: current can leave the shared node through R3, so R1 and R2 need not carry the same current
Yes: they are joined end to end
choices.feedback: Touching end to end is not enough. Series means one current through both, which needs the shared node to have no third connection; here R3 can take part of the current.

choices.text: Yes, if R1 and R2 have the same value
choices.feedback: Values don't decide it; the connections do. With a third branch at the node, the currents in R1 and R2 differ by R3's current (KCL).

drills.prompt: A 1.0 kΩ and a 2.2 kΩ resistor are in series across 6.4 V. What current flows?

choices.feedback: That uses the parallel combination, 1.0 kΩ ∥ 2.2 kΩ ≈ 688 Ω. In series one current crosses both, so the resistances add: 3.2 kΩ, and 6.4 V / 3.2 kΩ = 2.0 mA.
6.4 V / 1.0 kΩ leaves out the 2.2 kΩ. Every series resistor is in the current's path, so they add to 3.2 kΩ: 2.0 mA.
6.4 V / 2.2 kΩ leaves out the 1.0 kΩ. The resistances add to 3.2 kΩ: 2.0 mA.

drills.prompt: Which is true of every resistor in a single series string?

choices.text: Each has the same voltage across it.
choices.feedback: Only if they are equal. The current is shared; each voltage is I·R, so the larger resistor drops more.

choices.text: The current falls a little in each, as each uses some up.
choices.feedback: Charge isn't used up: whatever enters a resistor leaves it, so the current is the same all along the string. What each resistor takes is energy, the drop I·R.

choices.text: The largest resistor carries the least current.
choices.feedback: A single string has only one current. The largest resistor has the largest voltage across it, not the least current.

glossary.unit: R = R1 + R2 + …: one current, voltages that add
physics: Two parts are in series when they share a node that nothing else connects to. Charge cannot pile up at that node, so all the current leaving one part must enter the other: series parts carry the same current.

Each part drops I·R, and the drops add to the voltage across the whole string: V = I·(R1 + R2), so series resistances add. The voltage divides in proportion to resistance, the largest resistor taking the largest share; that is the voltage divider. One open anywhere in the string stops the current through all of it.

The same rule applies to other parts. Cells in series add their EMFs and their internal resistances. Series inductors add. Series capacitors do the opposite and combine as reciprocals, because their dielectric gaps effectively add: two 10 µF in series give 5 µF.
Judge series by the connections, never by the drawing. Parts drawn in a line are not in series if anything else joins the node between them, and parts drawn far apart can be.

glossary.definition: Parts are in parallel when both their ends connect to the same two nodes, so they have the same voltage across them. Their currents add, and the combined resistance is less than the smallest of them.

drills.prompt: An ideal 12 V supply lights a lamp. A second, identical lamp is connected across the same two supply terminals. What happens to the first lamp's current?

choices.text: It stays the same: the lamp still has 12 V across it.
It halves, because the two lamps share the current.
choices.feedback: The supply's current doubles instead. Each lamp has the full 12 V across it, so each draws what it drew alone.
The supply's total current doubles; the first lamp's own current is still set by 12 V across that lamp.

drills.prompt: What is a 10 kΩ resistor in parallel with a 15 kΩ resistor?

choices.feedback: That is the series sum. In parallel each resistor adds a path, so the pair conducts better than either alone: (10 × 15)/(10 + 15) = 6.0 kΩ, less than the smaller one.
That is the average. A parallel pair is always below its smaller resistor: 1/R = 1/10k + 1/15k gives 6.0 kΩ.
Half of 10 kΩ is what two 10 kΩ parts in parallel give. A 15 kΩ path conducts less than a second 10 kΩ would, so the result is a little higher: 6.0 kΩ.

drills.prompt: A 100 Ω resistor is put in parallel with a 1 MΩ resistor. The pair is:

choices.text: just under 100 Ω: the 1 MΩ barely changes it

choices.feedback: Parallel resistances don't average. Their conductances add: 1/100 + 1/1 000 000 comes almost all from the 100 Ω, so the pair is about 99.99 Ω.
Adding a parallel path always lowers the resistance, below the smaller of the two: just under 100 Ω.

glossary.unit: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + …: one voltage, currents that add
physics: Parts are in parallel when both their ends connect to the same two nodes. A part only "sees" the voltages of its two nodes, so parallel parts have the same voltage across them.

Each branch then draws its own current, V/R, and the branch currents add up to the total (Kirchhoff's current law). So conductances add: 1/R = 1/R1 + 1/R2, which for two resistors is R1·R2/(R1 + R2). Every branch adds current at the same voltage, so the combination is always below the smallest branch, and n equal resistors give R/n.

Fed from an ideal source, adding a branch leaves the other branches' currents unchanged; it only adds its own. From a real source with internal resistance, the extra current lowers the terminal voltage a little, and every branch's current falls with it.

Parallel capacitors add, because their plate areas add. Parallel inductors combine as reciprocals. Cells in parallel must be matched in voltage, or the higher one drives a large current into the lower.

glossary.definition: Two resistors in series across a voltage, with the output taken at the node between them, so the output is the fraction R2/(R1 + R2) of the input. That fraction holds only while the load draws little current compared with the current through the divider.

drills.prompt: A divider has R1 = 1.0 kΩ from 12 V to the output and R2 = 2.0 kΩ from the output to ground. What is the unloaded output?

choices.feedback: 12 V × 1.0/(1.0 + 2.0) is the drop across R1, the top resistor. The output is across R2: 12 V × 2.0/3.0 = 8.0 V.
That is 12 V × R2/R1. The fraction is R2 over the total, R2/(R1 + R2), and a divider can never give more than its input.
Half the input needs equal resistors. The larger resistor takes the larger share: R2 is two thirds of the total, so 8.0 V.

drills.prompt: Two 100 kΩ resistors divide 12 V to 6.0 V. A 100 kΩ load is then connected from the output to ground. The output:

choices.text: falls to 4.0 V, because the load in parallel with R2 makes 50 kΩ
stays 6.0 V, because the resistor ratio hasn't changed
choices.feedback: The load sits in parallel with R2, so the bottom of the divider becomes 100 k ∥ 100 k = 50 kΩ: 12 V × 50/(100 + 50) = 4.0 V.

choices.text: rises, because the load draws extra current
choices.feedback: A load only adds a path to ground. That lowers the bottom resistance, so the output falls, to 4.0 V here.

choices.text: falls to 3.0 V, because the load takes half the output
choices.feedback: Work it as a divider: R2 ∥ load = 50 kΩ, so the output is 12 V × 50/(100 + 50) = 4.0 V.

choices.text: Setting a reference voltage for an input that draws almost no current
Making a 5 V rail for a 1 A load from 12 V
choices.feedback: The load current would flow through the top resistor and move the output with every change in load, while the divider wastes power. A regulator does this job.

choices.text: Raising 5 V to 9 V for a sensor
choices.feedback: A divider's output is a fraction of its input, never more.

glossary.unit: none: the output is the fraction R2/(R1 + R2) of the input, unloaded
physics: With nothing connected to the output, R1 and R2 carry the same current, I = V_in / (R1 + R2), since charge has nowhere else to go. The output is the drop across R2: V_out = I·R2 = V_in·R2 / (R1 + R2). Only the ratio counts: 1 kΩ / 1 kΩ and 100 kΩ / 100 kΩ both give half the input.

A load across the output is a second path from the output to ground, in parallel with R2. It lowers the bottom resistance, so the output falls. Seen from the output, the divider is a Thevenin source: its unloaded output in series with R1 ∥ R2. For 10 kΩ / 10 kΩ from 12 V, that is 6 V behind 5 kΩ: a 100 kΩ load pulls the output to 5.71 V, and a 10 kΩ load to 4 V.

Smaller resistors hold up better under load but draw more current. 10 kΩ / 10 kΩ on 12 V draws 0.6 mA and dissipates 7.2 mW; 1 kΩ / 1 kΩ draws 6 mA and 72 mW. Choosing a divider is a trade between accuracy under load and wasted power.

glossary.definition: The currents flowing into any node add up to the currents flowing out, because charge cannot pile up at a node. It is conservation of charge applied to a junction.

drills.prompt: A supply delivers 50 mA to a board with three loads in parallel. Two of them draw 20 mA and 12 mA. What does the third draw?

choices.feedback: That is the two known loads together. The 50 mA from the supply splits three ways, so the third takes 50 − 20 − 12 = 18 mA.
Each load has the full supply voltage, but not the full current: the three branch currents add to 50 mA.

choices.text: It depends on the third load's resistance
choices.feedback: Its resistance sets its current, but KCL already tells you what it must be: 50 − 32 = 18 mA.

drills.prompt: Which statement follows from Kirchhoff's current law?

choices.text: The current into a resistor equals the current out of it.
A resistor uses up some of the current through it.
choices.feedback: Charge passes through; what the resistor takes is energy, seen as the voltage drop. The current out equals the current in.

choices.text: The voltages around any loop add to zero.
choices.feedback: That is Kirchhoff's voltage law, about energy around a loop. The current law is about charge at a node.

choices.text: Every branch at a node carries the same current.
choices.feedback: The branches can carry different currents; only their sum, in minus out, must be zero.

drills.prompt: An LED, a resistor, and a transistor's collector meet at one node. To find the transistor's current from the other two, which law do you write?

choices.text: Kirchhoff's current law at that node
Kirchhoff's voltage law around the loop
choices.feedback: KVL relates voltages around a loop. Relating the currents in the branches at one node is KCL.
A transistor is not a resistor, and Ohm's law only relates one part's voltage and current. At a junction, KCL ties the branch currents together.

glossary.unit: ampere (A): the currents into a node sum to the currents out
physics: At any node, the currents flowing in add up to the currents flowing out. This is conservation of charge: a node is a small piece of metal with almost no capacitance, so it cannot store charge. If more flowed in than out, the excess would raise the node's voltage within nanoseconds, and the higher voltage would push more current out through the branches until in and out were equal again.

To use it, pick a direction for each unknown current and mark it. Currents in count positive and currents out negative, and the sum is zero. If an answer comes out negative, the current flows the other way; its size is still right.

The law works backward as well as forward: if two of three currents at a node are known, the third needs no meter. It holds for any closed boundary, not only a single node: the currents into a whole subcircuit, or into a transistor, sum to zero, so a BJT's emitter current is its collector current plus its base current. Nodal analysis writes it at every node whose voltage is unknown, with each branch current written as a voltage difference over a resistance; circuit simulators solve the same equations.

glossary.definition: The voltages around any closed loop add to zero, counting rises and drops with their signs, because a charge carried around the loop returns to the same potential. It is conservation of energy for charge moving around a circuit.

drills.prompt: A 9.0 V battery drives a loop of a resistor and an LED. The LED has 2.0 V across it. What is across the resistor?

choices.feedback: The resistor gets only what the LED leaves: around the loop the drops add up to the 9.0 V rise, so 9.0 − 2.0 = 7.0 V.
Going around the loop, the battery is a rise and the LED and resistor are drops. Drops add up to the rise: 2.0 + V_R = 9.0, so V_R = 7.0 V.
Series parts carry the same current, not the same voltage. The resistor takes the remaining 7.0 V.

drills.prompt: A loop holds only a 12 V supply, R1, and R2. A meter reads 5.0 V across R1 and 9.0 V across R2. What does KVL say?

choices.text: Those readings can't both be right: the drops would total 14 V, more than the 12 V supply
Fine: R2 is the larger resistor, so it takes more
choices.feedback: The larger resistor does take more, but the two drops must still add to the 12 V supply; 5.0 + 9.0 = 14 V breaks KVL. Recheck the meter or the circuit.

choices.text: R2 must be getting extra voltage from the supply
choices.feedback: In a loop of one source and two resistors, the drops add to exactly the source voltage. A total of 14 V from 12 V means a reading is wrong or something else is in the loop.

drills.prompt: Which is true of Kirchhoff's voltage law in a circuit drawn with lumped parts?

choices.text: It holds around every loop, whatever parts are in it, diodes and transistors included.
It only applies to loops made of resistors.
choices.feedback: It is energy conservation for a charge carried around a loop, so it holds for any parts; a diode's drop counts like any other.

choices.text: It says the voltages across the parts of a loop are equal.
choices.feedback: It says they add to zero, rises and drops with their signs. They are equal only in special cases.

glossary.unit: volt (V): every term in the sum is a voltage, and the sum is 0 V
physics: The voltage between two points is the energy per coulomb a charge gains or loses in moving between them. In a circuit with steady currents it depends only on the two points, not on the path taken, so every node has one potential. A charge carried around a closed loop comes back to the potential it started at, so the rises and drops met on the way must cancel: ΣV = 0.

That gives a recipe. Pick a starting node and a direction, add each voltage met with its sign (a rise from − to + counts positive, a drop negative), and set the sum to zero. Neither the start nor the direction changes the result, and together with KCL at the nodes, enough loop equations fix every current in a network.

In a series loop one current flows through every part, so the drops share the source voltage in proportion to the resistances. With 10 V across 1 kΩ, 1.8 kΩ, and 2.2 kΩ, I = 10 V / 5 kΩ = 2 mA, and the drops are 2 V, 3.6 V, and 4.4 V, which add up to 10 V. Parts in parallel form a loop of their own, so KVL also says they share one voltage.

KVL is exact for a lumped circuit, where each part's voltage is defined between its terminals. A changing magnetic flux through the loop itself induces a voltage in the wiring, and then the path matters. Circuit analysis puts that effect into an element, an inductor's L·di/dt, and the stray inductance of real wiring is why two ends of a ground wire in a fast circuit can differ: 10 nH carrying a current that changes by 1 A in 10 ns drops 1 V.

confusions.title: An open switch has the voltage across it.
confusions.text: With the switch open no current flows, so every resistor in the loop drops I·R = 0 V, and KVL puts the whole supply across the gap: 12 V across an open switch in a 12 V lamp circuit. That is why a meter across a blown fuse reads the supply voltage.

confusions.title: The signs come from the direction of travel.
confusions.text: Going through a resistor in the direction of its current is a drop of I·R; going against it is a rise of I·R. Reversing the direction of travel multiplies every term by −1, and the sum is still zero.

confusions.title: The drops depend on the resistances, not on their order.

glossary.definition: Any linear network, seen from two of its terminals, behaves like one voltage source V_th in series with one resistance R_th. V_th is the open-circuit voltage at those terminals, and R_th is the resistance seen there with the independent sources set to zero, which equals V_th divided by the short-circuit current.

drills.prompt: A 12 V source feeds a divider of two 10 kΩ resistors, and the output is the middle node. What is its Thevenin equivalent?

choices.feedback: R_th is found with the source replaced by a short. Seen from the output, the two 10 kΩ resistors then both run to the shorted source: in parallel, 5 kΩ.
V_th is the open-circuit output, 12 V × 10/(10 + 10) = 6 V, not the source voltage.
Both resistors connect the output to the zeroed source, so both count, in parallel: 10 k ∥ 10 k = 5 kΩ.

drills.prompt: A sealed module has two output terminals. Which two measurements give its Thevenin equivalent?

choices.text: The open-circuit voltage, and the short-circuit current (or the voltage under a known load)
The open-circuit voltage, and an ohmmeter reading across the terminals while it runs
choices.feedback: An ohmmeter injects its own small current and reads nonsense across a live source. Use V_oc and I_sc: R_th = V_oc/I_sc.
That gives V_th but not R_th, so you still can't predict how far the voltage sags under a load.

drills.prompt: A source's Thevenin equivalent is 9.0 V in series with 1.0 kΩ. What voltage appears across a 2.0 kΩ load?

choices.feedback: 9.0 V is the open-circuit voltage. With a load, current flows through R_th and drops part of it: 9.0 V × 2.0/(1.0 + 2.0) = 6.0 V.
That is the drop across R_th. The load gets the rest, 9.0 − 3.0 = 6.0 V.

drills.prompt: Which is true of a Thevenin equivalent?

choices.text: It predicts the voltage and current for any load, but not the power dissipated inside the original network.
It also gives the power dissipated inside the original network.
choices.feedback: Only the behavior at the terminals is equivalent. An unloaded divider burns power in its resistors; its equivalent, a source in series with R_th, burns none with no load.

choices.text: It holds only for the one load it was worked out with.
choices.feedback: It holds for every load, which is its use, as long as the network is linear.

glossary.unit: volt (V) for the source and ohm (Ω) for the resistance; the short-circuit current, their ratio, is in amperes (A)
physics: A network of resistors and independent sources is linear: every voltage and current in it is a sum of terms proportional to the sources. Seen from two terminals, the voltage therefore falls in a straight line as the current drawn rises: V = V_th − I·R_th. A straight line is fixed by two numbers, so the whole network, however many parts it has, acts at those terminals like one source V_th behind one resistance R_th.

The two numbers come from the two ends of that line. With nothing connected, I = 0 and the terminal voltage is V_th, the open-circuit voltage. Shorted, V = 0 and the current is I_sc = V_th/R_th. R_th is also the resistance seen at the terminals with every independent source set to zero: a voltage source replaced by a short and a current source by an open, since that is what zero volts and zero amperes look like.

For a divider of 12 V with R1 = 10 kΩ and R2 = 10 kΩ, V_th = 12 V × 10 kΩ/20 kΩ = 6 V. With the source shorted, R1 and R2 both run from the output to ground, so R_th = 10 kΩ ∥ 10 kΩ = 5 kΩ. Check: shorting the output passes 12 V / 10 kΩ = 1.2 mA, and 6 V / 1.2 mA = 5 kΩ.

The equivalent predicts only what a load sees, not what happens inside. Unloaded, the divider dissipates (12 V)²/20 kΩ = 7.2 mW, while the equivalent's source delivers nothing. It also holds only while the network is linear: a diode or transistor inside makes R_th change with the current.

glossary.definition: The time τ that sets how fast a first-order circuit settles: RC for a resistor and capacitor, L/R for a resistor and inductor. After one τ the response has covered 63% of the way to its final value, and after five it is within 1%.
glossary.unit: second (s): Ω·F = (V/A)·(C/V) = C/A = s, and H/Ω = s
physics: While a capacitor charges through a resistor toward a step of V_S, the current is set by the voltage still to go: i = (V_S − v_C)/R. That same current is the rate the capacitor charges, i = C·dv_C/dt. So the closer v_C gets to V_S, the smaller the current and the slower v_C moves. Solving the two together gives v_C(t) = V_S(1 − e^(−t/τ)) with τ = RC.

Each τ closes 63.2% of the gap still left, since 1 − e^(−1) ≈ 0.632: 63.2% after 1τ, 86.5% after 2τ, 95.0% after 3τ and 99.3% after 5τ. If the starting slope, V_S/τ, kept up, the capacitor would reach V_S in exactly one τ. A discharge follows the same curve mirrored: v_C(t) = V_0·e^(−t/τ).
A resistor and an inductor work the same way with the roles swapped. The inductor's voltage, L·di/dt, is what the resistor leaves over, so the current rises toward V_S/R with τ = L/R.

confusions.title: τ is not the cutoff frequency.
confusions.text: 1/(RC) is the cutoff as an angular frequency, ω_c in rad/s; the RC low-pass cutoff in hertz is f_c = 1/(2πRC). For 1 kΩ and 100 nF, τ = 100 µs and f_c ≈ 1.59 kHz.

confusions.title: 63%, not 37%.
confusions.text: After one τ a charging capacitor has covered 63.2% of the way. e^(−1) ≈ 36.8% is what is still to go; on a discharge, it is what remains.

confusions.title: Not "full after one τ".
confusions.text: An exponential never quite arrives. Engineers call it settled after about 5τ (within 1%), or 7τ for 0.1%.

confusions.title: The supply voltage does not change τ.
confusions.text: Doubling V_S doubles every voltage on the curve but leaves the timing alone: τ depends on R and C only.

glossary.bench: the τ cursor, which finds where a step on a transient plot has covered 63.2% and reads τ off the time axis.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. I (DC), ch. 16 "RC and L/R Time Constants", section "Voltage and current calculations"
sources.note: τ = RC for a series RC circuit and L/R for a series RL circuit; each τ moves the voltage or current about 63% of the way still left; an empty capacitor first draws the supply voltage over R; and the current at any moment is the supply minus capacitor voltage over R.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Capacitors and Capacitive Circuits" (last update 15 October 2025), ch. 3 "Tutorial", section 3.4 "Inverse exponential growth/decay" (p. 47)

drills.prompt: A resistance in ohms times a capacitance in farads gives a time constant in:

choices.feedback: 1/(RC) is a rate, per second. RC itself is a time: Ω·F = (V/A)·(C/V) = C/A, and a coulomb per ampere is a second.

choices.text: ohm-farads, a unit with no simpler name
choices.feedback: It reduces: Ω = V/A and F = C/V, so Ω·F = C/A, which is a second.
Ω·F = (V/A)·(C/V) = C/A: coulombs per ampere, which is seconds.

drills.prompt: A 10 kΩ resistor charges a 100 µF capacitor from 0 V toward a 10 V supply. About what is the capacitor voltage after 1.0 s?

choices.feedback: An RC charge only approaches its end. τ = RC = 10 kΩ × 100 µF = 1.0 s, and one τ covers 63% of the way: 6.3 V. It is within 1% only after about 5τ.
37% (e⁻¹) is the part still to go after one τ, not the part covered. The capacitor is at 63%, 6.3 V.
Half the way is reached at about 0.69τ (ln 2 × τ), sooner than one τ. At τ = 1.0 s it is at 63%, 6.3 V.

drills.prompt: A capacitor charging through a resistor slows down as it nears the supply voltage. Why?

choices.text: The voltage left across the resistor shrinks, so the charging current shrinks.
Its capacitance falls as it fills.
choices.feedback: C is set by the plates and the dielectric and doesn't change with charge. What falls is the current, (V_S − v_C)/R.

choices.text: The resistor warms up and its resistance rises.
choices.feedback: The slowdown happens with a perfect resistor too: the charging current is proportional to the voltage still to go, which gives the exponential.

glossary.definition: The frequency at which a filter's output has fallen to 1/√2, about 70.7%, of its passband value: down 3 dB. For a first-order RC filter it is 1/(2πRC), where the capacitor's reactance equals the resistance.

drills.prompt: An RC low-pass uses R = 1.0 kΩ and C = 100 nF. What is its cutoff frequency?

choices.feedback: 1/(RC) = 10 000 is in radians per second. Divide by 2π for hertz: 1/(2π × 1.0 kΩ × 100 nF) ≈ 1.6 kHz.
RC = 100 µs is the time constant, a time. The cutoff frequency is 1/(2πRC) ≈ 1.6 kHz.
That is 2π/(RC); the 2π belongs with RC in the denominator: f_c = 1/(2πRC) ≈ 1.6 kHz.

drills.prompt: A sine at exactly the cutoff frequency passes through an RC low-pass. The output is:

choices.text: about 70.7% of the input amplitude, lagging it by 45°
zero, since the cutoff is where the filter stops passing signal
choices.feedback: A first-order filter rolls off gradually: down 3 dB at f_c, then 20 dB per decade. Nothing is cut off sharply there.
Half the power, not half the voltage: −3 dB is 1/√2 of the voltage, about 70.7%.

drills.prompt: You double the capacitor in an RC low-pass. The cutoff frequency:

choices.feedback: More capacitance means less reactance at each frequency, so X_C comes down to R at half the frequency: 1/(2πRC) halves.

choices.text: stays the same, because R sets it
choices.feedback: Both R and C set it: f_c = 1/(2πRC), so doubling C halves f_c.

glossary.unit: hertz (Hz); the same cutoff as an angular frequency, 2π times larger, is in rad/s
physics: In an RC low-pass filter the input divides between R and the capacitor's reactance, X_C = 1/(2πfC). The capacitor's voltage is 90° out of phase with the resistor's, so the two add at right angles, and the output is V_in·X_C/√(R² + X_C²). At low frequencies X_C ≫ R and nearly all of the input appears across the capacitor; at high frequencies X_C ≪ R and little does.

The cutoff is the boundary between those two regimes, where X_C = R: 1/(2πf_cC) = R, so f_c = 1/(2πRC). There the output is 1/√2 ≈ 70.7% of the input, which delivers half the power into a given resistance: −3.01 dB. The output also lags the input by 45° there.

Well above f_c the output is about V_in·X_C/R = V_in·f_c/f: ten times the frequency gives a tenth of the output, −20 dB per decade (−6 dB per octave). A filter with two reactive parts, such as an LC filter, is second order and falls at −40 dB per decade beyond its cutoff.
f_c = 1/(2πτ) ties the frequency picture to the time picture. An RC filter with τ = 100 µs has f_c = 1.59 kHz, and its step response rises from 10% to 90% in 2.2τ = 220 µs, so rise time × f_c ≈ 0.35.

confusions.title: The signal does not stop at f_c.
confusions.text: At f_c the output is still 70.7% of the input, and at 10f_c it is 9.95%: 1/√(1 + 10²) = 0.0995. A first-order filter only rolls off, at 20 dB per decade.

confusions.title: −3 dB is half the power, not half the voltage.
confusions.text: Half the voltage is −6.02 dB. In an RC low-pass that happens at √3·f_c: 2.76 kHz for 1 kΩ and 100 nF.

confusions.title: 1/(RC) is in radians per second.
confusions.text: For 1 kΩ and 100 nF, 1/(RC) = 10 000 rad/s. Dividing by 2π gives f_c = 1.59 kHz; reading 1/(RC) as hertz puts the cutoff at 10 kHz, 6.28 times too high.

confusions.title: A load moves the cutoff.
confusions.text: f_c = 1/(2πRC) assumes nothing draws current from the output. Load the 1 kΩ, 100 nF filter with 1 kΩ and the capacitor sees a Thevenin resistance of 1 kΩ ∥ 1 kΩ = 500 Ω: the cutoff doubles to 3.18 kHz and the passband output halves.

glossary.uses: Setting the bandwidth of an audio stage or a sensor input, anti-aliasing before an ADC, smoothing a PWM output to its average, supply decoupling, and reading an amplifier's bandwidth (its −3 dB point) off a datasheet.
glossary.bench: the −3 dB marker, which finds where an .ac sweep falls 3 dB below its passband and reads f_c.

sources.note: A low-pass filter's cutoff is where its output falls to 70.7% of the input; for one R and one C that is f = 1/(2πRC), where X_C = R; and the formula assumes no load, since a load resistor moves the response.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Elementary Filter Circuits" (last update 5 October 2025), ch. 3 "Tutorial", section 3.4 "Bode plots" (p. 29)
sources.note: The cutoff is conventionally the −3 dB (half-power) point, where the output voltage is √2/2 of the input and X = R, giving f_c = 1/(2πRC) for an RC filter.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Advanced Filter Circuits" (last update 20 April 2026), ch. 3 "Tutorial", section 3.6 "Improving roll-off" (p. 25)
sources.note: A first-order filter (one reactive part) rolls off at −20 dB per decade, a tenfold voltage drop per decade, and each added order of filtering, usually one more reactive part, makes the roll-off steeper.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Elementary Filter Circuits" (last update 5 October 2025), ch. 3 "Tutorial", section 3.6 "Roll-off" (p. 33)
sources.note: Roll-off is quoted in dB per octave or per decade; cascading two 20 dB/decade low-pass stages gives 40 dB/decade, and a series L with a shunt C rolls off more steeply than a series R with a shunt C.

glossary.definition: A logarithmic measure of a ratio: 10·log₁₀ of a power ratio, or 20·log₁₀ of a voltage ratio when both voltages are across equal resistances. The 20 comes from power going as voltage squared, so a change gives the same number of decibels whether you measure its power or its voltage.

drills.prompt: An amplifier's voltage gain is 100. What is that in decibels?

choices.feedback: 10·log₁₀(100) = 20 is the power formula. For a voltage ratio use 20·log₁₀: 20 × 2 = 40 dB.
Decibels are logarithmic: each factor of 10 in voltage adds 20 dB, so 100 = 10² is 40 dB.
log₁₀(100) = 2 is only the logarithm. Multiply by 20 for a voltage ratio: 40 dB.

drills.prompt: A filter attenuates a signal by 20 dB. By what factor did its voltage fall?

choices.feedback: 100 is the power ratio for 20 dB. The voltage ratio is 10^(20/20) = 10; power goes as voltage squared, so 10² = 100.
Decibels aren't a ratio themselves. The voltage ratio is 10^(dB/20) = 10.

drills.prompt: Two amplifier stages in cascade have gains of 20 dB and 6 dB. What is the total gain?

choices.feedback: Gains multiply, and logarithms turn products into sums, so decibels add: 20 + 6 = 26 dB. That is about 20 times in voltage (10 × 2).
Both stages amplify, so their decibels add: 20 + 6 = 26 dB, a voltage ratio of about 10 × 2 = 20.

glossary.unit: decibel (dB), a tenth of a bel: a ratio, so dimensionless. With a stated reference it names a level: dBm is relative to 1 mW, dBW to 1 W
physics: Signals in electronics span many orders of magnitude, from microvolts at an antenna to volts at an amplifier's output. A logarithm turns those ratios into small numbers that add: a stage with a gain of 10 followed by one of 100 gives 1000, and in decibels 20 dB + 40 dB = 60 dB.

The decibel is defined on power: 10·log₁₀(P₂/P₁). In a fixed resistance P = V²/R, so the power ratio is the voltage ratio squared, and 10·log₁₀((V₂/V₁)²) = 20·log₁₀(V₂/V₁). That is the only reason voltage takes 20: doubling a voltage is +6.02 dB because it quadruples the power, and the same change gets the same number of decibels whichever of the two you measure.

Positive decibels are a gain and negative ones a loss; 0 dB is a ratio of 1. Every 10 dB is a factor of 10 in power and every 20 dB a factor of 10 in voltage. 3 dB is almost exactly a factor of 2 in power and 6 dB a factor of 2 in voltage, since 10^0.3 = 1.995.
A plain dB figure is a ratio, not an amount. To name a level it needs a reference: 0 dBm is 1 mW and 30 dBm is 1 W.

typical.what: voltage ×0.707, an RC filter at f_c

confusions.title: 20 dB is ×10 in voltage and ×100 in power.
confusions.text: 10^(20/20) = 10 for voltage; 10^(20/10) = 100 for power. Reading 20 dB of voltage gain as ×100 uses the power rule on a voltage.

confusions.title: Decibels add; ratios multiply.
confusions.text: Stages of 20 dB and 6 dB give 26 dB, which is 10 × 2 = 20 in voltage, not 10 + 2 = 12.

confusions.title: −3 dB is not half the voltage.
confusions.text: −3 dB is half the power and 70.7% of the voltage. Half the voltage is −6 dB.

confusions.text: 1 V RMS across 50 Ω and 1 V RMS across 600 Ω are the same voltage, 0 dB apart as voltages, but they deliver 20 mW and 1.67 mW: 10.8 dB apart in power.

sources.note: A power ratio takes 10·log₁₀ and a voltage or current ratio 20·log₁₀, valid for the same load impedance (a voltage gain of 2 is a power gain of 4); a loss is negative and unity gain is 0 dB; and stage gains in dB add.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 1 "Amplifiers and Active Devices", section "Absolute dB scales"
sources.note: A dB figure names an absolute level only against a stated reference: 0 dBm is 1 mW (dissipated in 600 Ω for telephone work, 50 Ω for RF), and 0 dBW is 1 W.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Elementary Filter Circuits" (last update 5 October 2025), ch. 5 "Derivations and Technical References", section 5.1 "Decibels" (p. 58)
sources.note: Every 10 dB is a factor of 10 in power and every 3 dB about a factor of 2; the overall dB figure of a chain is the sum of its stages; dBm counts dB above 1 mW; and voltage takes 20·log₁₀ because power goes as voltage squared in a fixed resistance.

glossary.definition: The opposition a capacitor or inductor offers to alternating current, in ohms: X_C = 1/(2πfC) falls with frequency, and X_L = 2πfL rises with it. Its current is 90° out of phase with its voltage, so the energy it takes in during one quarter-cycle it returns in the next, and it dissipates nothing on average.
glossary.unit: ohm (Ω): the ratio of AC voltage amplitude to AC current amplitude
physics: A capacitor's current is set by how fast its voltage changes: i = C·dv/dt. Drive it with a sine of amplitude V_p at frequency f, and the current is a sine of amplitude 2πfC·V_p that peaks where the voltage crosses zero, a quarter-cycle ahead. The ratio of the amplitudes is the capacitive reactance, X_C = 1/(2πfC). The faster the voltage swings, the more current it takes to keep up, so X_C falls as the frequency rises.

An inductor is the mirror image: its voltage is set by how fast its current changes, v = L·di/dt. A current of amplitude I_p takes a voltage of amplitude 2πfL·I_p, peaking a quarter-cycle ahead of the current. So X_L = 2πfL rises with frequency. At DC an ideal inductor is a short and an ideal capacitor is an open circuit.

Reactance is in ohms because it is a voltage over a current, but it is not resistance. The energy a reactance takes in during one quarter-cycle goes back to the source in the next, so its average power is zero. With resistance in the same circuit, the two add at right angles: in series, |Z| = √(R² + X²).

confusions.title: Reactance is not resistance.
confusions.text: Both are in ohms, but a reactance dissipates no average power. An ideal capacitor with 5 V RMS across it and 10 mA RMS through it dissipates nothing: V·I gives the average power only when voltage and current are in phase.

confusions.title: It does not add straight onto resistance.
confusions.text: In series, 100 Ω of resistance and 100 Ω of reactance make |Z| = √(100² + 100²) ≈ 141 Ω, not 200 Ω.

confusions.title: X_C falls with frequency; X_L rises.
confusions.text: Ten times the frequency gives a tenth of X_C and ten times X_L. A capacitor blocks DC and passes high frequencies; an inductor passes DC and impedes high frequencies.

confusions.title: The 2π matters.
confusions.text: X_C = 1/(2πfC), not 1/(fC). At 1 kHz a 1 µF capacitor is about 159 Ω, not 1 kΩ.

confusions.title: The sign is a convention.
confusions.text: In Z = R + jX a capacitor's reactance is negative, X = −1/(2πfC), and an inductor's positive. Tables of X_C usually give the magnitude.

glossary.uses: Coupling capacitors (a low reactance at the signal frequency, an open circuit at DC), supply decoupling, RC and LC filters, chokes that keep high-frequency noise out of a supply, and resonance, where X_L = X_C.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. II (AC), ch. 4 "Reactance and Impedance -- Capacitive", section "AC capacitor circuits"
sources.note: A capacitor's current is proportional to dv/dt, so it leads the voltage by 90°; X_C = 1/(2πfC) = 1/(ωC) in ohms falls as frequency rises; and the capacitor absorbs and releases energy each cycle, dissipating none.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. II (AC), ch. 3 "Reactance and Impedance -- Inductive", section "AC inductor circuits"
sources.note: An inductor's voltage is proportional to di/dt, so its current lags by 90°; X_L = 2πfL = ωL rises with frequency; and over a full cycle it returns as much energy as it absorbs, dissipating none.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. II (AC), ch. 4 "Reactance and Impedance -- Capacitive", section "Series resistor-capacitor circuits"
sources.note: Resistance (0°) and capacitive reactance (−90°) add as complex numbers, so a series RC's impedance is the right-triangle combination of R and X_C.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. II (AC), ch. 11 "Power Factor", section "True, Reactive, and Apparent power"
sources.note: Reactive loads dissipate zero true power even though they drop voltage and draw current; their volt-amps are reactive power (VAR), and true power comes only from the resistances.

drills.prompt: In what unit is reactance measured?

choices.feedback: Farads measure capacitance, a property of the part. Reactance is the ratio of AC voltage to AC current, so it is in ohms, like resistance.
Reactance depends on frequency, but it is a ratio of voltage to current: ohms.

drills.prompt: What is the reactance of a 1.0 µF capacitor at 1.0 kHz?

choices.feedback: That is 2πfC itself, 6.3 mS, the capacitor's susceptance. Reactance is its reciprocal: 1/(2π × 1000 Hz × 1.0 µF) ≈ 159 Ω.
1/(f·C) = 1.0 kΩ leaves out the 2π: X_C = 1/(2πfC) ≈ 159 Ω.
That is the reactance of 0.1 µF, a slip of ten in the capacitance. With 1.0 µF: 1/(2π × 1000 Hz × 1.0 µF) ≈ 159 Ω.

drills.prompt: A capacitor and an inductor each sit across a sine source. The frequency is raised tenfold at the same amplitude. Their currents:

choices.text: the capacitor's rises tenfold and the inductor's falls tenfold

choices.feedback: Only the capacitor's: X_C = 1/(2πfC) falls as f rises, but X_L = 2πfL rises, so the inductor's current falls.

choices.text: neither changes, since only resistance limits current
choices.feedback: Reactance limits AC current too, and it depends on frequency: X_C falls tenfold, X_L rises tenfold.

drills.prompt: An ideal capacitor carries 10 mA RMS with 5 V RMS across it. What average power does it dissipate?

choices.feedback: V·I gives the average power only when voltage and current are in phase. In a capacitor they are 90° apart: it takes energy in one quarter-cycle and returns it in the next.
There is no factor of a half that applies here: voltage and current are 90° apart, so the average power is zero.

glossary.definition: The total opposition of a circuit to alternating current, combining resistance and reactance; its magnitude |Z| is the ratio of AC voltage to AC current, in ohms. Resistance and reactance are 90° apart, so in series they combine like the sides of a right triangle: |Z| = √(R² + X²).

drills.prompt: A 30 Ω resistor is in series with a reactance of 40 Ω. What is the magnitude of the impedance?

choices.feedback: Adding them directly treats R and X as in phase. They are 90° apart, so |Z| = √(30² + 40²) = 50 Ω.
Reactance doesn't subtract from resistance; they combine at right angles: √(30² + 40²) = 50 Ω.

drills.prompt: A series RC is driven at the frequency where X_C equals R = 1.0 kΩ. What is |Z|?

choices.feedback: R and X_C are 90° apart and don't add directly: |Z| = √(1.0² + 1.0²) kΩ ≈ 1.41 kΩ.
An inductor's and a capacitor's reactances can cancel; a resistance and a reactance can't. They combine at right angles: about 1.41 kΩ.
The reactance adds to the resistance at right angles, so |Z| is more than R: √2 × 1.0 kΩ ≈ 1.41 kΩ.

drills.prompt: Which is true of impedance?

choices.text: Its magnitude can change with frequency, because it includes reactance.
It is another name for resistance.
choices.feedback: Resistance dissipates and doesn't depend on frequency. Impedance also includes reactance, which stores energy and changes with frequency.

choices.text: A series RC has less impedance than its resistance alone.
choices.feedback: The reactance combines with R at right angles: |Z| = √(R² + X²) is never less than R.

glossary.unit: ohm (Ω): the ratio of AC voltage amplitude to AC current amplitude, together with the phase angle between them
physics: In a circuit driven by a sine, every voltage and current is a sine of the same frequency, described by an amplitude and a phase. Impedance relates the two for a part or a network: |Z| = V_p/I_p, and its angle is how far the voltage leads the current. A resistor is R at 0°, a capacitor 1/(2πfC) at −90°, and an inductor 2πfL at +90°.

Written as a complex number, Z = R + jX, resistance is the part in phase with the current and reactance the part 90° out of phase. That is why they combine like the sides of a right triangle: in series, |Z| = √(R² + X²) at an angle φ = arctan(X/R). Impedances in series add as complex numbers, and in parallel combine as 1/Z = 1/Z₁ + 1/Z₂, so Ohm's law, dividers, and Thevenin equivalents all carry over to AC with Z in place of R.

Because reactance depends on frequency, impedance does too. 1 kΩ in series with 100 nF is almost a pure 1 kΩ at high frequencies, where X_C is small; 1.41 kΩ at −45° at 1.59 kHz, where X_C = R; and mostly capacitive below that, 3.34 kΩ at 500 Hz.
Only the resistive part dissipates power: P = I_rms²·R, or V_rms·I_rms·cos φ. The reactive part takes energy in during one quarter-cycle and returns it in the next.

confusions.title: Magnitudes don't add.
confusions.text: 1 kΩ of resistance in series with 1 kΩ of reactance is 1.41 kΩ, not 2 kΩ, because the two voltages peak a quarter-cycle apart.

confusions.title: Impedance belongs to a frequency.
confusions.text: A part has one resistance but a different impedance at every frequency: 100 nF is 15.9 kΩ at 100 Hz and 15.9 Ω at 100 kHz.

confusions.title: Power goes only into the resistance.
confusions.text: With 10 mA RMS through 1 kΩ and 100 nF in series at 1.59 kHz, the voltage across both is 14.1 V RMS, but the power is (10 mA)² × 1 kΩ = 100 mW, not 14.1 V × 10 mA = 141 mW.

confusions.title: Inductive and capacitive reactances subtract.
confusions.text: They have opposite signs. In series at 1.59 kHz, 10 mH (+100 Ω) and 1 µF (−100 Ω) add to zero reactance, and a 10 Ω resistor in series with both makes |Z| = 10 Ω.

glossary.uses: Input and output impedance of amplifiers and instruments (why a scope probe loads a circuit more at high frequencies), filter design, 50 Ω signal sources and cables, loudspeaker loads, and the AC divider that every RC or RL filter is.
glossary.bench: the impedance readout, which divides the voltage across a part by the current through it on an .ac run and shows |Z| and φ.

glossary.definition: How far one sine wave is shifted in time from another of the same frequency, given as an angle in which a full period is 360°. A capacitor's current leads its voltage by 90°, an inductor's lags by 90°, and a resistor's is in phase.

drills.prompt: Two 1 kHz sine waves reach their peaks 0.25 ms apart. What is the phase difference?

choices.feedback: Time must be converted to a fraction of the period. At 1 kHz the period is 1 ms, and 0.25 ms is a quarter of it: 90°.
At 1 kHz a period is 1 ms, so 0.25 ms is a quarter period, 360°/4 = 90°.
The period at 1 kHz is 1 ms; 0.25 ms is 25% of it, and 25% of 360° is 90°.

drills.prompt: An ideal capacitor is driven by a sine voltage. Its current:

choices.text: peaks a quarter cycle before the voltage does

choices.feedback: That is a resistor. A capacitor's current is C·dv/dt, largest where the voltage changes fastest, at the zero crossings, a quarter cycle before the voltage peak.

choices.text: peaks a quarter cycle after the voltage does
choices.feedback: That is an inductor, whose voltage is L·di/dt. A capacitor's current leads its voltage.

drills.prompt: An inverting amplifier with a gain of −2 amplifies a low-frequency sine. The output's phase relative to the input:

choices.text: 180°: it peaks when the input is at its lowest

choices.feedback: The amplifier multiplies by a negative number at every instant, which turns the wave upside down: 180°. A quarter-cycle shift needs a reactance.
A positive gain wouldn't. The minus sign flips the wave, a 180° shift.

glossary.unit: degree (°) or radian: one period is 360° = 2π rad, so a time shift Δt at frequency f is φ = 360°·f·Δt
physics: Two sines of the same frequency can differ only in amplitude and in where their peaks fall. The phase difference measures the second: a shift of Δt in a period T is φ = 360°·Δt/T. The wave whose peaks come first leads; the other lags.

Phase shifts come from parts that store energy. A capacitor's current is C·dv/dt, largest where its voltage changes fastest, at the zero crossings: a quarter-period before the voltage peaks, so the current leads the voltage by 90°. An inductor's voltage is L·di/dt, so its current lags its voltage by 90°. A resistor's current follows its voltage with no shift.
Mixing resistance and reactance gives shifts in between. An RC low-pass output lags its input by arctan(f/f_c): almost nothing well below the cutoff, 45° at f_c, and approaching 90° far above it.

A fixed time delay is a phase shift that grows with frequency: 1 µs is 0.36° at 1 kHz but 36° at 100 kHz. An inverting amplifier shifts every frequency by 180°, because it multiplies the signal by a negative number rather than delaying it.

figures.caption: 1 kΩ and 100 nF, f_c = 1.59 kHz: φ = −arctan(f/f_c)

confusions.title: Phase compares sines of one frequency.
confusions.text: Between a 1 kHz and a 1.1 kHz sine the "phase difference" drifts by 36° every millisecond, so it is not a property of the pair. A fixed phase needs a common frequency.

confusions.title: Leading is not predicting.
confusions.text: A capacitor's current leads its voltage in the steady state, after the sine has run for many cycles; no current flows before a voltage is applied. Lead and lag describe where the peaks fall, cycle after cycle.

confusions.title: Inversion is not a 180° delay.
confusions.text: On a 1 kHz sine, inverting and delaying by 0.5 ms give the same trace, and so they do on any wave whose second half is the negative of its first. On a 1 kHz square wave with 25% duty cycle they differ: inversion gives 75% duty, a delay keeps 25%.

confusions.title: Degrees are not a time.
confusions.text: 45° is 125 µs at 1 kHz and 1.25 µs at 100 kHz: Δt = φ/(360°·f).

glossary.uses: Comparing two scope channels, the 90° shift between current and voltage in capacitors and inductors, power factor in AC loads, the phase response of filters and amplifiers, and why an inverting stage flips a signal.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. II (AC), ch. 1 "Basic AC Theory", section "AC phase"
sources.note: Phase shift is how far two waves of the same frequency are out of step, given in degrees of a 360° cycle; the one ahead leads and the other lags; and phase is always relative to a chosen reference.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. II (AC), ch. 4 "Reactance and Impedance -- Capacitive", section "AC capacitor circuits"
sources.note: A capacitor's current is largest where its voltage crosses zero and zero at the voltage peaks, so its current leads its voltage by 90°.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. II (AC), ch. 3 "Reactance and Impedance -- Inductive", section "AC inductor circuits"
sources.note: An inductor's voltage is proportional to di/dt, so its current lags its voltage by 90°.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. II (AC), ch. 4 "Reactance and Impedance -- Capacitive", section "Series resistor-capacitor circuits"
sources.note: Mixing resistance and capacitance gives a phase angle between 0° and −90°, and a resistor's voltage stays in phase with its current.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Single-Stage BJT Amplifiers" (last update 22 September 2026), ch. 3 "Tutorial", section 3.6 "Amplifier gain comparisons" (p. 52)
sources.note: Only the common-emitter stage has a negative (inverting) voltage gain, which shifts the output 180° from the input; the common-collector and common-base stages do not invert.

glossary.definition: A circuit that passes frequencies below its cutoff and attenuates those above it. The simplest is a series resistor followed by a capacitor to ground: at high frequencies the capacitor's falling reactance shunts the signal away from the output.

drills.prompt: Which arrangement is an RC low-pass filter?

choices.text: A resistor in series from input to output, and a capacitor from the output to ground
A capacitor in series from input to output, and a resistor from the output to ground
choices.feedback: That is a high-pass: the series capacitor blocks DC and passes high frequencies.

choices.text: A capacitor straight across the source, with nothing in series
choices.feedback: With no series resistance an ideal source simply drives the capacitor: the output equals the input at every frequency. The filter needs R to take the high-frequency part of the signal.

drills.prompt: A first-order low-pass has its cutoff at 1 kHz. About how much of a 10 kHz sine gets through?

choices.text: About a tenth of it (−20 dB)
None of it, since it is above the cutoff
choices.feedback: A first-order filter rolls off at 20 dB per decade. One decade above f_c the gain is about f_c/f = 0.1, not zero.
That is the gain at f_c itself. At ten times f_c it is about f_c/f = 0.1.

drills.prompt: A 5 V square wave at 20 kHz drives an RC low-pass whose time constant is 100 times the period. The output is:

choices.text: a nearly steady level at the wave's average, with a small ripple
a copy of the square wave
choices.feedback: The square wave's fundamental is far above the cutoff, so the filter strips it and its harmonics; only the average, the DC part, passes.

choices.text: 0 V, since the filter blocks the 20 kHz signal
choices.feedback: It blocks the switching, not the average. DC sits below every cutoff, so the average level passes unchanged.

physics: A low-pass filter is a divider whose ratio depends on frequency. In the RC version the resistor is in series and the capacitor is across the output. At DC the capacitor draws no current, so R drops nothing and the output equals the input. As the frequency rises the capacitor's reactance falls, it takes more current, and more of the input drops across R.

The output stays near the input up to the cutoff, f_c = 1/(2πRC), is 70.7% (−3 dB) at f_c, and falls in proportion to 1/f above it: −20 dB per decade for one capacitor. An inductor in series with the load is a low-pass too, since its reactance rises with frequency. An LC filter, inductor in series and capacitor across the output, has two energy-storing parts and falls at −40 dB per decade: a second-order filter.

In time, the same circuit averages. A square wave or PWM signal whose period is much shorter than RC comes out as its average plus a small ripple, and a step comes out as an exponential rise with τ = RC.

A passive filter's cutoff and passband gain depend on what follows it, because a load draws current from the output. An active filter buffers the capacitor with an op amp, so the load no longer moves the cutoff, and it can add gain.

typical.what: 10 Ω and 10 µF on a supply pin
10 kΩ and 1 µF after 20 kHz PWM
typical.value: f_c = 15.9 Hz; the 20 kHz part cut to about 0.08% (−62 dB)
