confusions.title: It does not remove everything above f_c.
confusions.text: A first-order filter with f_c = 1.59 kHz passes a 15.9 kHz signal at 10%, −20 dB. A steeper cut needs a higher-order filter.

confusions.title: The capacitor goes across the output.
confusions.text: A series capacitor with a resistor to ground is a high-pass: it blocks DC. In a low-pass the capacitor sits from the output to ground, where its falling reactance shunts high frequencies away.

confusions.title: Smoothing PWM needs RC much longer than the period.
confusions.text: With 1 kΩ and 100 nF (τ = 100 µs, f_c = 1.59 kHz), 1 kHz PWM is barely smoothed: its 1 kHz fundamental passes at 85%. With 10 kΩ and 1 µF (f_c = 15.9 Hz), it passes at 1.6%.

confusions.title: A filter delays as well as attenuates.
confusions.text: A step through 1 kΩ and 100 nF takes 2.2RC = 220 µs to rise from 10% to 90%, and a sine at f_c comes out 45° late.

glossary.uses: Smoothing PWM into an analog voltage, anti-aliasing before an ADC, keeping switching noise off a supply or sensor line, audio tone controls and crossovers, and the LC output filter of a buck converter.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. II (AC), ch. 8 "Filters", section "Low-pass filters"
sources.note: A series resistor with a shunt capacitor, or a series inductor alone, passes low frequencies; the cutoff is where the output is 70.7% of the input, f = 1/(2πRC) for one R and one C; and a load resistance shifts the response, so the formula holds only unloaded.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Elementary Filter Circuits" (last update 5 October 2025), ch. 3 "Tutorial", section 3.3 "Reactive filtering" (p. 25)
sources.note: Treating a capacitor as an open at DC and a short at very high frequency, and an inductor the other way round, shows why a series-R or series-L network with a shunt C passes slow signals and blocks fast ones.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Elementary Filter Circuits" (last update 5 October 2025), ch. 3 "Tutorial", section 3.6 "Roll-off" (p. 33)
sources.note: Cascading two 20 dB/decade low-pass stages gives 40 dB/decade, and a series L with a shunt C rolls off more steeply than a series R with a shunt C.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Advanced Filter Circuits" (last update 20 April 2026), ch. 3 "Tutorial", section 3.10 "Active filters" (p. 71)
sources.note: An active filter can have gain; its amplifier drives the load, so the load no longer shifts the cutoff; it works only while the amplifier's bandwidth is well above the signal's; and the single-capacitor topologies shown are first order.

glossary.definition: An integrated differential amplifier whose output is a very large open-loop gain, often 100 000 or more, times the difference between its two inputs. That gain is too large and too variable to use directly, so circuits set their gain with negative feedback through resistors.

drills.prompt: An op amp with negative feedback works in its linear range. Which is true?

choices.text: The output moves until the two inputs are at almost the same voltage.
Its two inputs are joined inside the chip.
choices.feedback: Nothing inside joins them, and they draw almost no current. Their equal voltages are the result of feedback, which is why the rule fails without it.

choices.text: Its inputs draw whatever current the circuit needs.
choices.feedback: An ideal op amp's inputs draw no current; real ones draw picoamps to nanoamps.

drills.prompt: An op amp on ±12 V supplies has no feedback, an open-loop gain of 200 000, V+ = 2.010 V, and V− = 2.000 V (ignore input offset). Its output sits:

choices.text: near the positive rail, a little below +12 V

choices.feedback: 10 mV × 200 000 asks for 2000 V, but the output can't go beyond its supplies; it stops near +12 V.
10 mV is the input difference. With no feedback, the whole open-loop gain multiplies it.

choices.text: at 0 V, since the inputs are almost equal
choices.feedback: The inputs are held equal only by negative feedback. Without it, 10 mV of difference drives the output to a rail.

drills.prompt: A voltage follower ties an op amp's output to its − input and feeds the signal to its + input. Why is V_out = V_in?

choices.text: Feedback drives the output until V− equals V+, and V− is the output itself.

choices.feedback: Its open-loop gain is huge. Feedback sets the closed-loop gain to 1.

choices.text: The input is wired straight through to the output.
choices.feedback: The output comes from the supplies through the op amp's output stage. That is why a follower can drive a load the signal source couldn't.

glossary.unit: the open-loop gain is a ratio (V/V), often quoted in dB (100 000 is 100 dB) or as V/mV on datasheets (100 V/mV is 100 000)
physics: An op amp amplifies the difference between its non-inverting (+) and inverting (−) inputs: V_out = A_OL·(V+ − V−), within the limits its supply allows. A_OL is huge, typically 10⁵ to 10⁶ at DC: with A_OL = 100 000 on ±15 V supplies, a difference of only 130 µV is enough to drive the output to about 13 V, where it stops.

That gain is useless as it stands: it varies several times over between parts, with temperature, and with frequency. So an op amp is almost always used with negative feedback, a resistor network that returns part of the output to the − input. The op amp then drives its output to whatever voltage makes V− equal V+ to within microvolts, and the circuit's gain is set by the resistor ratio, not by A_OL.

Two working rules follow, for an op amp with negative feedback inside its output limits: the inputs draw almost no current (nanoamps for bipolar inputs, picoamps for FET inputs), and the voltage between them is almost zero. Without feedback the second rule fails, and the op amp acts as a comparator: its output sits at one limit or the other.

Real op amps fall short in ways a datasheet quantifies. The output stops short of the supply rails unless it is rail-to-rail; the open-loop gain falls with frequency (the gain-bandwidth product); the output can change only so fast (the slew rate); and a small input offset voltage, microvolts to a few millivolts, is amplified along with the signal.

typical.what: output swing on ±15 V, bipolar output stage

figures.title: Open-loop transfer curve
figures.caption: no feedback, A_OL = 100 000, output limits ±13 V on ±15 V supplies: the whole linear range spans ±130 µV of input

confusions.title: V+ = V− is a result of feedback, not a property of the chip.
confusions.text: It holds only while negative feedback works and the output is inside its limits. Open loop, a 1 mV difference drives the output to its limit; with feedback, a saturated output lets the inputs drift apart.

confusions.title: The output current comes from the supply pins.
confusions.text: A follower putting 10 V across a 1 kΩ load delivers 10 mA, yet draws only nanoamps from the signal source. The 10 mA flows in through the op amp's positive supply pin.

confusions.title: The output does not reach the rails unless it is rail-to-rail.
confusions.text: A bipolar-output part on ±15 V swings to about ±13 V. A circuit that needs 14 V from it, or 4.9 V on a single 5 V supply, needs a rail-to-rail-output op amp, and even that stops tens of millivolts short under load.

confusions.title: A_OL is not the circuit's gain.
confusions.text: A non-inverting stage with R_f = 9.1 kΩ and R_g = 1 kΩ has a gain of 1 + 9.1 = 10.1 whether A_OL is 100 000 or 1 000 000: the two give 10.099 and 10.100.

glossary.uses: Amplifiers, active filters, buffers between a high-impedance source and a load, summing and difference amplifiers for sensors, precision current sources such as LED drivers, integrators, and, without feedback, comparators.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 8 "Operational Amplifiers", section "The "operational" amplifier"
sources.note: An op amp is a differential amplifier with a voltage gain of 200 000 or more, so with no feedback a differential input of tens of microvolts saturates its output, which is how it works as a comparator; the 741's inputs draw at most about half a microamp, and FET-input parts far less.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 8 "Operational Amplifiers", section "Negative feedback"
sources.note: Feedback to the inverting input drives the input difference to practically zero; the output current comes from the op amp's supply, not the signal source; and the output swings only to its saturation voltages, about +14 V and −13 V for a 741 on ±15 V, while FET-output parts such as the 3130 come within millivolts of the rails.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Operational Amplifiers" (last update 23 September 2026), ch. 3 "Tutorial", section 3.6 "Negative feedback" (p. 42)
sources.note: With the output fed back to the − input, V_out = A_V(V_in − V_out), so the closed-loop gain A_V/(A_V + 1) is almost exactly 1 and hardly changes when A_V falls tenfold; the output swings only within the supply rails.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Operational Amplifiers" (last update 23 September 2026), ch. 5 "Derivations and Technical References", section 5.7.3 "Input bias current" (p. 184); ch. 3 "Tutorial", section 3.12 "Differential amplification", footnote 10 (p. 69)
sources.note: Inputs are normally analyzed as drawing no current, while real inputs take a small bias current: tens of nanoamps for a 741, nanoamps for bipolar inputs and picoamps for FET inputs.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 8 "Operational Amplifiers", section "Offset voltage"
sources.note: Input offset voltage is modeled as a small source in series with one input of an otherwise perfect op amp, which accounts for a nonzero (often saturated) output with the inputs tied together.

glossary.definition: Returning part of an amplifier's output so that it subtracts from the input, which makes any error at the output partly cancel itself. With enough open-loop gain, the closed-loop gain is set by the feedback network, usually resistors, rather than by the amplifier.

drills.prompt: Which connection gives an op amp negative feedback?

choices.text: A resistor from the output to the inverting (−) input
A resistor from the output to the non-inverting (+) input
choices.feedback: That is positive feedback: a rise at the output raises V+, which pushes the output further up. It makes a Schmitt trigger, not an amplifier.

choices.text: A resistor from the output to ground
choices.feedback: That is a load; nothing returns to an input.

drills.prompt: A non-inverting stage with resistors for a gain of 10 is built with op amps whose open-loop gain ranges from 100 000 to 300 000. The stage's gain:

choices.text: is within about 0.01% of 10 for all of them
ranges over a factor of three, like the op amps
choices.feedback: Feedback makes the gain about 1/β = 10; the open-loop gain A only sets the small error: 10/(1 + 10/A) = 9.999 at A = 100 000.
That is the open-loop gain, with no feedback. The resistors set the closed-loop gain to 10.

drills.prompt: What does an amplifier give up when negative feedback makes its gain stable and predictable?

choices.text: Gain: the closed-loop gain is far below the open-loop gain.
Supply voltage: feedback needs a higher supply.
choices.feedback: Feedback costs no supply voltage. It gives up excess gain in return for accuracy, bandwidth, and lower distortion.

choices.text: Bandwidth: the closed-loop stage is slower than the open-loop amplifier.
choices.feedback: The other way around. Trading gain for feedback widens the bandwidth: about GBW divided by the noise gain, far beyond the open-loop corner.

glossary.unit: the feedback fraction β is a ratio (V/V) from 0 to 1; the loop gain A·β is a ratio too
physics: With negative feedback, an amplifier compares its output with its input. A fraction β of the output, set by a divider, is subtracted from the input, and only the difference is amplified: V_out = A·(V_in − β·V_out). Solving for the ratio gives the closed-loop gain, G = A/(1 + Aβ).

When the loop gain Aβ is large, G ≈ 1/β: the gain depends only on the divider. With A = 100 000 and β = 0.1, G = 100 000/10 001 = 9.9990; halve A to 50 000 and G = 9.9980. A 50% change in the amplifier moves the gain by 0.01%. Feedback trades raw gain, which is cheap, for gain that is precise and stable.

The mechanism is self-correction. If the output is too high, β·V_out rises, the difference at the input falls, and the output is pulled back. Any error that arises inside the amplifier, from nonlinearity, temperature, or the load, is reduced by the factor 1 + Aβ. The same factor lowers the output impedance and widens the bandwidth.

The correction works only while the loop is closed: while the output is inside its limits and the amplifier is fast enough to follow. Feedback to the + input does the opposite. It reinforces any change, drives the output to a limit, and gives hysteresis: that is positive feedback.

figures.title: Closed-loop gain against amplifier gain
figures.caption: β = 0.1: G = A/(1 + Aβ) approaches 1/β = 10 once A is large; A on a log scale

confusions.title: Lowering the gain is the point.
confusions.text: An op amp with A = 100 000 used at G = 10 gives up a factor of 10 000 in gain. That surplus is what holds the gain to 1/β within 0.01%.

confusions.title: The input it goes to decides the sign.
confusions.text: Output to the − input through a divider is negative feedback; to the + input it is positive. Swap the inputs of a working amplifier and it latches at one limit.

confusions.title: 1/β is not always the signal gain.
confusions.text: In an inverting amplifier with R_in = 10 kΩ and R_f = 100 kΩ, β = R_in/(R_in + R_f) and 1/β = 11, while the signal gain is −R_f/R_in = −10. The 11 is the noise gain, which sets the bandwidth.

confusions.title: Feedback can't fix a saturated output.
confusions.text: At G = 10 on ±15 V supplies, 2 V in asks for 20 V out. The output stops near 13 V, the loop no longer controls anything, and V− stops following V+.

confusions.title: This β is not a BJT's current gain.
confusions.text: Here β is the feedback fraction, a divider ratio from 0 to 1: β = 0.1 for a gain of 10. A BJT's β is its current gain, I_C/I_B, typically 100 or more. The two share a letter and nothing else.

glossary.uses: Every op-amp amplifier, the error amplifier of a voltage regulator, the emitter resistor that steadies a BJT's bias, LED and motor current control, and any loop that holds a quantity at a set point.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 8 "Operational Amplifiers", section "Negative feedback"
sources.note: Feeding the output back to the inverting input drives the input difference to practically zero and makes a self-stabilizing system; the exact open-loop gain hardly matters as long as it is very large; and this holds only inside the output's swing limits.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Operational Amplifiers" (last update 23 September 2026), ch. 3 "Tutorial", section 3.6 "Negative feedback" (p. 42)
sources.note: Solving V_out = A_V(V_in − V_out) gives a closed-loop gain of A_V/(A_V + 1): 0.999999 at A_V = 10⁶ and 0.99999 at 10⁵, so feedback makes the circuit's gain stable against changes in the amplifier, from part variation, temperature, or supply.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Operational Amplifiers" (last update 23 September 2026), ch. 3 "Tutorial", section 3.10 "Inverting and noninverting amplification" (p. 54)
sources.note: The closed-loop gain is the reciprocal of the feedback divider ratio, (RA + RB)/RB = 1 + RA/RB, found with zero input current and zero differential voltage.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 4 "Bipolar Junction Transistors", section "Biasing calculations", subsection "Emitter-bias"
sources.note: An emitter resistor gives negative feedback (degeneration): a rise in emitter current raises its drop, which reduces the base drive and pulls the current back, so the bias depends less on temperature, tolerances, and β.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 8 "Operational Amplifiers", section "Positive feedback"
sources.note: Feeding the output back to the + input instead latches the output at one limit and gives hysteresis, while negative feedback creates an equilibrium.

glossary.definition: The inverting input of an op amp whose non-inverting input is grounded, held at almost exactly 0 V by negative feedback although nothing connects it to ground. It draws no current itself, so all the current arriving through the input resistor continues through the feedback resistor.

drills.prompt: An inverting amplifier has R_in = 10 kΩ and V_in = 2.0 V. What current flows through R_in?

choices.text: 0 mA, since op-amp inputs draw no current
choices.feedback: The input pin takes none, but R_in does carry current: its far end sits at the virtual ground, 0 V, so (2.0 V − 0 V)/10 kΩ = 0.20 mA flows on into R_f.
The virtual ground fixes R_in's inner end at 0 V whatever R_f is, so the current is 2.0 V / 10 kΩ = 0.20 mA. R_f sets the output instead.

drills.prompt: You probe the inverting input of a working inverting amplifier with an oscilloscope. You see:

choices.text: almost nothing: microvolts to a few millivolts
a copy of the input signal
choices.feedback: Feedback holds that node at the + input's voltage, 0 V; the input signal appears across R_in instead.
The output appears across R_f. The inverting input sits at the virtual ground, about 0 V.

drills.prompt: Why is it called a virtual ground rather than a ground?

choices.text: Its 0 V is held by feedback, not by a connection, and it vanishes if the output saturates.
It connects to ground through a high resistance inside the op amp.
choices.feedback: There is no internal path to ground; the op amp's inputs draw almost no current. The 0 V comes from the output adjusting itself.

choices.text: It is ground for AC signals only.
choices.feedback: It holds 0 V for DC and AC alike, as long as feedback works. It is virtual because no wire makes it so.

glossary.unit: volt (V): the inverting input sits the output voltage divided by the open-loop gain away from ground, microvolts in practice
physics: In an inverting amplifier the + input is grounded, the signal reaches the − input through R_in, and R_f feeds the output back to it. If the − input rose above 0 V, the output would swing negative and pull it back down through R_f; if it fell below, the output would swing positive. The output settles where V− is almost exactly 0 V.

How close it gets follows from the gain: V_out = −A_OL·V−, so V− = −V_out/A_OL. For −10 V out with A_OL = 100 000, V− = 100 µV. It measures as ground, but nothing connects it to ground, and it stays there only through feedback: a virtual ground.

So the input current is set by R_in alone: I = V_in/R_in. The op amp's input takes only its bias current, nanoamps, so all of that current continues through R_f, and V_out = −I·R_f = −V_in·R_f/R_in. The source sees an input resistance of R_in. Several inputs, each through its own resistor, can feed the node without affecting each other, which is how a summing amplifier mixes signals.
The virtual ground holds only while feedback works. If the output saturates, or the signal is so fast that A_OL has fallen to a small value, V− moves away from 0 V and the rules built on it fail.

typical.what: V− for −10 V out, A_OL = 1000 (at a high frequency)

typical.value: 100 µA, all of it through R_f

typical.what: input resistance of an inverting stage
current into the op amp's − input

confusions.title: It is not connected to ground.
confusions.text: Wire the − input to ground and the 100 µA from R_in flows into that wire instead of through R_f. The output then no longer depends on the input: with 0 V between its inputs, it drifts to a limit on the op amp's offset voltage.

confusions.title: It takes no current.
confusions.text: Its potential is 0 V, but it is not a path to ground: the input pin draws only nanoamps, so the 100 µA through R_in all continues through R_f, making V_out = −100 µA × 100 kΩ = −10 V.

confusions.title: A non-inverting amplifier has no virtual ground.
confusions.text: There the signal is on the + input, and feedback makes V− follow it: with 1 V in, both inputs sit at 1 V. The inputs are equal, not grounded.

confusions.title: It fails when the output saturates.

glossary.definition: The ratio of a circuit's output signal to its input signal, such as V_out/V_in for voltage gain; a negative gain means the output is inverted. It is often given in decibels, 20·log₁₀ of the voltage ratio.

drills.prompt: A non-inverting amplifier has R_f = 47 kΩ and R_g = 4.7 kΩ. What is its voltage gain?

choices.feedback: R_f/R_g = 10 is the inverting stage's gain. A non-inverting stage gives 1 + R_f/R_g = 11, because its output must also lift the − input up to V_in.
That is the inverting configuration. Fed at the + input, the output is in phase: 1 + 47/4.7 = 11.

drills.prompt: What unit does a voltage gain carry?

choices.feedback: A gain compares an output voltage with an input voltage; the volts cancel.
Volts per ampere would be ohms. A voltage gain is volts per volt, a pure number.

drills.prompt: A voltage follower has a voltage gain of 1. Which is true?

choices.text: It can still deliver far more power than the source, from its own supply.

choices.feedback: Its input draws almost nothing while its output can supply tens of milliamps, so it keeps a weak source from being loaded.

choices.text: Its gain in decibels is 1 dB.
choices.feedback: 20·log₁₀(1) = 0 dB. A gain of 1 is 0 dB.

glossary.unit: a ratio (V/V for voltage gain), so unitless; or decibels, 20·log₁₀ of the voltage ratio
physics: Gain compares an output with the input that caused it: A_v = V_out/V_in for voltage, and likewise for current or power. The energy for a larger output comes from the power supply; the input only controls how much of it reaches the load. A circuit of resistors, capacitors, and inductors alone can never deliver more power than it receives.

The sign carries the polarity. An inverting amplifier with R_in = 10 kΩ and R_f = 100 kΩ has A_v = −R_f/R_in = −10: 0.5 V in gives −5 V out. A non-inverting amplifier with R_g = 10 kΩ from the − input to ground and the same R_f has A_v = 1 + R_f/R_g = 11 and keeps the polarity. A magnitude below 1 is attenuation: a divider of 10 kΩ and 10 kΩ has A_v = 0.5.

In decibels, a voltage gain is 20·log₁₀|A_v|: 10 is 20 dB and 0.5 is −6.02 dB. The sign does not appear in decibels; an inversion shows as a 180° phase shift instead. Stages in a chain multiply their gains, so their decibels add, provided each stage's gain is worked out with the next stage as its load.

Gain is not one number for every signal. It falls at high frequencies (the gain-bandwidth product), and it stops at the output's limits: with a gain of −10 on ±15 V supplies, any input beyond about ±1.3 V is clipped at about ∓13 V.

typical.what: common-emitter stage, R_C = 4.7 kΩ, unbypassed R_E = 1 kΩ

glossary.definition: For an internally compensated op amp, the closed-loop gain times the bandwidth stays about constant, equal to the frequency where the open-loop gain has fallen to 1. A stage with noise gain G therefore has a bandwidth of about GBW/G.

drills.prompt: An op amp with a 1 MHz gain-bandwidth product is used in a non-inverting stage with a gain of 20. About what bandwidth does it have?

choices.feedback: That multiplies the GBW by the gain. Gain and bandwidth trade against each other, so bandwidth ≈ GBW/gain = 1 MHz / 20 = 50 kHz.
That is the bandwidth at a gain of 1, as a follower. At a gain of 20 it is 1 MHz / 20 = 50 kHz.

drills.prompt: A design needs a non-inverting gain of 100 with 50 kHz of bandwidth. What gain-bandwidth product must the op amp have, at least?

choices.feedback: That would do only at a gain of 1. Gain × bandwidth = 100 × 50 kHz = 5 MHz.
That divides instead of multiplying: the product is 100 × 50 kHz = 5 MHz.

drills.prompt: A gain of 100 is needed from op amps with a 1 MHz GBW. Compared with one stage of 100, two stages of 10 in cascade give:

choices.text: much more bandwidth: about 64 kHz instead of 10 kHz
the same bandwidth, because the GBW is fixed
choices.feedback: The GBW is per op amp, and two stages use two. Each stage of 10 reaches 100 kHz; together about 64 kHz, against 10 kHz for one stage of 100.

choices.text: less bandwidth, because each stage adds its own roll-off
choices.feedback: Each stage does roll off, but at 100 kHz instead of 10 kHz; the pair is down 3 dB at about 64 kHz, still far above 10 kHz.

drills.prompt: Does the bandwidth set by the GBW depend on the signal's amplitude?

choices.text: No: it is a small-signal limit; the slew rate is the limit that depends on amplitude.
Yes: larger signals get less bandwidth.
choices.feedback: That describes slew-rate limiting, a separate effect. The GBW limit applies the same way to any small signal.

choices.text: Yes: larger signals get more bandwidth.
choices.feedback: Amplitude doesn't widen any op-amp limit. The GBW limit is the same for any small signal; slew rate cuts large ones further.

glossary.unit: hertz (Hz): a gain (V/V) times a frequency
physics: An internally compensated op amp contains a small capacitor that makes its open-loop gain start falling at a low frequency, often a few hertz, and keep falling at 20 dB per decade. Along that slope A_OL × f is constant, and equals the frequency where A_OL has fallen to 1: the gain-bandwidth product. An op amp with GBW = 1 MHz has an open-loop gain of 1000 at 1 kHz and 10 at 100 kHz.

Negative feedback holds the closed-loop gain G only while A_OL is well above G. A stage keeps its gain up to roughly the frequency where the open-loop curve comes down to meet it, then follows that curve down. Its −3 dB bandwidth is therefore f = GBW/G: 100 kHz at G = 10 on a 1 MHz part, and 10 kHz at G = 100.

The G in that formula is the noise gain, 1/β = 1 + R_f/R_in, not the signal gain. In a non-inverting stage the two are equal. An inverting stage with a gain of −1 has a noise gain of 2, so its bandwidth is GBW/2.

The compensation capacitor is there for stability: rolling the gain off early, from a single dominant corner, keeps the op amp's phase shift from reaching 180° while its gain is still above 1, so even a follower, with all of its output fed back, does not oscillate.

typical.what: inverting gain of −1 (noise gain 2) on a 1 MHz part

figures.caption: A_OL = 200 000 (106 dB) falling from 5 Hz, so GBW = 200 000 × 5 Hz = 1 MHz; a stage with G = 10 (20 dB) is flat to 100 kHz

confusions.title: The bandwidth is where the gain is already 3 dB down.
confusions.text: A G = 10 stage on a 1 MHz part gives 7.07 at 100 kHz. To stay within 1% of 10, the signal must stay below about 14 kHz.

confusions.title: Use the noise gain, not the signal gain.
confusions.text: An inverting stage with a gain of −1 has 1/β = 2, so a 1 MHz part gives it 500 kHz, not 1 MHz.

confusions.title: Two stages beat one.
confusions.text: A gain of 100 in one stage on a 1 MHz part has 10 kHz of bandwidth. Two stages of 10 have 100 kHz each, and together about 64 kHz: 100 kHz × √(√2 − 1).

confusions.title: GBW is not the slew rate.
confusions.text: The GBW sets one bandwidth for every amplitude; the slew rate limits how fast a large output can move. A 1 MHz, 0.5 V/µs part at G = 1 passes a 100 kHz sine of 0.5 V peak cleanly, but a 10 V peak sine slews above about 8 kHz.

glossary.uses: Choosing an op amp for a signal's gain and bandwidth, splitting a high gain across stages, checking that an active filter's amplifier is fast enough, and reading the open-loop gain plot on a datasheet.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Amplifier Performance" (last update 27 September 2026), ch. 2 "Tutorial", section 2.6 "Bandwidth" (p. 24)
sources.note: The gain-bandwidth product is the measured gain times the test frequency, roughly constant over a wide range, so a GBW of 1.2 million means a gain of 1 at 1.2 MHz; no amplifier can have both arbitrarily high gain and arbitrarily wide bandwidth.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Lessons in Electric Circuits, Vol. III (Semiconductors), ch. 8 "Operational Amplifiers", section "Frequency response"
sources.note: An internally compensated op amp such as the 741 has a built-in capacitor that makes its differential gain fall as frequency rises, and that falling gain limits the usable bandwidth of a feedback circuit.

sources.cite: Tony R. Kuphaldt, Modular Electronics Learning (ModEL), module "Operational Amplifiers" (last update 23 September 2026), ch. 5 "Derivations and Technical References", section 5.7.5 "Frequency compensation" (p. 189)
sources.note: Op amps are compensated by deliberately reducing open-loop gain as frequency rises, so that the fed-back signal's gain is below 1 at the frequency where the loop's phase shift would reach 360°; most do it with an internal capacitor.

glossary.definition: The fastest rate at which an amplifier's output voltage can change, usually given in V/µs. A sine of peak V_p and frequency f needs a slope of 2πf·V_p at its zero crossings, and when that exceeds the slew rate it is distorted toward a triangle.

drills.prompt: Which unit is a slew rate given in?

choices.feedback: Frequency enters through the sine's slope, but the slew rate itself is a rate of change of voltage: volts per microsecond.
Volts per volt is a gain. A slew rate is volts per unit time.
A time alone is a rise time. The slew rate is how many volts the output moves per microsecond.

drills.prompt: An op amp slews at 0.5 V/µs and must deliver a sine of 10 V peak. About what is the highest clean frequency?

choices.feedback: 0.5 V/µs divided by 10 V is 50 000 per second, but a sine's steepest slope is 2πf·V_p, not f·V_p: divide by 2π, about 8.0 kHz.
That uses the 20 V peak-to-peak swing. The steepest slope is 2πf·V_p with the peak, 10 V: f = 500 000 V/s / (2π × 10 V) ≈ 8.0 kHz.

drills.prompt: A sine is slew limited at the output. You halve its amplitude at the same frequency. What happens?

choices.text: It may come out clean: the slope it needs has halved.
Nothing changes: bandwidth limits don't depend on amplitude.
choices.feedback: That holds for the GBW limit. The slew rate limits slope, 2πf·V_p, which halves with the amplitude.
A smaller swing needs a smaller slope, 2πf·V_p, so the output is less likely to hit the slew limit.

glossary.unit: volts per microsecond (V/µs); 1 V/µs = 10⁶ V/s
physics: Inside an op amp, a stage that can deliver only a limited current drives the compensation capacitor, and a capacitor's voltage can change only as fast as i = C·dv/dt allows. With at most I_max available, the output can change no faster than SR = I_max/C. When the input asks for more, the output becomes a straight ramp at the slew rate until it catches up.

A sine of peak V_p at frequency f, v = V_p·sin(2πft), is steepest at its zero crossings, where its slope is 2πf·V_p. It passes undistorted only while 2πf·V_p ≤ SR. Above that, the sine is bent toward a triangle whose sides have slope SR, and its amplitude falls. The highest frequency at which a sine of a given amplitude passes whole, f = SR/(2πV_p), is the full-power bandwidth.

Slew rate is a large-signal limit: it depends on the output's amplitude, not on the gain. A 0.5 V/µs op amp passes a 1 V peak sine up to 79.6 kHz but a 10 V peak sine only up to 7.96 kHz. The gain-bandwidth product, in contrast, sets a bandwidth that is the same at every amplitude.

typical.what: needed by a 10 V peak sine at 20 kHz
a 0 V to 10 V step at 0.5 V/µs

confusions.title: Small signals rarely slew.
confusions.text: A 741-class op amp (0.5 V/µs, 1 MHz) could pass a 100 mV peak sine up to 796 kHz as far as slewing goes. At a gain of 10 its gain-bandwidth product already ends the bandwidth at 100 kHz, so for small signals the GBW is the limit that bites.

confusions.title: Slewing is not clipping.
confusions.text: Clipping flattens the peaks at the output's limits. Slewing bends the sine into a triangle with straight sides of slope SR and shrinks it, with its peaks still well inside the limits.

confusions.title: The 2π matters.
confusions.text: A 10 V peak sine at 20 kHz needs 2π × 20 kHz × 10 V = 1.26 V/µs, not 20 kHz × 10 V = 0.2 V/µs. A 0.5 V/µs op amp can't deliver it.

confusions.title: Lowering the gain does not raise the slew rate.
confusions.text: The output's dv/dt limit is the same at a gain of 1 or 100. Less gain helps only by making the output smaller.

glossary.definition: A circuit, often an op amp with no negative feedback or a dedicated comparator chip, whose output switches to one of two levels depending on which input is higher. It turns an analog voltage into a logic decision at a threshold.

drills.prompt: A comparator powered from 0 V and 5 V has 2.5 V from a divider on its + input and a sensor on its − input. The sensor reads 3.1 V. The output is:

choices.feedback: The output goes high when V+ is above V−. Here the sensor on the − input is higher, so the output goes low.
With no feedback the output doesn't follow the input; it goes to one level or the other. V− > V+ sends it low.

drills.prompt: Which is true of an op amp used as a comparator?

choices.text: Its inputs can sit far apart: the equal-inputs rule needs negative feedback.
Its inputs are held equal, as in an amplifier.
choices.feedback: Only negative feedback holds them equal. Without it, they sit wherever the circuit puts them, and the output reports which is higher.

choices.text: Its output is proportional to the input difference.
choices.feedback: Only within microvolts of the switching point. Beyond that the huge open-loop gain sends the output to a rail.

drills.prompt: A comparator's reference comes from a divider across 5.0 V: 30 kΩ on top, 20 kΩ to ground. At what input voltage does it switch?

choices.feedback: That is the drop across the top resistor. The reference is across the bottom one: 5.0 V × 20/(30 + 20) = 2.0 V.
5.0 × 20/30 uses the ratio of the two resistors. The divider fraction is R2 over the total: 20/50, so 2.0 V.

physics: A comparator answers one question: is V+ above V−? Its output goes to its high level if so and to its low level if not. Inside it is a differential amplifier with very high gain and no feedback, so with a gain of 100 000 a difference of 50 µV is enough to move a 5 V output all the way.

A reference on one input sets the threshold. With 2.5 V from a divider on V− and a sensor on V+, the output goes high whenever the sensor is above 2.5 V. Swapping the inputs inverts the output; the threshold stays at 2.5 V.

A dedicated comparator is built to switch: it leaves either output state quickly, and many have an open-collector output that can only pull down, so a pull-up resistor to the logic supply sets the high level. An op amp also works as a comparator, but it is designed for feedback and is slow to recover from sitting at its limits.

A slow, noisy input causes trouble. Near the threshold the noise carries the input back and forth across it, and the output switches each time: it chatters. Hysteresis, added with positive feedback, cures it.

typical.what: input difference to swing a 5 V output at a gain of 100 000
threshold from a 10 kΩ/10 kΩ divider on 5 V

confusions.title: An op amp used as a comparator has no virtual ground.
confusions.text: Without negative feedback nothing makes V− equal V+. The inputs can sit volts apart; the output simply reports which is higher.

confusions.title: An open-collector output needs a pull-up.
confusions.text: Without one the output can only pull low. When it should be high it floats, and a logic input reads no defined level.

confusions.title: One threshold chatters on a slow, noisy input.
confusions.text: A 0.1 V/ms ramp carrying 100 mV of noise stays within 100 mV of the threshold for 2 ms, and the output can switch at any moment during it. Two thresholds more than 200 mV apart stop it.

confusions.title: Swapping the inputs inverts the output, not the threshold.
confusions.text: With the sensor on V− and 2.5 V on V+, the output goes low, not high, when the sensor rises above 2.5 V; the switching point is still 2.5 V.

sources.note: A noisy input near the threshold makes a plain comparator's output chatter at the noise frequency, and positive feedback through a large resistor to the + input gives two thresholds that stop it.

glossary.definition: A difference between the input level that switches a circuit one way and the level that switches it back. In a Schmitt trigger, positive feedback creates the two thresholds, so noise smaller than the gap between them can't make the output chatter.

drills.prompt: Why doesn't a Schmitt trigger chatter on a slow, noisy input?

choices.text: Once it switches, its threshold jumps away from the input, so noise must cross the whole gap to switch it back.
A capacitor inside it filters the noise out.
choices.feedback: No capacitor is needed. The two thresholds, made by positive feedback, do the work.

choices.text: Its output switches more slowly than a comparator's.
choices.feedback: It switches just as fast; it switches once, because the second threshold is out of the noise's reach.

drills.prompt: A Schmitt trigger switches high when its input rises past 2.6 V and low when it falls past 2.4 V. The input carries 50 mV peak-to-peak of noise. Does it chatter at a crossing?

choices.text: No: the 0.2 V gap is wider than the noise
Yes: any noise near a threshold causes chatter
choices.feedback: That is true for a plain comparator, with one threshold. Here the input must fall 0.2 V to switch back, and 50 mV of noise can't do that.

choices.text: Only if the noise exceeds 2.4 V
choices.feedback: What matters is the gap between the thresholds, 2.6 − 2.4 = 0.2 V, against the 50 mV of noise. The gap is larger, so the output doesn't chatter.

drills.prompt: Which connection gives a comparator hysteresis?

choices.text: Positive feedback: a resistor from the output to the + input
Negative feedback: a resistor from the output to the − input
choices.feedback: That makes a linear amplifier; the output no longer snaps between two levels.

choices.text: A capacitor between the two inputs
choices.feedback: That only slows the input. Hysteresis needs the output to move the threshold, through positive feedback.

glossary.unit: volt (V): the gap between the upper and lower thresholds
physics: A Schmitt trigger is a comparator with positive feedback: a resistor from its output to its + input. The output's state then moves the threshold. While the output is low, the + input is pulled down, and the input must rise further to switch it; once the output is high, the + input is pulled up, and the input must fall further to switch it back.

In the figure, the output swings from 0 to 5 V, R1 = 10 kΩ runs from the input to the + input, R2 = 100 kΩ from the output, and the − input sits at 2.5 V. With the output low, the + input is V_in·R2/(R1 + R2), which reaches 2.5 V at V_in = 2.5 V × 110/100 = 2.75 V. With the output high, it is V_in + (5 V − V_in)·R1/(R1 + R2), which falls to 2.5 V at V_in = 2.25 V. The hysteresis is 0.5 V, which is 5 V × R1/R2.

Noise smaller than that gap can't make the output chatter: once the input has crossed 2.75 V going up, it must fall all the way to 2.25 V to switch it back. The positive feedback also sharpens the edge, since a change in the output pushes the + input further past the threshold and the switch completes itself.
The word comes from magnetism. A magnetic core's magnetization also depends on its history, and the energy lost going around that loop each cycle is part of a transformer's core loss.

confusions.text: The feedback resistor goes to the + input. Taken to the − input instead, it makes a linear amplifier with no thresholds at all.

confusions.title: The thresholds need not straddle the reference evenly.
confusions.text: In the same circuit with a 1 V reference, the thresholds are 1.1 V and 0.6 V: the gap is still 0.5 V, but it is not centered on 1 V.

confusions.title: Too much hysteresis is a fault too.
confusions.text: The gap must be wider than the noise but narrower than the signal's swing. With thresholds at 2.25 V and 2.75 V, a sensor that only moves between 2.4 V and 2.6 V never switches the output.

confusions.title: It does not clean the signal.
confusions.text: It stops the output from responding to noise smaller than the gap. The input is unchanged, and noise larger than 0.5 V peak to peak still causes extra switching.

glossary.definition: A two-terminal part, usually a PN junction, that conducts readily when its anode is more positive than its cathode and blocks current the other way. A conducting silicon diode drops about 0.6–0.7 V over a wide range of current.

drills.prompt: Which way does a diode conduct, judged from its symbol?

choices.text: Along the triangle's point, from anode to cathode, toward the bar
Toward the triangle's flat side, from cathode to anode
choices.feedback: The triangle points the way conventional current flows: anode to cathode. The bar marks the cathode.

choices.text: Either way, depending on the voltage
choices.feedback: In normal use it conducts only from anode to cathode; reverse current flows only in breakdown, which a Zener uses on purpose.

drills.prompt: A silicon diode in series with 1.0 kΩ is forward biased by a 5.0 V supply. About what current flows?

choices.feedback: That ignores the diode's drop. About 0.7 V stays across the diode, so the resistor gets 4.3 V: 4.3 mA.
That puts the diode's 0.7 V across the resistor. The resistor takes the rest, 5.0 − 0.7 = 4.3 V.

drills.prompt: The same diode is turned around in that 5 V circuit. The current is:

choices.text: almost none: nanoamps to microamps of leakage

choices.feedback: Reversed, the junction blocks. Only a tiny leakage flows until breakdown, which for a rectifier or small-signal diode is tens of volts or more.

choices.text: large, because the diode breaks down
choices.feedback: 5 V is far below a typical diode's breakdown voltage, tens of volts or more. It simply blocks.

physics: A silicon diode is a PN junction: p-type silicon, whose majority carriers are holes, against n-type, whose majority carriers are free electrons. Where they meet, carriers diffuse across and recombine, leaving a thin depletion region with no free carriers, whose electric field turns back further diffusion.

Forward bias, anode (p side) more positive than cathode, works against that field and lets carriers cross; the current grows exponentially with the voltage, about tenfold for every 60–120 mV at room temperature. At 0.5 V a small silicon diode passes microamps; at 0.6–0.7 V it passes milliamps, and from there the circuit around it, not the diode, sets the current.

Reverse bias adds to the field and widens the depletion region, so only a tiny leakage current flows, nanoamps for a small silicon diode at room temperature, until the reverse voltage reaches breakdown. A rectifier must never get there; a Zener diode is made to work there.

A diode that has been conducting holds charge near its junction, and when the voltage reverses it conducts backward briefly until that charge is cleared: the reverse recovery time, a few nanoseconds for a small switching diode and microseconds for a standard rectifier. A Schottky diode, a metal–semiconductor junction, stores almost no such charge and drops only 0.2–0.4 V.

glossary.definition: The voltage across a conducting diode from anode to cathode: about 0.6–0.7 V for a silicon junction, 0.2–0.4 V for a Schottky at small currents, and about 1.2 V (infrared) to 3.3 V (blue) for an LED, rising with the photon energy. It rises only about 60–120 mV for each tenfold increase in current, which is why a diode is often modeled as a fixed drop.
glossary.unit: volt (V), from anode to cathode while the diode conducts
physics: Forward bias lowers a PN junction's built-in barrier, and the number of carriers able to cross it grows exponentially with the voltage. The Shockley equation describes it: I = I_S(e^(V/(nV_T)) − 1), where V_T = kT/q ≈ 25.9 mV at 300 K, the ideality factor n is between 1 and 2, and the saturation current I_S is tiny: around 10⁻¹⁴ A for a small silicon junction modeled with n = 1.

Because the current is exponential in the voltage, the voltage is logarithmic in the current: each tenfold rise in current adds only n·V_T·ln 10, about 60 mV for n = 1 and 120 mV for n = 2. From 1 mA to 100 mA the drop of a silicon diode moves by roughly 0.1 to 0.25 V, plus the drop across its bulk resistance at high current. That is why a fixed 0.6–0.7 V is a good model for most circuit work.

The barrier depends on the junction. A Schottky's metal–semiconductor junction drops about 0.2–0.4 V. In an LED the forward voltage tracks the band gap, which also sets the color of the light: about 1.2–1.5 V for infrared, 1.8–2.2 V for red, and about 3 V for blue.

At a fixed current the drop falls by about 2 mV for each degree Celsius the junction warms, because I_S rises steeply with temperature. That makes a diode a simple thermometer, and it is why diodes in parallel don't share current well: the warmer one drops less, takes more current and warms further.

confusions.title: 0.7 V is a model, not a constant.

confusions.title: A diode is not a resistor.
confusions.text: V_F divided by the current gives a different "resistance" at every current. Use the drop for bias, and the slope n·V_T/I for small signals.

confusions.title: An LED does not drop 0.7 V.
confusions.text: Its drop is set by its band gap: about 2 V for red and about 3 V for blue. For a red LED at 10 mA from 5 V, the resistor should be (5 − 2) V / 10 mA = 300 Ω. Sizing it as if the LED dropped 0.7 V gives 430 Ω, and then only (5 − 2) V / 430 Ω ≈ 7 mA flows, so the LED runs dimmer than planned.

confusions.title: A Schottky's low drop has a cost.
confusions.text: Its reverse leakage is far higher than a silicon junction's: typically tens of microamps to milliamps for a 1 A Schottky near its rated reverse voltage, against well under a microamp for a small silicon diode. It also rises steeply with temperature, roughly doubling every 10 °C or so. In a hot or high-impedance circuit, that leakage can matter more than the 0.3 V saved.

drills.prompt: A red LED with a forward voltage of 2.0 V runs from 5.0 V at 10 mA. What series resistor does it need?

choices.feedback: 5.0 V / 10 mA ignores the LED. The resistor only gets what the LED leaves: (5.0 − 2.0) V / 10 mA = 300 Ω.
2.0 V / 10 mA uses the LED's voltage. The resistor takes the other 3.0 V: 300 Ω.

drills.prompt: A silicon diode carries a fixed current and warms up. Its forward voltage:

choices.feedback: At a fixed current the drop falls as the junction warms, about 2 mV per °C; that is how a diode works as a temperature sensor.
0.7 V is a model. The real drop falls about 2 mV per °C, and it also shifts with current.

drills.prompt: At the same current, which has the lowest forward voltage?

choices.feedback: A silicon junction drops about 0.6–0.7 V; a Schottky's metal–semiconductor junction drops about 0.2–0.4 V.
A blue LED drops about 3 V: its wide band gap, which sets the photon energy, also sets a high forward voltage.

glossary.definition: A diode made to break down at a specified reverse voltage V_Z, so it can conduct in reverse with its voltage held nearly constant over a wide range of current. With a series resistor to set its current, it makes a simple voltage reference or regulator.

drills.prompt: A 5.1 V Zener diode is fed from 12 V through 680 Ω, with no load. About what current does it carry?

choices.feedback: 12 V / 680 Ω forgets the Zener's voltage. The resistor gets only 12 − 5.1 = 6.9 V: about 10 mA.
5.1 V / 680 Ω uses the Zener's voltage. The resistor takes the difference, 6.9 V: about 10 mA.

drills.prompt: Which is true of a Zener regulator with a series resistor?

choices.text: The Zener takes whatever current the load doesn't, so it dissipates most with no load.
The Zener's current stays constant as the load changes.
choices.feedback: The resistor's current is nearly constant, set by (V_in − V_Z)/R. The load and the Zener share it, so the Zener's current falls as the load draws more.

choices.text: It works without the series resistor.
choices.feedback: The Zener's voltage barely moves with current, so a stiff supply across it alone would drive a destructive current. The resistor sets the current.

drills.prompt: A 5.1 V Zener diode is forward biased. About what does it drop?

choices.feedback: V_Z applies only in reverse breakdown. Forward, it is an ordinary PN junction.
Forward, it still has a junction to cross: about 0.7 V, like any silicon diode.

glossary.unit: volt (V): the Zener voltage, specified at a stated test current
physics: Every diode breaks down if its reverse voltage is high enough: the field across the depletion region grows strong enough to move carriers across in large numbers, and the reverse current rises steeply while the voltage barely changes. In a rectifier that happens at hundreds of volts and is a fault. A Zener diode is doped so that it happens at a chosen, low voltage, and built to conduct there continuously.

Below about 5 V the breakdown is mainly by tunneling, the Zener effect proper, and its voltage falls as the diode warms; above about 6 V it is by avalanche multiplication, and its voltage rises as the diode warms. Between them the two effects nearly cancel, so Zeners of about 5–6 V drift least with temperature.

A Zener needs a series resistor to set its current. From V_in = 12 V through R = 470 Ω to a 5.1 V Zener, the resistor carries (12 − 5.1) V / 470 Ω = 14.7 mA. A 1 kΩ load takes 5.1 mA of it and the Zener the remaining 9.6 mA. If the load changes, the Zener's current changes to make up the difference, while its voltage stays near 5.1 V.

That works only while the Zener keeps enough current to stay in breakdown, typically a few milliamps at least, and while its dissipation V_Z·I_Z stays inside its rating. With the load removed, the Zener above takes all 14.7 mA and dissipates 5.1 V × 14.7 mA = 75 mW.

glossary.definition: A light-emitting diode: a PN junction in a direct-band-gap semiconductor that emits light when electrons and holes recombine. Its forward voltage rises with the photon energy, from about 1.8 V for red to about 3 V for blue and white.

drills.prompt: Why does an LED on a voltage supply need a series resistor or a current driver?

choices.text: Its current rises steeply with its voltage, so something else must set the current.
Its forward voltage is too high otherwise.
choices.feedback: Its forward voltage is set by its band gap; nothing lowers it. The problem is that a small change in voltage changes the current a lot.

choices.text: To protect it against reverse voltage.
choices.feedback: Reverse protection is a separate matter. The series resistor sets the forward current.

drills.prompt: Two white LEDs with a forward voltage of 3.0 V each run in series from 9.0 V at 20 mA. What series resistor do they need?

choices.feedback: That allows for only one LED: (9.0 − 3.0) V / 20 mA. Both drop 3.0 V, leaving 3.0 V for the resistor: 150 Ω.
9.0 V / 20 mA ignores both LEDs. They take 6.0 V, leaving 3.0 V: 150 Ω.

drills.prompt: At the same current, which LED has the highest forward voltage?

choices.feedback: Red photons carry the least energy of the visible colors, so a red LED drops the least, about 1.8–2 V.
Infrared photons carry less energy than visible light, so an IR LED drops even less than red, about 1.2–1.5 V.

physics: In a forward-biased LED, electrons cross the junction and recombine with holes. In a direct-band-gap semiconductor, such as the alloys of gallium with arsenic, phosphorus, or nitrogen that LEDs are made of, a recombination can release its energy as a photon whose energy is close to the band gap. In silicon, whose band gap is indirect, that energy goes almost entirely into heat, which is why silicon diodes give off practically no light.

The photon energy sets the color: E = hc/λ, about 1240 eV·nm divided by the wavelength. Red light at 630 nm carries 1.97 eV and blue at 470 nm 2.64 eV, so a red LED conducts at about 1.8–2.2 V and a blue one at about 3 V: at working current the forward voltage is close to the photon energy in volts, plus resistive and contact losses that are larger in blue and white parts. A white LED is a blue one coated with a phosphor that turns part of the blue into yellow.

Light output follows current, not voltage, and like any diode's, an LED's current rises steeply with its voltage. So an LED is driven with a set current: through a series resistor, R = (V_supply − V_F)/I, or from a constant-current driver. From 5 V, a red LED dropping 2.0 V at 20 mA needs (5 − 2.0) V / 20 mA = 150 Ω.
LEDs tolerate little reverse voltage, often only about 5 V, and their forward voltage falls as they warm.

glossary.definition: A bipolar junction transistor: three layers, NPN or PNP, in which a small base current controls a collector current about β times larger. Its base–emitter junction is a diode, so a conducting silicon BJT has about 0.6–0.7 V from base to emitter.

drills.prompt: An NPN transistor switches a load from 12 V. Where does the load go?

choices.text: Between 12 V and the collector, with the emitter grounded
Between the emitter and ground, with the collector on 12 V
choices.feedback: That makes an emitter follower: the emitter sits about 0.7 V below the base, so the load gets at most the drive voltage less 0.7 V, never the full 12 V. A switch puts the load in the collector.
The base carries only the small control current. The load current flows from collector to emitter.

drills.prompt: An NPN with β = 100 is in its active region with a base current of 20 µA. What is the collector current?

choices.feedback: That is the base current. In the active region the collector carries β times it: 100 × 20 µA = 2.0 mA.
100 × 20 µA = 2000 µA = 2.0 mA. Check the prefixes.

drills.prompt: In a BJT's active region, its junctions are:

choices.text: base–emitter forward biased, base–collector reverse biased

choices.feedback: That is saturation, where the transistor acts like a closed switch.
That is cutoff, where no collector current flows.

physics: An NPN transistor is a thin p-type base between an n-type emitter and an n-type collector. Forward-bias the base–emitter junction, by about 0.7 V, and the emitter injects electrons into the base. The base is so thin and lightly doped that most of them reach the base–collector junction before they can recombine, and that reverse-biased junction's field sweeps them into the collector. Only a small fraction recombine in the base; supplying them is the base current.

The split is fixed by the device's construction: roughly 100 electrons reach the collector for each one the base supplies, so I_C = β·I_B, and I_E = I_C + I_B. As long as the base–collector junction stays reverse biased, the collector current hardly depends on the collector voltage: the collector acts as a current source controlled by the base. That is the active region, where amplifiers work.

Switches use the other two states. With the base–emitter junction off, below about 0.5 V, the transistor is cut off and passes almost no collector current. With more base current than the load needs, the collector falls until the base–collector junction is forward biased too: the transistor saturates, and V_CE drops to about 0.1–0.3 V.

A PNP transistor is the mirror image: its emitter sits at the most positive point, its base is pulled about 0.7 V below the emitter, and its currents flow the other way. The arrow in the symbol is on the emitter and points the way conventional current crosses the base–emitter junction: out of an NPN, into a PNP.

confusions.text: The emitter is heavily doped and the collector built to block voltage. Used backward, a BJT's β drops to a small fraction of its normal value, and its emitter–base junction breaks down at only a few volts.

glossary.definition: A BJT's current gain, the ratio of collector current to base current in the active region (h_FE on datasheets), typically 50 to 300 and varying widely between parts and with temperature. A switch is driven with a forced β, I_C/I_B, of about 10, so every part saturates.

drills.prompt: An NPN switch must carry 100 mA. With a forced β of 10, what base current do you supply?

choices.feedback: A part with β = 100 would sit just at the edge of saturation, and any lower-β part wouldn't saturate. A forced β of 10 leaves margin: 100 mA / 10 = 10 mA.
The base current is the collector current divided by the forced β, 100 mA / 10 = 10 mA, not multiplied by it.

drills.prompt: Which is true of β?

choices.text: It can differ by a factor of three or more between parts of the same type.
It is fixed for each part number.
choices.feedback: Datasheets give a wide range, often 100 to 300 for one part number, and it shifts with current and temperature. Good designs work over the whole range.

choices.text: It is the voltage gain of a common-emitter stage.
choices.feedback: β is a current ratio. A common-emitter stage's voltage gain is set by its resistors, about −R_C/R_E.

drills.prompt: A bias circuit gives I_C = 1.0 mA with a β = 100 part. Swapped for a β = 300 part, the collector current triples. Which bias did it use?

choices.text: A single resistor from the supply to the base, which fixes the base current
A stiff divider on the base with an emitter resistor
choices.feedback: That fixes the base voltage, so the emitter current is about (V_B − 0.7 V)/R_E whatever β is. Swapping parts would barely change I_C.

choices.text: A current source in the emitter
choices.feedback: An emitter current source fixes I_E directly; I_C ≈ I_E for any large β, so it wouldn't triple.

glossary.unit: a ratio (A/A), so unitless: collector current over base current in the active region; datasheets call it hFE
physics: In the active region, the base current supplies the small fraction of carriers that recombine in the thin base, so it is a fixed fraction of the collector current: β = I_C/I_B. The fraction depends on the base's width and doping, which vary from part to part, so two transistors of one type can differ in β by a factor of three or more.

β also changes with the collector current, falling at very low and very high currents, and it rises with temperature. A datasheet gives a minimum, and often a typical value, at stated currents; a sound design works with any β above the minimum.

Since I_E = I_C + I_B, the emitter current is (β + 1)·I_B, and the fraction of the emitter current that reaches the collector is α = β/(β + 1), 0.990 for β = 100. Seen from the base, a resistor in the emitter appears about (β + 1) times larger, which is why an emitter follower has a high input resistance.

In a switch, β is not the ratio that flows. A saturated transistor carries whatever current its load allows, and its base is overdriven on purpose. The ratio I_C/I_B there is the forced β, chosen around 10 so that even the lowest-β part saturates.

confusions.text: A base current of 43 µA gives 4.3 mA with β = 100, and would ask for 12.9 mA with β = 300, more than a 12 V, 1 kΩ load can pass: that part saturates. Emitter feedback, or a switch's forced β, removes the dependence.

confusions.title: In saturation, I_C/I_B is not β.
confusions.text: A switch passing 11.8 mA with 1.2 mA of base drive runs at a forced β of about 10, whatever its h_FE.

confusions.title: I_E is (β + 1)·I_B.
confusions.text: With β = 100 and I_B = 43 µA, I_C = 4.3 mA and I_E = 4.343 mA.

confusions.title: h_FE and h_fe are different figures.
confusions.text: h_FE is the DC ratio I_C/I_B; h_fe is the small-signal ratio of changes, ΔI_C/ΔI_B, measured at a stated frequency. Many texts write β for either, and for most estimates they are close, but datasheets list them separately.

glossary.uses: Sizing a base resistor for a switch (from the minimum h_FE, with a forced β of about 10), bias design, the input resistance of an emitter follower, and Darlington pairs, whose β values multiply.

sources.note: Seen from the base, the emitter path r'_E + R_E appears β + 1 times larger, so the stage input impedance is R1 ∥ R2 ∥ (β + 1)(r'_E + R_E).

glossary.definition: The state in which more drive no longer raises the output: a saturated BJT has both junctions forward biased and only about 0.2 V from collector to emitter, an op amp's output stops near a supply rail, and an inductor's core can magnetize no further, so its inductance falls sharply. For a MOSFET the same word names the region in which the drain current stops rising with V_DS, the counterpart of a BJT's active region, not its saturation.

drills.prompt: An NPN switch with β = 100 gets 5.0 mA of base current and drives a 220 Ω load from 9.0 V, with V_CE(sat) = 0.2 V. What is the collector current?

choices.feedback: β·I_B = 100 × 5.0 mA is what the base could support, but the load allows only (9.0 − 0.2) V / 220 Ω = 40 mA. With the base overdriven the transistor saturates, and the supply and the load set the current.
That is the base current. The collector carries the load current, set in saturation by the supply and the load: (9.0 − 0.2) V / 220 Ω = 40 mA.

drills.prompt: A BJT switch should be on, but its collector reads 4 V on a 12 V supply with the load connected. What is wrong?

choices.text: It isn't saturated: too little base current leaves it in the active region, where it runs hot.
Nothing: 4 V is a normal saturation voltage.
choices.feedback: V_CE(sat) is about 0.2 V. At 4 V the transistor is in its active region, limited by β·I_B, and dissipating 4 V times the collector current.
Off, no current flows, so the load drops nothing and the collector sits at the full 12 V. At 4 V current is flowing; there just isn't enough base drive.

drills.prompt: A MOSFET in a current driver is said to be "in saturation," and so is a BJT in a switch. Which is true?

choices.text: The MOSFET is in its constant-current region; the BJT is fully on, like a closed switch.
Both are fully on, with little voltage across them.
choices.feedback: That is the BJT meaning. A MOSFET that is fully on, acting as a resistor, is in its triode region; its saturation region is where the current levels off and V_DS can be large.

choices.text: Both are in their constant-current region.
choices.feedback: That is the MOSFET meaning. A BJT's constant-current region is the active region; a saturated BJT has only about 0.2 V across it.

drills.prompt: An inductor runs above its rated saturation current. What happens?

choices.text: Its inductance drops sharply, so the current rises much faster than expected.
Its inductance rises, smoothing the current more.
choices.feedback: A saturated core can carry no more flux, so its permeability, and with it the inductance, falls.
Heating is set by the RMS current and the winding resistance. Saturation is a separate, magnetic limit: the inductance falls as soon as the peak current passes it.

physics: In a BJT switch the load limits the collector current: from 12 V through 1 kΩ, no more than about (12 − 0.2) V / 1 kΩ = 11.8 mA can flow, however hard the transistor is driven. While β·I_B is below that, the transistor is in its active region and I_C = β·I_B. Once β·I_B exceeds it, the collector has fallen so low that the base–collector junction is forward biased as well: the BJT is saturated, V_CE ≈ 0.2 V, and more base current changes almost nothing.

A BJT switch is meant to saturate. It then dissipates little, 11.8 mA × 0.2 V = 2.4 mW here, and its on state no longer depends on β. Designers drive the base with about a tenth of the collector current, a forced β of 10. The cost is extra charge stored in the base, which slows the turn-off.

In a MOSFET the same word names a different region. A MOSFET is in saturation when V_DS is large enough, V_DS ≥ V_GS − V_t, that the channel pinches off at the drain end and the drain current stops rising with V_DS: I_D is then set by V_GS, as I_C is set by the base in a BJT's active region. MOSFET amplifiers work there. A fully on MOSFET switch is in the other region, called triode or ohmic, where it behaves as a small resistance, R_DS(on). Many switching guides borrow the BJT usage and call a fully on MOSFET "saturated" and the flat region "active"; tell which is meant from V_DS: a few tenths of a volt or less means fully on, several volts means the current is being limited.

So a saturated BJT is a closed switch, while a MOSFET in saturation is a current source. What the two uses share is only that something has stopped rising: a BJT's collector current with more base current, a MOSFET's drain current with more drain voltage. An op amp's output stopped at its limit and a magnetic core that can take no more flux are called saturated too.

confusions.title: A saturated BJT is fully on; a MOSFET in saturation is not.
confusions.text: A BJT switch is designed to saturate, with V_CE ≈ 0.2 V. A MOSFET switch must not sit in saturation: there it holds a large V_DS and dissipates I_D·V_DS. Fully on, it is in the triode region: 2 A through 50 mΩ drops 0.1 V and dissipates 0.2 W. Switching guides that call a fully on MOSFET "saturated" mean this triode state.

confusions.title: In BJT saturation, I_C/I_B falls below β.
confusions.text: The load sets I_C. With 1 mA of base drive and an 11.8 mA load the ratio is 11.8, even if h_FE is 200.

confusions.title: Driving harder lowers V_CE only a little.
confusions.text: Past saturation, more base current barely moves V_CE, and it adds stored charge that the base must clear before the switch can turn off.

confusions.title: An op amp's saturation is a third meaning.
confusions.text: Its output stops near a supply rail because the output stage has run out of voltage. The feedback loop is then broken, and the inputs no longer sit at equal voltages.

glossary.uses: BJT switches for relays, LEDs, and lamps (designed to saturate), MOSFET amplifiers and current sources (biased in saturation), op amps used as comparators (output saturated on purpose), and choosing inductors that stay below their core's saturation current.

glossary.definition: A metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistor: the gate voltage, insulated from the channel by a thin oxide, controls the current from drain to source. The gate draws no steady current, only a brief current to charge or discharge its capacitance at each switching edge.

drills.prompt: What controls an N-channel MOSFET's drain current?

choices.text: The gate current, as a base current controls a BJT
choices.feedback: The gate is insulated by oxide, so it draws essentially no steady current. The voltage on it controls the channel.
The channel forms with respect to the source: V_GS sets it. V_DS then decides between the triode and saturation regions.

drills.prompt: A microcontroller pin switches a MOSFET at 20 kHz. Which is true of the pin's current?

choices.text: Brief pulses at each edge to charge and discharge the gate, and none in between
None at all, since the gate is insulated
choices.feedback: There is no steady current, but the gate is a capacitance, often nanofarads, so each edge must move its gate charge Q_g.

choices.text: A steady current of I_D divided by the transistor's gain
choices.feedback: That is how a BJT's base works. A MOSFET's gate draws current only while its voltage changes.

drills.prompt: A MOSFET's gate is left unconnected. Which is true?

choices.text: It may sit partly on: charge stranded on the gate capacitance holds a voltage, so a pull-down resistor is needed.
It turns off, since no gate current flows.
choices.feedback: With no path to discharge it, the gate keeps whatever charge it picked up, and stray fields can add more. A pull-down resistor holds it off.

choices.text: It conducts fully, as an open gate reads as high.
choices.feedback: Its state is undefined, not high: anything from off to partly on, which can overheat it. A pull-down resistor fixes the state.

physics: In an n-channel enhancement MOSFET, the source and drain are n-type regions in a p-type body, so with no gate voltage there are two back-to-back junctions between them and no current flows. The gate is a conducting plate separated from the body by a thin oxide. Raise the gate above the source and its field draws electrons to the surface under the oxide; above the threshold voltage V_t there are enough to form an n-type channel joining source to drain.

The oxide is an insulator, so the gate draws no steady current: it is a capacitor, of hundreds of picofarads to a few nanofarads in a power MOSFET, which must be charged to turn the MOSFET on and discharged to turn it off. A logic pin can hold a MOSFET on without supplying any current, but switching it fast takes a large current for a short time: moving 20 nC of gate charge in 20 ns takes 1 A.

With a small V_DS the channel behaves as a resistance whose value V_GS sets: the triode, or ohmic, region, where a switch works, with V_DS = I_D·R_DS(on). With a larger V_DS the channel pinches off at the drain end and the current levels off at about K(V_GS − V_t)²: the saturation region, where an amplifier works. Switching guides often call a fully on MOSFET "saturated" in the BJT sense; here it is in the triode region.

In a power MOSFET the source is tied to the body, which leaves a diode between them and the drain: anode at the source, cathode at the drain in an n-channel part. It conducts whenever the drain goes below the source, whatever the gate does, so a MOSFET blocks in one direction only.

confusions.title: It conducts backward through its body diode.
confusions.text: With the drain below the source, the body diode conducts at about 0.7 V whatever the gate does. Blocking both ways takes two MOSFETs back to back.

confusions.title: V_GS is measured to the source, not to ground.
confusions.text: In a low-side switch the source is at ground, so they are the same. In a high-side N-channel switch the source rises to the load voltage, and the gate must be driven above the supply to keep it on.

confusions.text: SPICE netlists name MOSFETs M (M1, M2); schematics usually use Q, the same letter as a BJT. Q1 on a board and M1 in its simulation can be the same part.

glossary.definition: The gate-to-source voltage V_t at which a MOSFET's channel just forms and drain current begins to flow, often 1–4 V for power parts. At its threshold a MOSFET is barely on; full conduction needs the higher V_GS at which its datasheet specifies R_DS(on).

drills.prompt: A MOSFET's datasheet gives a gate threshold of 2–4 V and specifies R_DS(on) at V_GS = 10 V. Can a 3.3 V logic pin switch it fully on?

choices.text: No: 3.3 V lies inside the 2–4 V threshold range, where the channel barely conducts, if at all.

choices.feedback: At threshold a MOSFET only starts to conduct, and a part can have a threshold up to 4 V. Full conduction needs V_GS near the 10 V its R_DS(on) is specified at, or a logic-level part.

choices.text: Yes: any gate voltage above 0 V turns it fully on.
choices.feedback: Below threshold there is no channel at all; just above it, a weak one. The datasheet's R_DS(on) needs 10 V here.

drills.prompt: An NMOS has V_t = 1.5 V and K = 2 mA/V², and is in saturation with V_GS = 2.5 V. What is its drain current, I_D = K(V_GS − V_t)²?

choices.feedback: That squares V_GS itself: 2 × 2.5². Only the overdrive above threshold counts: V_GS − V_t = 1.0 V, so 2 × 1.0² = 2.0 mA.
That squares the threshold, 2 × 1.5². The current depends on the overdrive above it: 2 mA/V² × (2.5 V − 1.5 V)² = 2.0 mA.

drills.prompt: A MOSFET warms up. Its threshold voltage:

choices.text: falls, by a few millivolts per °C
rises, so it switches off when hot
choices.feedback: The threshold falls with temperature. At a fixed gate voltage near threshold, a warm MOSFET conducts more, not less.

choices.text: stays fixed: it is set by the oxide thickness
choices.feedback: The oxide matters, but the threshold also depends on temperature: it falls a few millivolts per °C.

glossary.unit: volt (V), from gate to source; written Vt in the course and VGS(th) on datasheets
physics: The gate, oxide, and body of a MOSFET form a capacitor. In an n-channel part, a positive gate first pushes holes away from the surface, leaving a depletion layer with no free carriers. Only when the gate is high enough does the surface hold more free electrons than the body holds holes: an inversion layer, which is the channel. The gate–source voltage at which that happens is the threshold, V_t.

Above threshold, the charge in the channel grows in proportion to the overdrive, V_GS − V_t. In saturation the drain current follows the square law, I_D = K(V_GS − V_t)², so doubling the overdrive quadruples the current. In the triode region the channel's resistance falls roughly as 1/(V_GS − V_t).

Datasheets give V_GS(th) as the voltage at which a small, stated drain current flows, often 250 µA or 1 mA, with a wide spread: 2–4 V for one standard power part. It also falls by a few millivolts for each degree the die warms. So the threshold is never a design target for a switch; R_DS(on) is specified at a V_GS well above it, 10 V for a standard part, or 4.5 V or 2.5 V for a logic-level one.
A P-channel MOSFET has a negative threshold: its gate must go below its source, by 1–4 V for power parts, before it conducts.

about 1–2 V; specified at 4.5 V or 2.5 V

confusions.title: At V_t a MOSFET is barely on.
confusions.text: The threshold is where current starts, at 250 µA on many datasheets. A switch needs V_GS several volts above it. Texts that call V_t the "turn-on voltage" mean that turn-on begins there, not that it is complete.

confusions.title: A 3.3 V gate drive may not be enough.
confusions.text: With V_t up to 4 V, a standard part may not turn on at all from 3.3 V; even with V_t = 2 V, 1.3 V of overdrive leaves a high R_DS(on). Use a logic-level part specified at 2.5 V or lower.

confusions.title: The threshold varies between parts.
confusions.text: A datasheet range of 2–4 V means two parts from one reel can differ by 2 V. A circuit that biases a MOSFET near its threshold needs feedback to set the current.

confusions.title: The threshold falls as the part warms.
confusions.text: At a fixed V_GS near threshold, a hotter MOSFET conducts more, so in linear use paralleled MOSFETs can hog current unless each has its own source resistor or control loop. Fully on, the opposite holds: R_DS(on) rises with temperature, so paralleled switches share current.

confusions.title: V_t is not the thermal voltage V_T.
confusions.text: The MOSFET threshold V_t, 1–4 V for power parts, differs only by case from the thermal voltage V_T = kT/q, about 26 mV at room temperature, which appears in the diode and BJT equations.

glossary.definition: The resistance R_DS(on) from drain to source of a MOSFET driven fully on: milliohms for power parts, ohms for small-signal ones. It is specified at a stated gate voltage and rises with temperature, often by 1.5 to 2 times between 25 °C and 125 °C.

drills.prompt: A fully on MOSFET with R_DS(on) = 50 mΩ carries 4.0 A. What does it dissipate?

choices.feedback: 4.0 A × 50 mΩ = 0.20 V is the voltage across it. The power is I²·R = 4.0² × 0.050 = 0.80 W.

drills.prompt: Why does a MOSFET switch's conduction loss quadruple when its current doubles?

choices.text: P = I²·R_DS(on): the voltage across it doubles along with the current.

choices.feedback: At a given gate voltage and temperature it is roughly constant. The square comes from P = I·(I·R).
The voltage across the switch, I·R_DS(on), also doubles, so the power I²·R_DS(on) goes up four times.

drills.prompt: What gate drive does a MOSFET need for its datasheet R_DS(on)?

choices.text: At least the V_GS stated with the R_DS(on) figure, such as 4.5 V or 10 V
Anything just above the threshold voltage
choices.feedback: Just above threshold the channel is weak and the resistance high. R_DS(on) is guaranteed only at the stated V_GS.

choices.text: Any gate voltage: R_DS(on) is fixed
choices.feedback: The channel resistance falls as V_GS rises; the datasheet figure holds only at the V_GS it states.

glossary.unit: ohm (Ω); milliohms (mΩ) for power MOSFETs
physics: Fully on, a MOSFET's channel is a thin layer of electrons between source and drain, and at small V_DS it behaves as a resistor: V_DS = I_D·R_DS(on). More gate overdrive puts more electrons in the channel and lowers its resistance, until the channel's share is small next to the fixed resistance of the rest of the die, the bond wires and the package, and further V_GS gains little.

Because it is a resistance, the conduction loss is P = I²·R_DS(on), which makes it the key figure of a MOSFET switch. 5 A through 20 mΩ drops 0.1 V and dissipates 0.5 W; a BJT saturated at 0.2 V would dissipate 1 W at the same current. Doubling the current quadruples the loss.

R_DS(on) rises with temperature, often 1.5 to 2 times between 25 °C and 125 °C, because the electrons' mobility falls as the silicon warms. A hot MOSFET therefore dissipates more. The same effect helps MOSFETs in parallel share current: the warmer one's resistance rises and pushes current to the others.

It is specified only at a stated V_GS: 10 V for a standard part, 4.5 V or 2.5 V for a logic-level one. At lower gate voltages the resistance rises steeply, and near the threshold the MOSFET is not a switch at all.

confusions.text: 10 A through one 10 mΩ part dissipates 1 W. Through two in parallel, 5 A each, it is 0.25 W each and 0.5 W in total.
