glossary.definition: A circuit of diodes that turns AC into DC of one polarity: a half-wave rectifier passes one half of each cycle, and a full-wave bridge flips the other half up as well. Its output pulses, so a reservoir capacitor usually follows to hold it near the peak.

drills.prompt: A transformer winding of 12 V RMS feeds a silicon bridge rectifier and a large reservoir capacitor. About what is the DC output at light load?

choices.feedback: 12 V RMS is the heating value. The capacitor charges to the peak, √2 × 12 ≈ 17.0 V, less two diode drops.
That subtracts one diode drop. In a bridge two diodes conduct in series on each half-cycle: 17.0 − 1.4 ≈ 15.6 V.
That is the winding's peak. The two conducting diodes drop about 1.4 V: 15.6 V.

drills.prompt: With the same capacitor and load, why does a full-wave rectifier give half the ripple of a half-wave one?

choices.text: It refills the capacitor twice per cycle, so the capacitor discharges for half as long.
Its output voltage is twice as high.
choices.feedback: The peak is the same, less one more diode drop. The ripple halves because the gap between refills halves.

choices.text: It has more diodes, which filter the output.
choices.feedback: Diodes don't filter. The capacitor does, and it has half as long to sag between refills.

drills.prompt: In a rectifier feeding a reservoir capacitor, the current through the diodes is:

choices.text: short pulses near each peak, much larger than the load current
a steady current equal to the load current
choices.feedback: The diodes conduct only while the input is above the capacitor's voltage, a short part of each cycle. All the charge the load used must go back in then, so the pulses are large.

choices.text: a sine wave in phase with the input
choices.feedback: The diodes are reverse biased for most of the cycle, while the capacitor holds the output above the input.

physics: A rectifier uses diodes to let current reach the load in one direction only. A half-wave rectifier is a single diode in series: it conducts while the source is positive and blocks while it is negative, so the load gets one half of each cycle and nothing during the other. Its output pulses at the line frequency, 60 Hz.

A bridge uses four diodes so that both halves of the cycle drive current through the load the same way: on one half two diagonally opposite diodes conduct, on the other half the other two. The output pulses at twice the line frequency, 120 Hz, and since two diodes are always in the path, its peak is about 1.4 V below the source's peak instead of 0.7 V.

The peak of a sine is √2 times its RMS value. A 12 V RMS transformer secondary peaks at 16.97 V, so a bridge gives about 15.6 V peak and a half-wave rectifier about 16.3 V. A reservoir capacitor after the diodes charges to near that peak and feeds the load between peaks, leaving a ripple.

Each diode must block the reverse voltage across it. In a bridge each diode blocks about the source's peak. In a half-wave rectifier with a reservoir capacitor, the diode has the capacitor's +V_peak on one side and the source's −V_peak on the other: about twice V_peak, 34 V for a 12 V RMS secondary.

half-wave output peak from 12 V RMS
average of a full-wave output with no capacitor

confusions.title: A rectifier alone does not make steady DC.
confusions.text: Without a capacitor a bridge's output falls to 0 V twice per cycle. A DC meter reads its average, not its peak: about 0.637 × 16.97 V less the 1.4 V of the two diodes, or 9.4 V, against a 15.6 V peak.

confusions.title: A bridge's output repeats at 120 Hz.
confusions.text: Both half-cycles produce a pulse, so on 60 Hz the output repeats every 8.33 ms. A half-wave rectifier's repeats every 16.7 ms.

confusions.title: A bridge loses two diode drops.
confusions.text: On each half-cycle the current passes through two diodes in series: 16.97 V − 1.4 V = 15.6 V peak, not 16.3 V.

confusions.title: A transformer's rating is RMS, not peak.
confusions.text: A 12 V transformer is 12 V RMS. With a capacitor the output charges toward its 16.97 V peak less the diodes, so a lightly loaded 12 V bridge supply sits near 15.6 V, not 12 V.

glossary.definition: The periodic variation left on a DC voltage or current after rectification or switching, usually given peak to peak. With a reservoir capacitor it is about I/(f·C) for a half-wave rectifier and half that for full-wave; a switching converter's ripple is at its switching frequency.

drills.prompt: A full-wave rectifier on the 60 Hz line feeds 0.50 A from a 2200 µF reservoir capacitor. About what is the peak-to-peak ripple?

choices.feedback: I/(f·C) is the half-wave figure. A bridge refills at 120 Hz, twice per cycle, which halves it: 0.50 / (120 × 0.0022) ≈ 1.9 V.
2200 µF is 2.2 × 10⁻³ F. Then 0.50 / (2 × 60 × 0.0022) ≈ 1.9 V, not millivolts.

drills.prompt: The load current on a capacitor-input rectifier doubles. The ripple:

choices.feedback: More current drains the capacitor faster between peaks: ΔV ≈ I/(2f·C) for full-wave rises with I.

choices.text: stays the same, set by the capacitor and the frequency
choices.feedback: The capacitor loses charge I·Δt between peaks, so ΔV ≈ I/(2f·C) is proportional to the load current.

drills.prompt: Which change reduces a buck converter's inductor ripple current, with the same inductor and the same input and output voltages?

choices.feedback: Each on-time would be longer, so the current ramps further: ΔI = (V_in − V_out)·D/(f·L) grows as f falls.
In continuous conduction the load sets the average inductor current, not its ripple. ΔI = (V_in − V_out)·D/(f·L) has no load term.

glossary.unit: volt (V) peak to peak, or ampere (A) for a ripple current
physics: After a rectifier, a reservoir capacitor charges to near the peak, then supplies the load on its own until the rectified voltage rises above it again, while every diode is off. With a load current I it discharges at dV/dt = I/C, so its voltage falls in a nearly straight line between peaks.

If that discharge lasts the whole time between peaks, the drop is V_r ≈ I·t/C, with t = 1/f for half-wave and 1/(2f) for full-wave rectification: V_r ≈ I/(fC) or I/(2fC). For 0.5 A from 2200 µF after a bridge on 60 Hz, V_r ≈ 0.5 A / (2 × 60 Hz × 2200 µF) = 1.89 V peak to peak. The estimate is a little high, and so errs on the safe side: recharging starts before the next peak. In the figure the rising sine catches the capacitor 7.1 ms after the peak, so it falls 227 V/s × 7.1 ms = 1.6 V.

Ripple falls with more capacitance and with full-wave rectification, and a regulator after the capacitor removes most of what remains, provided the bottom of the ripple stays above the regulator's minimum input. The capacitor's current arrives in short, high pulses while the diodes conduct, so its ripple-current rating, which limits its heating, matters as much as its capacitance.

A switching converter's output ripples too, at its switching frequency: the inductor current rises and falls in a triangle, and the output capacitor absorbs the alternating part. At hundreds of kilohertz rather than 120 Hz, a much smaller capacitor holds the ripple to millivolts.

glossary.definition: Pulse-width modulation: switching a load fully on and fully off at a fixed frequency and varying the fraction of each period it is on, the duty cycle. The load, or a filter after the switch, responds to the average, D times the full voltage, while the switch wastes little power because it is never half on.

drills.prompt: A 12 V supply drives a motor through a MOSFET switched by PWM at a 25% duty cycle. Ignoring the drops in the switch and the flyback diode, what average voltage does the motor see?

choices.feedback: The motor sees 12 V only while the switch is on, a quarter of the time, and about 0 V otherwise: the average is 0.25 × 12 V = 3.0 V.
That is the off fraction, 75%, of 12 V. The switch is on for 25%: 3.0 V.

drills.prompt: Why does PWM dim a lamp more efficiently than a series resistor?

choices.text: The switch is either fully on, with little voltage across it, or off, with no current, so it dissipates little.

choices.feedback: The supply stays the same; the switch connects it for only part of each period. The saving comes from the switch never being half on.
The lamp is unchanged. A series resistor burns power whenever current flows; a switch that is fully on or off burns almost none.

drills.prompt: An LED is driven by PWM at 1 kHz with a 50% duty cycle. What does the eye see?

choices.text: Steady light, with half the average light output of the LED fully on

choices.feedback: The eye can't follow 1 kHz. It averages the pulses into steady light.

choices.text: Full brightness, since the LED is fully on when it is on
choices.feedback: The LED is fully on half the time and off the rest; the eye integrates that into half the average output.

physics: PWM switches a load between fully on and fully off at a fixed frequency and varies only how long each on-time lasts. The fraction of each period spent on is the duty cycle D, so the average voltage across the load is D·V_supply: 25% of 12 V averages 3 V.

The switch wastes little because it is never half on. Off, it carries no current; on, it has almost no voltage across it. Driving a 6 Ω load at 25% from 12 V, the switch carries 2 A while on, and with 50 mΩ of on-resistance it dissipates (2 A)² × 50 mΩ × 0.25 = 50 mW, plus a little at each edge. A transistor holding the same load at a steady 6 V, which gives it the same 6 W, would itself drop 6 V at 1 A and dissipate 6 W.

What the load responds to depends on how fast it is. A motor's inductance and inertia, a heater's thermal mass, and an eye watching an LED all average the pulses if the frequency is high enough. For a true DC voltage, a low-pass filter follows the switch: the LC filter of a buck converter, or an RC filter on a microcontroller's PWM pin.

Average voltage and power scale differently. Power goes as V², so a resistor switched at duty D receives D·V²/R, while a steady D·V would give D²·V²/R. At 25% from 12 V into 6 Ω the load gets 6 W, four times the 1.5 W that a steady 3 V would give.

typical.value: hundreds of hertz to tens of kilohertz

typical.what: switch loss, 2 A on, 50 mΩ, D = 25%

confusions.title: The average is not the RMS.
confusions.text: A 6 Ω heater on 12 V at 25% duty receives 6 W, not the 1.5 W a steady 3 V would give: the RMS voltage is √0.25 × 12 V = 6 V.

confusions.title: The frequency does not set the average.
confusions.text: At one duty cycle, 1 kHz and 20 kHz PWM have the same average. The frequency decides how much of the switching gets through the load or filter, and how often the switch pays its edge losses.

confusions.title: A meter reads the average; the load sees the pulses.
confusions.text: A DC meter shows about 3 V on a 12 V, 25% PWM line, but every pulse is 12 V. An LED or a logic input on that line sees 12 V, not 3 V.

confusions.title: Faster switching is not free.
confusions.text: Each edge passes through a moment with both voltage and current on the switch. Ten times the frequency means ten times as many edges, and ten times the switching loss.

glossary.definition: The fraction D of each switching period during which a switch is on, from 0 to 1, or 0% to 100%. In an ideal buck converter the output voltage is D times the input.

drills.prompt: A switch is on for 3.0 µs of every 10 µs. What are its duty cycle and switching frequency?

choices.feedback: The switching frequency is 1/period = 1/(10 µs) = 100 kHz. 1/(3.0 µs) is the reciprocal of the on-time.
3/7 compares the on-time with the off-time. The duty cycle is the on-time over the whole period: 3.0/10 = 0.30.

drills.prompt: An ideal buck converter makes 3.3 V from 12 V. What duty cycle does it run at?

choices.feedback: That is the off fraction, 1 − D. A buck gives V_out = D·V_in, so D = 3.3/12 ≈ 0.28.
12/3.3 is upside down, and a duty cycle can't exceed 1: D = V_out/V_in = 3.3/12 ≈ 0.28.

drills.prompt: In what unit is a duty cycle given?

choices.feedback: The on-time is in seconds; the duty cycle is the on-time divided by the period, so the seconds cancel.
Hertz measures the switching frequency. The duty cycle is a fraction of each period.

glossary.unit: a ratio from 0 to 1, or a percentage: the on-time divided by the period
physics: The duty cycle is the fraction of each period a switch spends on: D = t_on/T. At 100 kHz the period is 10 µs, so an on-time of 4.2 µs is D = 0.42, or 42%. A signal with D = 0.5 is a square wave.
What makes D useful is averaging. A voltage switched between V and 0 has an average of D·V, which is what a filter, a motor, or a meter responds to.

In a converter, D follows from the inductor. In steady state the inductor's current ends each cycle where it began, so its average voltage is zero: the volt-seconds while the switch is on cancel those while it is off. In a buck, the inductor has V_in − V_out across it for D·T and −V_out for (1 − D)·T; setting (V_in − V_out)·D = V_out·(1 − D) gives V_out = D·V_in. A boost's balance gives V_out = V_in/(1 − D), which climbs steeply as D approaches 1.

Real converters need a little more duty than the ideal formula to cover the drops in the switch, diode, and inductor, and a controller adjusts D continuously to hold the output as the input and the load change.

confusions.title: Duty cycle is a fraction of the period, not a time.
confusions.text: A 5 µs on-time is D = 0.5 at 100 kHz but D = 0.05 at 10 kHz.

confusions.title: V_out = D·V_in assumes continuous inductor current.
confusions.text: At a light load the inductor current of a buck with a diode reaches zero during each cycle, and the output rises above D·V_in at the same duty until the controller lowers D. Losses work the other way: under load a real buck needs a little more than the ideal D.

confusions.title: A boost's output is not D·V_in.
confusions.text: From 12 V, a boost at D = 0.5 gives 24 V and at D = 0.8 gives 60 V: V_in/(1 − D).

confusions.title: Duty cycles near 0 or 1 are hard to reach.
confusions.text: The switch needs time to turn on and off. At 1 MHz a duty of 2% is an on-time of 20 ns, about as long as the switching edges themselves.

glossary.uses: Setting a converter's output, PWM motor and LED control, reading a controller's duty on a scope to diagnose a supply, and timer and servo signals.

glossary.definition: A switching converter that steps a DC voltage down: a switch chops the input, and an inductor and capacitor pass on its average, so V_out = D·V_in. It wastes little power, so it draws less current from its input than it delivers to its load.

drills.prompt: An ideal buck converter makes 5.0 V at 2.0 A from 20 V. What current does it draw from the 20 V supply?

choices.feedback: That is what a linear regulator would draw: the same current in as out. A buck trades voltage for current: 10 W in at 20 V is 0.50 A.
Power in equals power out, so the higher voltage means less current, not more: 10 W / 20 V = 0.50 A.

drills.prompt: Why can a buck converter be far more efficient than a linear regulator?

choices.text: Its switch is never half on, and the inductor stores energy rather than burning the difference.
It drops the voltage across a smaller resistor.
choices.feedback: There is no dropping resistor. The switch is fully on or fully off, and the inductor and capacitor average the chopped voltage.
It uses more: a switch, an inductor, a capacitor, and a controller. Its efficiency comes from never dissipating the voltage difference.

drills.prompt: Why does a buck converter's average inductor current equal its load current?

choices.text: The output capacitor passes no steady current, so on average all the inductor's current goes to the load.
The inductor regulates its own current to match the load.
choices.feedback: An inductor doesn't regulate anything; it carries whatever its voltage builds up. The capacitor can't take a steady current, so the average must go to the load.

choices.text: The switch carries the load current all the time.
choices.feedback: The switch conducts only during the on-time, so its average current is D times the load current. The inductor carries current all period.

physics: A buck converter chops its input with a switch and filters the result with an inductor and a capacitor. While the switch is on, the switch node sits at V_in, and the inductor, with V_in − V_out across it, ramps its current up. When the switch opens, the inductor keeps its current flowing through the diode (or a second switch); the switch node falls to one diode drop below 0 V, and the current ramps down with about −V_out across the inductor.

In steady state the inductor's current ends each cycle where it began, so its average voltage is zero and the output equals the average of the switch node: V_out = D·V_in, as long as the inductor current never falls to zero. From 12 V at D = 0.5 the output is 6 V.

The inductor current is a triangle around the load current. Its peak-to-peak ripple is ΔI = (V_in − V_out)·D/(f·L): from 12 V to 6 V at 100 kHz with 100 µH, ΔI = 6 V × 0.5 / (100 kHz × 100 µH) = 0.3 A. The output capacitor absorbs that triangle and leaves only a small voltage ripple on the output.

Because the switch is either fully on or fully off, a buck converter wastes little power; efficiencies above 90% are routine. Power in is then about power out, so it draws less current than it delivers: 6 V at 1 A from 12 V at 90% efficiency takes 0.56 A. A linear regulator doing the same would draw the full 1 A and turn 6 W into heat.

typical.value: about 100 kHz to a few MHz

typical.what: inductor ripple, 12 V to 6 V, 100 kHz, 100 µH
input current for 6 V at 1 A, 90% efficient

confusions.title: It does not burn off the difference.
confusions.text: A linear regulator from 12 V to 6 V at 1 A dissipates 6 W. A buck converter at 90% efficiency takes 6.67 W in and loses 0.67 W.

confusions.title: Its input current is less than its output current.
confusions.text: 6 V at 1 A from 12 V at 90% efficiency draws 0.56 A, not 1 A.

confusions.title: The diode carries the current while the switch is off.
confusions.text: The inductor's current can't stop at once; with the switch open it flows up from ground through the diode. Without the diode, the switch node would be driven far below ground, as at a coil switched off without a flyback diode.

confusions.title: V_out = D·V_in assumes the current never reaches zero.
confusions.text: At light load the triangle touches zero, and with a diode as the second switch the current stays at zero for part of each cycle; the output then rises above D·V_in, toward V_in with no load at all, unless the controller lowers D. A synchronous buck in forced-PWM mode lets its inductor current go negative, so it stays continuous and holds near D·V_in.

glossary.definition: A diode across an inductive load such as a relay coil or a motor, reverse biased in normal operation, that gives the coil's current a path when the switch opens. Without it the current would be forced to stop at once, and the kickback L·di/dt could reach hundreds of volts and destroy the switch.

drills.prompt: An NPN low-side switch drives a 12 V relay coil. Where does the flyback diode go?

choices.text: Across the coil, cathode to the 12 V end
Across the coil, anode to the 12 V end
choices.feedback: Then it is forward biased whenever the switch is on and short-circuits the supply through the transistor.
In series it can only block current. The coil's current needs a loop that bypasses the opened switch: a diode across the coil.

drills.prompt: A 100 mH coil carries 50 mA. With no flyback diode, the switch forces the current to zero in 1 µs. About what voltage would the coil produce?

choices.feedback: That would be a fall over 1 ms. Over 1 µs, v = L·di/dt = 0.1 H × 0.05 A / 10⁻⁶ s = 5000 V: the short time is what makes it huge.
0.1 H × 0.05 A = 0.005 Wb is the coil's flux linkage, not a voltage. The voltage is how fast it changes: divide by 1 µs, v = L·di/dt = 5000 V.

drills.prompt: A plain flyback diode makes a relay release a little later. Why?

choices.text: The coil's current circulates through the diode and decays slowly, opposed only by about 0.7 V and the coil's resistance.
The diode stores charge that holds the relay closed.
choices.feedback: A diode stores very little charge. The delay comes from the coil's current circulating through the diode, decaying at a rate set by L and its small loop voltage.

choices.text: It doesn't; the relay releases at the same moment.
choices.feedback: The coil's current, and so its magnetic pull, now dies away over a time of about L/R instead of at once, so the release comes later.

physics: An inductor's current can't change instantly: v = L·di/dt, so forcing it to change fast takes a large voltage. When a transistor turns off a relay coil carrying 100 mA, the coil drives the collector as high as it must to keep that current flowing. Stopping 100 mA in 1 µs through 100 mH would take 100 mH × 100 mA / 1 µs = 10 kV; in practice the voltage climbs until something conducts, usually the transistor in breakdown, which is what destroys it.

A diode across the coil, cathode to the positive supply, is reverse biased while the transistor is on and carries nothing. At turn-off, the coil's current moves into the diode and circulates around the loop of coil and diode. The collector rises only to the supply plus one diode drop: 12.7 V on a 12 V supply.

The circulating current then decays through the coil's own resistance, with a time constant of about L/R: 0.83 ms for 100 mH and 120 Ω. That slow decay delays the relay's release. A Zener in series with the diode lets the voltage rise to about the supply plus V_Z and one diode drop, which ends the current sooner, at the cost of a higher voltage on the transistor.

Any switch that interrupts an inductive load needs such a path: relay coils, solenoids, and motors. In an H-bridge or a buck converter, diodes (or the MOSFETs' body diodes) do the same job, giving the inductor current somewhere to go each time a switch opens.

confusions.title: It is fitted "backward" on purpose.
confusions.text: Cathode to the positive supply, it is reverse biased in normal operation and carries nothing. Fitted the other way, it would short the supply through the transistor as soon as the transistor turned on.

confusions.title: The spike is set by how fast the current stops, not by the supply.
confusions.text: v = L·di/dt has nothing to do with the 12 V: a coil interrupted in a microsecond can produce hundreds or thousands of volts.

confusions.title: It slows the relay's release.
confusions.text: The current decays through the diode with τ ≈ L/R, 0.83 ms for 100 mH and 120 Ω, so the contacts open later. Where release time matters, a Zener in series with the diode shortens the decay.

confusions.title: It works only on a DC-driven coil.
confusions.text: Across a coil driven from AC, the diode would conduct on every half-cycle of one polarity and short the supply.
